anchor_text: In Troy, there lies the scene. From isles of Greece
summary: The Prologue is 'arm'd' (suited in armour), not in the author's or actor's conventional costume. He announces that the play starts in the middle of the ten-year siege — a direct nod to the classical epic principle of beginning in medias res ('in the middle of things'). Shakespeare assumes his audience already knows the story of Helen's abduction and the Greek fleet; see the reference card for the layered sources.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad (Chapman) / Horace
sources.citation: George Chapman, Seauen Bookes of the Iliades (1598), which Englished Books 1-2 and 7-11 of Homer (not Books 1-7); the in medias res principle is named by Horace, Ars Poetica 148-149 ('in medias res...auditorem rapit').

sources.name: Caxton, Recuyell
sources.citation: William Caxton, Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (1474), the first book printed in English, a primary prose source for the Troy plot.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1

Rescued in 2026-06-02 review sweep — Corrected the false Chapman 1598 scope (Books 1-2 and 7-11, not Books 1-7) and pinned the verified Horace Ars Poetica 148-149 locus for in medias res; gloss unchanged.

The in medias res observation is textually sound (TLN 27-28 'Leaps o'er the vaunt and firstlings of those broils, / Beginning in the middle'), and the armed Prologue's combative self-presentation is mainstream critical consensus; the Chapman/Caxton source layering is defensible context.

anchor_text: princes orgulous, their high blood chaf'd
summary: 'Orgulous' is an archaic adjective meaning proud, haughty, or arrogant (from Old French orguilleux). 'Chaf'd' means heated or inflamed. The Prologue is saying that the Greek princes, proud and furious, have launched their ships against Troy.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'orgulous, adj.': 'Proud, haughty; arrogant.' From Old French orguilleus; rare after the 16th century.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'orgulous': 'proud, haughty.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2
OED 'orgulous, adj.' (proud, haughty, from Old French orguilleus) and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon gloss are both correct and well-established.
'Orgulous' meaning proud/haughty from Old French orguilleux is uncontroversial and well-attested; the reading of 'chaf'd' as inflamed or heated is standard and fits the syntax.

anchor_text: ransack Troy, within whose strong immures
summary: 'Immures' (singular 'immure') means walls, from Latin immurare, to wall in. Troy's 'strong immures' are its famous fortification walls — the walls so strong that it took the Greeks ten years and the trick of the wooden horse to breach them.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'immure, n.': 'A wall; a fortification.' From Latin murus.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 8
OED 'immure, n.' as wall/fortification exists and is attested; the Latin root murus is correct, and the noun form is documented in early 1600s usage including Shakespeare.
'Immures' as walls (from Latin murus/immurare) is well-documented and the gloss is accurate; the note about ten years and the wooden horse is background context, not a misreading.

anchor_text: ravish'd Helen, Menelaus' queen, With wanton Paris sleeps
summary: Helen, wife of the Greek king Menelaus, ran off with (or was carried off by) the Trojan prince Paris — the act that launched the ten-year war. 'Ravish'd' here can mean seized or abducted; whether Helen consented was debated in antiquity and in Shakespeare's play itself. 'Wanton' means lascivious or sexually careless. The war's cause is thus reduced to a single bed.
detail: The Prologue's phrasing is pointed: 'ravish'd' implicates force, but Paris and Helen appear at ease in their shared bed. The tension between abduction and consent is the play's foundational irony — thousands die for what may be an adulterous elopement. Homer's Iliad gives no clear verdict on consent; the medieval tradition tended to condemn Helen as the faithless wife.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 3 (Helen on the wall, Paris and Menelaus duel for her); Ovid, Heroides 16-17 (the correspondence of Paris and Helen).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ravish, v.' senses 1 and 2: 'to carry off by force'; also 'to seize and carry away.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 9
Iliad Book 3 (the duel for Helen) and Ovid Heroides 16-17 (the Paris-Helen correspondence) are real texts that directly support the summary and detail claims.

The gloss correctly identifies the ambiguity in 'ravish'd' (seized/abducted versus the ease implied by 'sleeps') and the tension between abduction and consent is a genuine irony foregrounded in the Prologue's own phrasing; mainstream reading.

anchor_text: Priam's six-gated city, Dardan, and Tymbria, Ilias, Chetas, Troien, And Antenorides
summary: The Prologue names Troy's six gates: Dardanian, Timbrian, Helias (Ilias), Chetas, Troien, and Antenorides. This topographical precision comes from Caxton's Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, the main Elizabethan prose Troy chronicle. No classical source gives exactly this list; it establishes the play's debt to the medieval Troy tradition rather than to Homer directly.

sources.name: Caxton, Recuyell
sources.citation: William Caxton, Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (1474): the names of Troy's gates appear in the medieval Troy narratives (Lydgate, Caxton) that derive ultimately from Guido delle Colonne's Historia destructionis Troiae (c. 1287).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 15
The attribution of Troy's gate-names to Caxton's Recuyell via the Guido delle Colonne/Lydgate medieval tradition is accurate and represents standard source-study consensus for this passage.

The attribution of the six gate-names to Caxton/Guido delle Colonne rather than Homer is accurate and the claim that no classical source gives this exact list is defensible; the annotation correctly identifies the play's debt to the medieval Troy tradition.

anchor_text: Call here my varlet; I'll unarm again. Why should I war without the walls of Troy
summary: 'Varlet' is an archaic term for a personal attendant or servant (the armour-bearer who helps a knight arm and disarm). Troilus is refusing to go to battle: he is having his armour removed before he has even left the palace, because his desire for Cressida has overtaken his will to fight. He will 'war' (fight) inside himself instead of on the battlefield.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'varlet, n.' sense 1: 'A personal attendant or manservant; a servant-boy, page'; by the 16th century often contemptuous for a rascal, but here used neutrally.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 32
OED 'varlet, n.' sense 1 as personal attendant or servant is correct, and the note that the word later became contemptuous while used neutrally here is accurate.

'Varlet' as armour-bearer/personal attendant is correct for this context, and the interpretation that Troilus is unarmour-ing before going to battle because love has overcome his will to fight is exactly what the text says (TLN 32-36).

anchor_text: Will this gear ne'er be mended?
summary: 'Gear' here means business, affair, or matter (a very common Elizabethan usage). Pandarus's exasperated question — 'will this business never be put right?' — is his response to Troilus's lovesick moping. Pandarus is playing the reluctant go-between while Troilus refuses to be satisfied with the progress of the courtship.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'gear, n.' sense 7: 'Business, affair, matter' (colloquial, 16th-17th century).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 37
OED 'gear, n.' sense 7 ('business, affair, matter', colloquial 16th-17th century) correctly supports the gloss.
'Gear' meaning business/affair/matter is a standard Elizabethan usage and the reading of Pandarus's line as exasperated commentary on Troilus's lovesick moping is clearly supported by context.

anchor_text: a cake out of the wheat must tarry the grinding
summary: Pandarus uses an extended simile of bread-making — grinding, bolting (sifting flour), leavening (adding yeast), kneading, heating the oven, baking, and cooling — to tell Troilus that love, like baking, cannot be hurried at any single stage. Each time Troilus says he has 'tarried' (waited), Pandarus names the next step still ahead. The speech is a small comic set-piece in the tradition of the patient-counsellor.
detail: 'Bolting' means sifting flour through a cloth ('bolter') to remove the bran — a step between grinding the grain and making the dough. 'Leavening' is the rising of the dough before baking. Pandarus's laborious list of seven stages mocks Troilus's impatience by reducing erotic longing to kitchen work — and anticipates his role as a domestic go-between who pedantically manages the lovers' progress to bed.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bolting, n.' sense 1: 'The action of sifting meal or flour.' OED s.v. 'leavening, n.': 'The action of causing fermentation in dough.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 45
OED 'bolting, n.' (sifting flour through a bolter) and 'leavening, n.' (causing fermentation in dough) are correctly cited and support the gloss.

The extended bread-making simile (TLN 44-55) is accurately described and each stage (grinding, bolting, leavening, kneading, baking, cooling) corresponds to the actual text; the characterization of it as a comic set-piece mocking Troilus's impatience is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: Patience herself, what goddess e'er she be, Doth lesser blench at suff'rance than I do
summary: Troilus personifies Patience as a goddess ('Patience herself') to show how far beyond ordinary human endurance his pain is: even the divine embodiment of patient suffering, he claims, would flinch ('blench') less at pain than he does. 'Suff'rance' means suffering or endurance. The hyperbole signals the grandiose, self-dramatizing love-language the play is simultaneously staging and gently mocking.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'blench, v.' sense 1: 'To shrink back, flinch, quail.' OED s.v. 'sufferance, n.' sense 1: 'endurance of pain or hardship.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 56
OED 'blench, v.' sense 1 (to flinch) and 'sufferance, n.' sense 1 (endurance of pain or hardship) are correctly cited and directly support the gloss.

Personifying Patience as a goddess and the claim that Troilus says even she would flinch less than he does is an accurate reading of TLN 56-57; the identification of self-dramatizing hyperbole as simultaneously staged and mocked is a mainstream interpretation of the play's mode.

anchor_text: cygnet's down is harsh, and spirit of sense Hard as the palm of ploughman
summary: Troilus piles up comparisons to Cressida's hand: compared to it, even a baby swan's ('cygnet's') downy feathers feel rough, and the most delicate sense perception ('spirit of sense') feels as hard and callused as a farm-worker's hand. This is a rhetorical device called a blazon — a catalogue of a beloved's physical perfections, each likened to something superlatively fine. The speech strains so hard for superlatives that it becomes almost absurd.
detail: The blazon was a standard Petrarchan and Renaissance lyric convention: to praise a woman by listing her parts (eyes, hair, hand) and measuring each against some ideal. Shakespeare's Troilus delivers the convention at length and in earnest, but Pandarus's breezy response — 'I speak no more than truth' / 'Thou dost not speak so much' — deflates it comically. The hyperbole is part of the play's anatomy of idealised love: the higher Troilus builds Cressida on words, the worse the eventual fall.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cygnet, n.': 'A young swan.' OED s.v. 'spirit, n.' sense 18: 'spirit of sense' — the most refined perceptual faculty, drawn from Galenic physiology's 'animal spirits.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 85
OED 'cygnet, n.' (young swan) is correct; the Galenic 'animal spirits' reading for 'spirit of sense' is a defensible and standard editorial gloss for this passage.

The blazon identification is accurate, the cygnet/ploughman's-palm comparisons are correctly described from TLN 83-86, and the observation that Pandarus's deflating responses undercut the hyperbole is textually grounded; 'spirit of sense' as refined perceptual faculty from Galenic physiology is mainstream.

anchor_text: I have had my labour for my travail, ill thought on of her and ill thought on of you; gone between and between
summary: 'Labour' and 'travail' were near-synonyms (both meaning toil or effort), but the pairing is a pun: 'travail' also carries the French sense of travel (going back and forth as a messenger). Pandarus has literally been 'going between' the two — a 'go-between' — and the word 'between' puns on the pimp's role of being in between lovers. The scene establishes Pandarus as the agent of their affair, whose name will give English the word 'pander.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'travail, n.' sense 1: 'Painful or laborious effort' and sense 2 (archaic): 'a journey, travel.' OED s.v. 'pander, n.': 'A go-between in an illicit amour; a pimp. [f. Pandarus of Troilus and Cressida].' First cited in Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385).

sources.name: Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde
sources.citation: Geoffrey Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385): Pandarus is Criseyde's uncle and the lovers' go-between, the source of the English word 'pander.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 97

The OED citation claims 'pander' is 'First cited in Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385),' but available evidence indicates OED's earliest attestation for the generalized noun 'pander' is c. 1450, postdating Chaucer's poem — the word derives from Chaucer's character name but is not itself first recorded in his text.

The labour/travail near-synonym pairing and the pun on 'travail' as travel (going between) is well-attested and the 'go-between' / 'between' wordplay is textually present (TLN 97-99); the etymology of 'pander' from Pandarus via Chaucer is accurate.

anchor_text: Tell me, Apollo, for thy Daphne's love, What Cressid is, what Pandar, and what we?
summary: Troilus invokes Apollo, the sun-god who was hopelessly in love with the nymph Daphne: she fled him and prayed to be transformed into a laurel tree at the very moment of his grasp. The allusion sets Troilus's situation — desperate, close but unable to reach his beloved — against Apollo's eternally frustrated love. The question 'what Cressid is, what Pandar, and what we?' is Troilus asking the god to name the roles in their strange, pander-brokered courtship.
detail: In Ovid's Metamorphoses 1.452-567, Cupid shot Apollo with a golden arrow of love and Daphne with a leaden arrow of aversion; Apollo pursued and Daphne escaped by metamorphosis. The parallel: Troilus pursues but cannot reach Cressida, and needs Pandarus to broker access. By praying to Apollo 'for thy Daphne's love' — by the god's own history of blocked desire — Troilus is inviting a god who failed as a lover to explain why he, Troilus, is also failing.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.452-567 (Apollo and Daphne; Golding's English translation, 1567).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 124
Ovid Metamorphoses 1.452-567 (Apollo and Daphne, including Cupid's gold and lead arrows) is confirmed correct; Arthur Golding's English translation of 1567 is the standard date.

The Ovid Metamorphoses 1 allusion (Apollo and Daphne) is correctly identified and the parallel — Troilus pursues but cannot reach Cressida, needing a go-between — is a defensible and mainstream reading of Troilus's prayer at TLN 124-125.

anchor_text: Her bed is India; there she lies, a pearl; Between our Ilium and where she resides Let it be call'd the wild and wandering flood; Ourself the merchant, and this sailing Pandar Our doubtful hope, our convoy, and our bark
summary: Troilus builds an elaborate metaphor (a conceit) in which Cressida is a pearl in distant India — the world's byword for fabulous, unreachable wealth — and Pandarus is the merchant-ship that might bring her to him across a dangerous sea. 'Ilium' is another name for Troy. 'Our bark' means our sailing vessel; 'convoy' means escort or transport. The imagery links the lovers' courtship to risky long-distance trade, with Pandarus as the doubtful instrument of profit.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bark, n.2': 'A small sailing vessel.' The India-pearl image for unattainable feminine beauty is a Renaissance lyric commonplace; cf. Shakespeare's Othello 5.2 ('pearl richer than all his tribe').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 126
OED 'bark, n.2' as small sailing vessel is correct; the Othello 5.2 pearl parallel is a real and apt cross-reference.

The mercantile conceit (Cressida as pearl in India, Pandarus as the merchant-ship) is accurately described from TLN 126-130, and the India-pearl image for unattainable feminine beauty as a Renaissance lyric commonplace is defensible; the cross-reference to Othello 5.2 is apt.

anchor_text: Let Paris bleed: 'tis but a scar to scorn; Paris is gor'd with Menelaus' horn
summary: The 'horn' is a sexual pun: a cuckold (a man whose wife has been unfaithful) was said in Elizabethan slang to wear invisible horns. Menelaus has been cuckolded by Paris — Paris stole his wife Helen — so Menelaus's 'horn' is the cuckold's horn that has now, in battle, 'gored' Paris back. The play launches its persistent mockery of Menelaus as the play's most visibly wronged and least dignified man.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'horn, n.' sense 7: 'The horn (or horns) imagined as growing on the forehead of a cuckold.' The cuckold's horn is documented from at least the 13th century; cf. also 'the-cuckolds-horns' reference card (Much Ado).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 138
OED 'horn, n.' sense 7 (the cuckold's horn, documented from at least the 13th century) correctly supports the bawdy reading.

The cuckold's horn pun is unambiguous in context (Paris has cuckolded Menelaus by sleeping with Helen, and Menelaus has now literally wounded Paris in battle), and the play's persistent mockery of Menelaus as the most wronged yet least dignified figure is a mainstream critical observation.

anchor_text: Whose height commands as subject all the vale
summary: 'Commands as subject' here means 'dominates as its overlord' — the tower is so high that the whole valley below it lies subject to its view, as a vassal lies subject to a lord. 'Vale' is a valley.
detail: The political metaphor (height = sovereignty, the lowlands = subject peoples) was a Renaissance commonplace for any elevated vantage point. It also quietly frames the scene: Cressida and Alexander will shortly observe the warriors from this tower, positioned as spectators rather than actors in the war's theatre.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'subject, adj.' sense 4a: 'Under the dominion or rule of a sovereign'; s.v. 'vale, n.1' sense 1a.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 149
OED s.v. 'subject, adj.' sense 4a and 'vale, n.1' sense 1a are real entries supporting the archaic meanings glossed.

The sovereignty/vassal political metaphor for an elevated viewpoint is a Renaissance commonplace and the reading of 'commands as subject' as 'dominates as overlord' is standard; the brief interpretive extension about Cressida as spectator rather than actor stays well within the scene's framing.

anchor_text: Hector, whose patience Is as a virtue fix'd
summary: 'Patience' here means steadiness of temper under provocation — a settled, almost permanent quality (hence 'fix'd') rather than passive endurance. Alexander is saying Hector is famously unflappable, which makes today's anger extraordinary.
detail: The phrase echoes Stoic descriptions of virtue as a stable disposition of the soul ('recta ratio,' a right reason fixed in the character); in Renaissance moral philosophy 'patience' was both a cardinal virtue and a warrior's prerequisite. The contrast with 'mov'd' (line 151) is deliberate: what shifts an immovable man shifts the world.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'patience, n.' sense 1a: 'The suffering or enduring of pain or trouble with calmness; the quality of being patient.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 150
OED s.v. 'patience, n.' sense 1a is a real entry; the Stoic context in the detail is conventional scholarship that does not overreach the OED citation.
Reading 'patience' as settled Stoic steadiness (fixed disposition) rather than passive endurance is defensible and mainstream, and the contrast with 'mov'd' is explicitly cued in the text at TLN 151.

anchor_text: a very man per se, And stands alone
summary: 'A man per se' — Latin for 'in and of himself' — means an individual so exceptional that he is a category of one, a man without parallel or comparison. Alexander is praising Ajax as absolutely singular. Cressida immediately punctures this: any man stands alone if he is not drunk, sick, or legless.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'per se': 'by himself, alone, without equal' (Latin, 'in and of itself').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 163
Rescued in 2026-06-02 review sweep — Dropped the fabricated 'also in Love's Labour's Lost 5.1' cross-reference (the phrase does not occur in LLL); kept the verified Schmidt gloss.
The scholastic/philosophical sense of 'per se' as 'a category of one' is correct, and Cressida's deadpan literal reinterpretation of 'stands alone' is exactly what the exchange shows; no overreach.

anchor_text: hath robb'd many beasts of their particular additions
summary: 'Additions' means distinguishing qualities or attributes — titles, badges of excellence — taken from specific animals. Ajax has stolen the lion's courage, the bear's churlishness, the elephant's slowness, having crammed all of them into one body. The idea is that he is a catalogue of virtues and faults without any balance or coherence.
detail: The portrait of Ajax as a grotesque anthology of animal qualities belongs to the play's wider satiric habit of reducing human excellence to a bestiary. 'Addition' in Shakespeare frequently means a title or attribute appended to a name (as 'Most Royal Majesty' is an addition to a king's name); here those badges of excellence have been filched from beasts.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'addition': 'attribute, title, quality appended.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 166
Onions s.v. 'addition' is a real entry supporting 'attribute, title, quality appended'; the card reference to 'the-greek-and-trojan-heroes' is non-source material not judged here.

The sense of 'additions' as distinguishing attributes or badges (cf. Othello, Hamlet) is well-attested in Shakespeare and fits the context of animal-qualities being 'robbed' from specific beasts; the bestialized portrait reading is mainstream.

anchor_text: any man an attaint but he carries some stain of it
summary: 'Attaint' means a fault, a stain of dishonour, or a moral blemish. Alexander is saying Ajax carries some taint of every vice there is — he is a complete sample of human weakness as well as human virtue. The word comes from legal usage (attainder, the corruption of blood) and carries a sense of inherited disgrace.
detail: In law, 'attainder' was the consequence of being found guilty of felony or treason: it 'corrupted the blood' and stripped the convicted person of civil rights. Shakespeare uses 'attaint' in a looser, moral sense meaning any blemish of character. The dovetailing of 'virtue... a glimpse' and 'attaint... some stain' makes Ajax a kind of walking moral average: no quality in full, no vice to the bottom.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'attaint, n.' sense 3: 'A stain upon one's honour or reputation; disgrace.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 171
OED s.v. 'attaint, n.' sense 3 is a real entry confirming 'stain upon honour'; the legal background in the detail is accurate and does not overreach the source.

The legal-to-moral extension of 'attaint' as moral stain or blemish is the standard Shakespearean usage; the gloss is accurate, and the reading of the paired 'virtue... glimpse / attaint... stain' chiasm is defensible.

anchor_text: merry against the hair
summary: 'Against the hair' means against the grain — contrary to one's natural inclination or disposition. Ajax is merry when he has no reason to be and melancholy without cause: his moods are permanently out of step with circumstances.
detail: The idiom compares the direction of a disposition to the lie of an animal's coat: stroking against the hair rubs against the natural direction, causes resistance and discomfort. The phrase was current in Shakespeare's day (cf. Twelfth Night 5.1); here it completes the portrait of Ajax as a man chronically at odds with himself as much as with others.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'hair': 'against the hair, against the grain, contrary to nature or inclination.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 172
Onions s.v. 'hair' documenting 'against the hair = against the grain' is a real entry; the Twelfth Night cross-reference in the detail is a real parallel use.

'Against the hair' as 'against the grain / contrary to natural inclination' is a well-documented idiom and the reading that Ajax's moods are permanently out of step with circumstances follows directly from the text.

anchor_text: a gouty Briareus, many hands and no use, or purblind Argus, all eyes and no sight
summary: Briareus was a hundred-handed giant of Greek myth; Argus was the hundred-eyed giant set to watch the cow-goddess Io. Alexander is mocking Ajax: he has Briareus's many hands but is gouty (too stiff and pained to use them), and Argus's many eyes but is purblind (nearly blind). Maximum equipment, zero effectiveness.
detail: Briareus (also called Aegaeon) is named in the Iliad (1.402-404) as the giant the gods summoned to defend Zeus; Hesiod's Theogony (617-735) describes him and his brothers Cottus and Gyges as the Hecatoncheires ('hundred-handed ones'). Argus Panoptes ('all-seeing') is named by Ovid (Metamorphoses 1.625-750) as the hundred-eyed guardian Hera set to watch Io, eventually killed by Hermes; the name 'Argus' was a byword for vigilance, while 'purblind' means nearly or partially blind. Both allusions appear here in grotesquely inverted form: excess without function, which is the satiric portrait of Ajax the play builds throughout.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 1.402-404 (Briareus called to help Zeus); Hesiod, Theogony 617-735 (the Hecatoncheires).

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.625-750 (Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed watcher of Io, killed by Hermes).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 174

Homer Iliad 1.402-404 (Briareus passage confirmed at lines 401-403 by Perseus) and Hesiod Theogony 617-735 (Hecatoncheires) are real passages; Ovid Metamorphoses 1.625-750 is slightly stretched (Argus episode runs 622-688) but the source is real and the core claims are correct, though calling the killer 'Hermes' conflates Greek and Roman names for the Ovidian killer Mercury.

Briareus (Hecatoncheires) and Argus Panoptes are correctly identified; the inverted form — maximum equipment, zero effectiveness — is the obvious satiric point Shakespeare is making, and the sources cited are appropriate.

anchor_text: O Jupiter! there's no comparison
summary: Cressida swears by Jupiter — the king of the Roman gods, and the strongest oath available in this classical Trojan setting — to emphasize how obviously superior Troilus is to Hector. The exclamation works like a modern 'Good God!' and signals exasperated sarcasm, since she is mocking Pandarus's obvious partiality.
detail: Characters in Shakespeare's Troy plays swear by classical gods (Jupiter, Juno, Apollo) as appropriate to the setting; audiences recognized these as the equivalent of Christian oaths. The use of 'Jupiter' as an expletive is consistent with the play's world: it is Troilus's own oath of astonishment in other scenes. Here Cressida deploys it with theatrical irony — she does not actually believe Troilus superior to Hector and is playing with Pandarus.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'Jupiter': used as an exclamation or oath throughout the Roman and Trojan plays.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 203
Schmidt s.v. 'Jupiter' as exclamation or oath in the Roman and Trojan plays is a real lexicographic observation; the claim is modest and supported.

The exclamation 'O Jupiter!' as a classical-setting oath equivalent to 'Good God!' is correct and uncontroversial; reading Cressida's line as exasperated sarcasm (she does not actually believe Troilus superior to Hector) is strongly supported by her conduct throughout the scene.

anchor_text: Condition I had gone barefoot to India
summary: 'Condition' here means 'even on condition that' or 'even if.' Pandarus is saying he would have wagered his willingness to walk barefoot to India (an extreme, absurd hardship) on the proposition that Troilus IS himself — meaning fully his own glorious self. It is comic hyperbole to stress how exceptional Troilus is.
detail: India was the far edge of the known world for Elizabethans, synonymous with boundless distance and hardship. Barefoot pilgrimage was a medieval Catholic penance requiring extreme sacrifice. Pandarus combines both for maximum comic exaggeration. The phrase has no conditional logic that resolves clearly — it is broken-backed hyperbole, which Cressida dryly ignores with 'He is not Hector.'

sources.name: Onions

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 213

The conjunctive sense of 'Condition' ('even on condition that') is standard Early Modern usage, and reading the phrase as broken-backed hyperbole that Cressida coolly ignores is accurate to the scene's comic rhythm.

anchor_text: for a brown favour, for so 'tis, I must confess
summary: 'Favour' means face or complexion. Pandarus is saying Troilus has a brownish, sun-darkened face — the natural result of a soldier's outdoor life — but even so, Helen praised his looks above Paris's. 'Brown' in this period was not entirely negative, but a fair (light) complexion was the Elizabethan beauty ideal, so it is a mild concession.
detail: Elizabethan beauty ideals for men and women both prized paleness over darkness; a 'brown' face suggested outdoor labour, military exposure to the sun, or simply an unfashionable skin tone. The passage that follows — Pandarus and Cressida sparring over 'brown and not brown,' 'true and not true' — is a comedy of polite evasion in which each tries to avoid committing to a clear statement.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 231

'Favour' as face or complexion is standard, and the identification of a light/fair complexion as the Elizabethan beauty ideal making 'brown' a mild concession is correct; the comedy of mutual hedging in the exchange is exactly what the text plays.

anchor_text: Helen's golden tongue had commended Troilus for a copper nose
summary: A 'copper nose' was in this period specifically associated with the effects of advanced syphilis, which caused facial disfigurement including erosion of the nose. Cressida implies that Helen's praise ('golden tongue') is so worthless it could as easily commend a symptom of venereal disease as a beauty. The insult targets both Helen's judgment and, obliquely, the sexual disorder the war conceals.
detail: Syphilis ('the pox') was epidemic in early modern Europe; advanced cases destroyed cartilage and left a characteristic sunken or reddened nose, recognizable on the street. 'Copper-nose' and 'bottle-nose' were slang for the condition. The joke therefore also plants the play's controlling metaphor: the entire Trojan War, launched by an adultery, is a kind of venereal sore disfiguring everyone involved. Pandarus himself will end the play diseased. The gold/copper contrast also parodies the motif of the three caskets (gold, silver, lead) that is more explicit in The Merchant of Venice.

The association of 'copper nose' with syphilitic disfigurement is well-documented in the period, the gold/copper contrast with Helen's 'golden tongue' is clearly intentional, and the annotation is appropriately placed at scholar depth; the final sentence about the three-caskets motif is a reach but is marked as an aside and does not distort the core reading.

anchor_text: she's a merry Greek indeed
summary: 'A merry Greek' was Elizabethan slang for a dissolute, loose-living person. Cressida applies it pointedly: if Helen loves Troilus while living with Paris, she is not just cheerful but sexually promiscuous — a 'merry Greek' in the bawdy sense, and an ironic one at that, since Helen is Trojan by adoption.
detail: The phrase was common enough to appear in Middleton and other contemporaries. It collapses the play's two worlds — the Greek and Trojan camps — into a single term for moral disorder, while Cressida's wit insists on calling Helen by what she is rather than what Pandarus's fawning rhetoric would make her. The scene consistently uses irony and double entendre to strip away romantic inflation.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'Greek': 'a merry Greek, a boon companion, reveller, loose liver.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 245
Onions s.v. 'Greek' documenting 'a merry Greek = boon companion, reveller, loose liver' is a real entry that directly supports the summary.

'A merry Greek' as slang for a dissolute or loose-living person is attested in Onions and contemporaries, and Cressida's pointed application to Helen (living with Paris while allegedly loving Troilus) is exactly the wit the line performs.

anchor_text: into the compass'd window
summary: A 'compass'd window' is a bay window or bow window — one that projects outward from the wall in a curved or angled (compass = circular, rounded) shape. Helen came into Troilus's room via this fashionable architectural feature. The detail places the scene in a prosperous Trojan interior.
detail: Bay or compass windows were a common feature of Elizabethan town houses and great halls. 'Compass'd' can mean curved, semicircular (from the compass's arc), or simply bowed out. Shakespeare often uses the detail as a mark of domestic intimacy or architectural specificity; here it lends the anecdote a vivid, believable domesticity that heightens the comedy of the chin-inspection that follows.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 247

anchor_text: a tapster's arithmetic may soon bring his particulars therein to a total
summary: A tapster (bartender) was proverbially the lowest form of arithmetic — counting small sums of money on his fingers. Cressida jokes that Troilus's four hairs need nothing beyond a tapster's counting ability to add up. 'Particulars' (individual items) and 'total' (the sum) carry the commercial language of a bartender's bill.
detail: The joke mocks Troilus's youth and sparse beard — signs that he is not yet fully grown — by framing his face as an accounts ledger with very few entries. The commercial register also has a faint edge: Cressida's wit tends to place courtly and romantic objects in a marketplace of plain evaluation, preparing her closing soliloquy in which she reasons about the economics of desire.

The tapster-as-low-reckoner joke is well-founded — tapsters counted small sums, and the commercial vocabulary of 'particulars' and 'total' is clearly in play; the light extension about Cressida's marketplace wit is consistent with the scene and does not overread.

anchor_text: Without the rack
summary: Pandarus says Helen has a 'marvell's white hand'; Cressida replies 'Without the rack' — meaning no one had to torture the admission out of Helen. The rack was a device of torture that stretched the body. The joke is: yes, she confesses it freely, no stretching required. The wit also implies this 'confession' cost little, since it is not exactly controversial.
detail: Judicial torture by rack was a real (if theoretically illegal) practice in Elizabethan England, used in treason cases. The pun on 'confess without the rack' (confess without being forced) was a recognizable comic formula. Cressida deploys it here to deflate Pandarus's reverence for Helen: the concession that Helen has a white hand is so trivial it requires no compulsion.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 272

The rack-as-torture-device and 'confess without the rack' as a comic formula for a freely-given admission is correct and well-suited to the context; Cressida is deflating Pandarus's reverence for Helen, exactly as glossed.

anchor_text: 'The forked one,' quoth he, 'pluck't out and give it him.'
summary: Troilus identifies Paris's hair among his own beard-hairs as the 'forked one' — a forked hair being a phallic shape, but also carrying the sense of 'forked' as the mark of a cuckold's horns (a man whose wife has cheated on him). Helen is Paris's woman; Troilus's joke implies Paris is a cuckold, since Helen loves Troilus. The court laughs; Paris 'chaf'd' (raged).
detail: The cuckold's horns were the standard Elizabethan emblem of a deceived husband — imagined as two horns sprouting from the forehead, hence 'forked.' A forked hair from Troilus's beard therefore neatly encodes the double insult: Paris wears the cuckold's emblem within Troilus's own chin-hairs. The anecdote is also structurally important: it shows Helen and Troilus in easy, flirtatious intimacy inside the court at Troy, the very situation the war's defenders claim to be protecting.

The cuckold's-horns reading of 'forked' is unimpeachable — it is the standard Elizabethan emblem — and the text provides direct confirmation: Paris 'chaf'd' (raged), which only makes sense if the insult lands as a cuckolding joke.

anchor_text: he will weep you, and 'twere a man born in April
summary: April was proverbially the month of rain and showers (spring weeping), so 'a man born in April' would weep readily and at length. Pandarus is saying Troilus is so deeply in love with Cressida that he weeps over her as naturally and abundantly as April showers. The 'you' is not a direct object but an ethical dative — 'he will weep, I tell you.'
detail: The ethical dative ('weep you') is a common Early Modern English construction: 'you' or 'me' inserted into a clause not as its grammatical object but as a loose gesture toward the listener, roughly equivalent to 'he will weep, I promise you' or 'he'll go and weep.' The April rain comparison is a conventional image of plentiful, involuntary weeping; Cressida's riposte ('I'll spring up in his tears, an 'twere a nettle against May') turns the weather metaphor into a weed-garden joke, implying her own thorny, prickly resistance.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 302

The ethical dative reading of 'weep you' is correct, the April-showers proverbial comparison is standard, and Cressida's nettle-against-May riposte is well-glossed as a weed-garden joke about her prickly resistance; no overreach.

anchor_text: He's one of the flowers of Troy
summary: 'Flowers' means the best, the finest examples — the choicest individuals of a group. Pandarus praises Aeneas as one of Troy's most distinguished warriors. The phrase was a conventional aristocratic compliment.
detail: The 'flowers of chivalry' or 'flowers of a city' was a standard phrase of aristocratic praise in medieval and Renaissance usage, treating excellence as the highest bloom of a collection. Pandarus applies it to Aeneas as the warriors file past — part of his running commentary that will climax with his lavish description of Troilus. Aeneas appears only briefly; he has a larger dramatic role elsewhere in the play as Troy's emissary.

'Flowers' as 'finest examples, pick of the group' is the standard sense and the aristocratic compliment reading is uncontroversial.

anchor_text: he has a shrewd wit
summary: 'Shrewd' here does not mean dishonest; it means sharp, piercing, or penetrating — a keen intelligence. Pandarus is praising Antenor's cleverness. Later in the play Antenor's value as an intelligence asset is exactly why the Trojans trade Cressida for him — making this offhand compliment retrospectively ominous.
detail: In Early Modern English 'shrewd' usually meant keen, sharp, or cutting (as a 'shrewd wind' cuts) rather than deceitful. 'A shrewd wit' was a positive quality: quick, incisive intelligence. The same word is applied to women ('a shrew' = a sharp-tongued woman), but here is straightforwardly complimentary. The irony for an audience that knows the story: Antenor's 'soundness of judgment' (line 320) includes, in the chronicle tradition, an eventual role as a traitor who helps the Greeks take Troy.

anchor_text: If he do, the rich shall have more
summary: Pandarus says Troilus will 'nod' to him if he sees him; Cressida replies 'If he do, the rich shall have more' — punning on 'nod' as a rhythmic head movement that can mean either greeting or sleepiness. 'The rich shall have more' is a sardonic proverbial observation (the wealthy always accumulate more wealth), here applied to the meaningless increment of one more nod.
detail: The proverb 'to them that have, more shall be given' echoes Matthew 25:29 (the parable of the talents), but Cressida deflates it into a world-weary shrug: Pandarus already has Troilus's nod, and getting another one is merely the rich getting richer. The wordplay also mocks Pandarus's self-importance — he expects a public acknowledgment from a prince as proof of his significance.

The proverbial Matthew 25:29 echo is a plausible background, but the gloss primarily argues Cressida is punning on 'nod' as greeting versus sleepiness, which is not clearly present in the text — the more direct reading is simply that 'the rich shall have more' deflates the significance of one nod via the proverb about accumulation alone; the sleepiness pun is not established.

anchor_text: chaff and bran, chaff and bran! porridge after meat! I could live and die in the eyes of Troilus. Ne'er look, ne'er look; the eagles are gone. Crows and daws
summary: Pandarus distinguishes the common soldiers (chaff, bran, porridge, crows, daws) from the noble warriors (the wheat, the eagle, the meat itself). 'Chaff' is the husks left after threshing grain; 'bran' is the rough outer husk of wheat; 'porridge' is a humble filler after the main course; 'daws' are jackdaws — noisy, common birds. All are images of what is cheap, coarse, and left over.
detail: 'Crows and daws' versus 'eagles' is the standard Elizabethan image of common versus noble: the eagle was the king of birds and an emblem of heroic greatness, while jackdaws were proverbially empty chatterers who stole bright things. 'Porridge after meat' (filling food eaten after the real substance is gone) is Pandarus's way of saying the common soldiers are an afterthought, a mopup after the feast of heroes. The passage captures his absolute and comic idolatry of Troilus.

Chaff, bran, porridge, crows, and daws as images of the common and worthless versus eagles and meat as images of the noble are all correctly glossed; Pandarus's comic idolatry of Troilus is accurately described.

anchor_text: birth, beauty, good shape, discourse, manhood, learning, gentleness, virtue, youth, liberality, and such like, the spice and salt that season a man
summary: Pandarus lists the Renaissance ideal of the complete courtier — noble birth, physical beauty, good bearing, eloquence ('discourse'), martial courage, scholarship, courtesy, virtue, youth, and generosity — arguing these qualities 'season' (give flavour to) a man as spices and salt season food. He claims Troilus possesses them all.
detail: This catalogue echoes Castiglione's The Book of the Courtier (Hoby's English translation, 1561), which systematised exactly these qualities as the marks of a perfect gentleman and courtier. Shakespeare's audience would recognise the list as a genre-piece — the encomium or blazon of male virtue. The irony is that Cressida's response refuses the whole framing: she turns the heroic spice-list into a recipe for a 'minc'd man baked in a pie' (minced, cut small, cooked through). The play's satiric project is to show this gallery of heroes as equally diminished.

The parallel to the Castiglionean courtier-ideal is well-established and the list in the text closely matches the categories Castiglione enumerates; noting that Cressida's mince-pie riposte deflates the whole frame is accurate to the scene.

anchor_text: a minc'd man; and then to be bak'd with no date in the pie, for then the man's date is out
summary: Pandarus says Troilus has all the qualities of a perfect man — 'spice and salt.' Cressida takes the culinary metaphor literally: fine, then he is a 'minc'd man' (the spiced, minced-meat filling of a mince pie), baked without a 'date' (a date fruit used in medieval spiced pies). But 'date' also means a span of time: a man without a date has 'his date out' — his time is up, he is past his best, out of date. The joke mocks romantic inflation with market logic.
detail: Minced pies (or 'mince pies') were sweetened with spices, dried fruits, and dates, a popular Elizabethan dish. The triple pun on 'date' (the fruit / a calendar date / the duration of a man's prime) is characteristic of Cressida's wit, which consistently translates courtly idealism into marketplace accounting. This is a key moment: she is not impressed by Pandarus's catalogue, and she shows it through wordplay rather than open argument.

anchor_text: A man knows not at what ward you lie
summary: A 'ward' is a defensive position or guard stance in fencing — the posture a swordsman takes to block an attack. Pandarus says he cannot tell what Cressida's guard is, meaning she is impossible to catch off balance or out-argue. It is an admission of defeat by a man who cannot keep up with her wit.
detail: Fencing vocabulary was widely used metaphorically in Elizabethan English; to 'lie at a ward' meant to hold a defensive position (the stance held between attacks). Pandarus's concession that he cannot find Cressida's ward sets up the extended martial-fencing metaphor she then develops through 'wards' and 'watches,' turning her whole strategy of emotional self-defence into a mock-tactical position. The fencing register points toward the play's underlying theme that love is war by another name.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 378

The fencing-vocabulary reading of 'ward' as a defensive posture is standard, and the subsequent development of wards and watches in Cressida's speech confirms the extended fencing metaphor; the thematic extension to 'love is war' is defensible as a characterisation of the play's overall conceit.

anchor_text: Upon my back, to defend my belly; upon my wit, to defend my wiles; upon my secrecy, to defend mine honesty
summary: Cressida lists her 'wards' — defensive positions. 'Upon my back to defend my belly' is simultaneously a fencing stance (lying back to shield the torso) and a bawdy double entendre: lying on her back (in the sexual position) to guard her belly (her chastity, or the womb). The whole speech plays between genuine self-analysis and sexual wordplay.
detail: The speech is Cressida's most candid moment before her closing soliloquy. Read literally, it is a remarkably modern articulation of how a woman must manage every aspect of her presentation — wit, secrecy, physical appearance, social dependency — to maintain 'honesty' (chastity/reputation) in a world where men control the field. Read bawdily, 'upon my back to defend my belly' stages the fundamental paradox: the defensive posture for sex is also the vulnerable one. That Cressida sees this double-bind with clear eyes is the play's most sympathetic presentation of her. 'Honesty' in Shakespeare = chastity, truthfulness, and reputation together.

anchor_text: unless it swell past hiding, and then it's past watching
summary: Cressida's fencing-metaphor speech ends here with a pregnancy joke: if the 'blow' (the sexual strike) makes her belly 'swell past hiding' — makes her visibly pregnant — then no guard or watch can conceal it. The pun closes the extended mock-tactical speech with its most explicit double meaning.
detail: The sequence 'ward... watch... swell past hiding' threads a consistent bawdy subtext through apparently abstract tactical language. A woman made pregnant by a blow she could not ward off is past all defending — her body announces the breach. This is the play's darkest articulation of Cressida's situation before her soliloquy: she is aware that love and its consequences, once visible, become public property, removing her last defensive position. The play will literalise this when she is handed over to the Greeks.

anchor_text: By the same token, you are a bawd
summary: Pandarus says he will bring Cressida a 'token' (a love-gift or message) from Troilus. Cressida turns 'by the same token' (meaning 'and moreover' — a linking phrase) back into a literal meaning: by the same act that makes him a token-carrier, you are a bawd (a procurer of illicit sex). It is the scene's clearest statement of what Pandarus is doing.
detail: A 'token' in the period was both a small gift (a glove, a ring) exchanged between lovers as a pledge of love, and a linking phrase ('by the same token, meaning likewise'). Cressida exploits the ambiguity: Pandarus's literal act of token-bearing marks him as what he is. The moment is tonally ambiguous — playful banter, or a hard accusation? — but it squarely names what the play does more explicitly in the Epilogue, when Pandarus bequeaths his 'diseases' and calls himself the broker of the affair.

anchor_text: Words, vows, gifts, tears, and love's full sacrifice, He offers in another's enterprise
summary: Cressida's closing soliloquy reveals she genuinely loves Troilus but has calculated that women who yield immediately lose value ('Things won are done; joy's soul lies in the doing'). She will 'hold off' to sustain desire. The soliloquy shows her as strategically self-aware, not simply passive — but also trapped in a logic where her own feelings must be hidden to have any power.
detail: The soliloquy is the scene's most important passage for understanding the play's treatment of Cressida. She articulates a painful double bind: a woman who shows love is immediately devalued ('Achievement is command; ungain'd, beseech'), so she must conceal the very feeling that drives her. Modern readers often read this as an indictment of the social structures that force such concealment, not of Cressida's character. The observation that 'Men prize the thing ungain'd more than it is' is not cynicism but accurate social analysis. anchor_text: The heavens themselves, the planets, and this centre
summary: This is Ulysses's famous 'degree' speech: he argues that the entire universe operates on a principle of fixed hierarchy — the sun presides over the planets, which follow ranked orbits — and that any disruption of this cosmic order produces catastrophe on earth. The speech expresses a widespread Elizabethan idea that social hierarchy mirrors and is guaranteed by the structure of the cosmos.

The official Homily Against Disobedience, read in every parish church, taught that rebellion against authority was as disordered as the planets running amok. Ulysses is the play's most eloquent voice for this ideal of degree, yet his elaborate scheme to manipulate Ajax and humble Achilles shows the gap between the doctrine he preaches and the cynical maneuvering he practices. The speech is simultaneously the play's most lofty political statement and one of its central ironies.

Ulysses's astrology is orthodox early modern astronomy, not mere metaphor.

anchor_text: he is Ajax
summary: Thersites's 'he is Ajax' is a pun on 'a jakes' — Elizabethan slang for a privy or toilet. anchor_text: you as under an impress
summary: An 'impress' (or impressment) was compulsory military service — being forcibly pressed into service against your will, as opposed to serving voluntarily. Achilles is mocking Thersites by applying Elizabethan military law to the Trojan War: Thersites claimed he serves voluntarily, but Achilles says the beatings he just received make him a conscript, not a volunteer. Impressment — especially of sailors — was a live grievance in Elizabethan England.

Achilles's joke maps modern English legal categories ('voluntary service' versus 'under an impress') onto the heroic world of Troy, which is characteristic of the play's anachronistic, debunking technique: the great epic war treated as if it were a contemporary labour dispute.

anchor_text: Ulysses and old Nestor--whose wit was mouldy ere your grandsires had nails on their toes--yoke you like draught oxen, and make you plough up the wars
summary: Thersites, briefly at his sharpest, accuses Ulysses and old Nestor of using Achilles and Ajax as dumb work-animals. 'Draught oxen' are plough-oxen, controlled by a yoke — powerful beasts that do all the hard labour while their drivers get the benefit. The image exposes the play's real power structure: the clever men (Ulysses, Nestor) manipulate the mighty men (Achilles, Ajax) for their own ends. This is also a compression of a major theme of the play.

Thersites punctures the scheme in two lines: the 'wisdom' of the counsellors is mere craft, yoking powerful fools to fight their battles for them. The joke about Nestor's wit being 'mouldy' (stale, covered in age's mould) before even Achilles's grandfather was born captures Nestor's characterisation as a windy elder.

anchor_text: Achilles' brach bids me

The nature of the Achilles-Patroclus relationship was debated since antiquity — Plato's Symposium argues over it, and Homer himself leaves it ambiguous. This is Thersites's nastiest voice, reported here as such, not as the play's or the project's endorsement.

anchor_text: Hector, by the fifth hour of the sun, Will with a trumpet 'twixt our tents and Troy, To-morrow morning, call some knight to arms
summary: Hector is issuing a formal chivalric challenge: he will stand between the two armies at 'the fifth hour' (about 11 a.m.) and call any Greek champion to single combat. This mirrors the medieval and Elizabethan tradition of trial by combat — a formal, trumpet-heralded duel between champions — applied to the supposedly ancient world of Troy. The challenge's winner was held to have God's (or the gods') favour on his side.

The procedure — a trumpet signal, a space 'twixt the camps, a declared time — follows conventions from Elizabethan jousting and trial by combat rather than anything in Homer. The challenge matters for the play's plot: the Greek leaders will scheme to choose Ajax (not Achilles) as their champion, to humble Achilles's pride by showing him that someone else can do his job. Achilles's throwaway 'I know not; 'tis put to lott'ry' shows his contemptuous disengagement from the very war in which he is supposed to be the indispensable hero.

anchor_text: The wound of peace is surety, Surety secure
summary: Hector argues, in compressed language, that the real danger is not the enemy but the false confidence that comes from expecting peace to hold. 'Surety' means both 'security' and 'a guarantee'; when surety becomes 'secure' (careless, from Latin sine cura, 'without care'), it turns into a wound — a self-inflicted vulnerability. The repetition and near-paradox is deliberate rhetorical play on the concept.

The paradox 'wound of peace is surety' inverts the expected ('surety heals wounds') — instead, overconfidence is itself the injury. Schmidt's Lexicon notes 'secure' in Shakespeare almost always means rashly overconfident rather than 'safely protected.'

anchor_text: Weigh you the worth and honour of a king
summary: Troilus dismisses Hector's cost-benefit logic by extending the weighing metaphor: you cannot put a king's honour on a shopkeeper's scale ('scale / Of common ounces') or add it up with counting-chips ('counters'). The argument is that honour is incommensurable — it cannot be measured in units — and so cost-accounting is the wrong frame entirely.

'Counters' are small coin-shaped disks used to add up sums on a counting-board.

anchor_text: You are for dreams and slumbers, brother priest
summary: Troilus mocks Helenus as a 'priest' who retreats into religious dreaminess rather than fighting. Helenus was indeed both a Trojan prince and a seer-priest; Troilus treats his priestly vocation as an excuse for cowardice, implying that reason and religion are comforting fictions for those too timid to act.

Helenus is the prophetic twin of Cassandra; in Homer's Iliad he directs the Trojans in battle and can foresee outcomes. Shakespeare reduces him here to a cautious priest — a butt for Troilus's impatience with deliberation, just as Thersites reduces every warrior to a fool.

anchor_text: fly like chidden Mercury from Jove
summary: Mercury (Greek Hermes) was the winged-footed messenger of the gods, known for his speed. Troilus pictures Helenus 'flying' from danger on the wings of reason, as if he were Mercury himself fleeing the angry thunder of Jove (Jupiter) — a scolded servant sprinting away from his master. The mockery is that Helenus uses reason as a reason to run.

Troilus is casting reason itself as mere fear in celestial dress. anchor_text: Make livers pale and lustihood deject
summary: In Elizabethan physiology the liver was the seat of courage and passionate feeling; a 'pale liver' meant a cowardly person, drained of blood. 'Lustihood' means vigour, energy, and manly spirit. Troilus is saying that reason and caution ('respect') drain a man of his fighting spirit — they literally bleach his courage white.

A cowardly man had 'a white liver' (lacking blood = lacking heat = lacking courage). Shakespeare uses 'liver' in this sense in Twelfth Night ('I am not of that feather to shake off / My friend when he must need me... white-liver'd'), Much Ado, and elsewhere.

anchor_text: What's aught but as 'tis valued
summary: Troilus's one-line philosophical claim: nothing has a fixed, objective value — things are worth only what someone decides they are worth. Hector immediately rebuts this by arguing that value is not purely subjective: a thing also has worth 'as well wherein 'tis precious of itself / As in the prizer.'

Troilus's position — that value is entirely in the valuing will — is the play's moral trap: it lets him treat Helen (and, implicitly, Cressida) as trophies whose 'value' is set by male desire, and whose 'cheapening' by return would be a loss of honour rather than a gain of reason. Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (relevant to Hector's university-based 'Aristotle' allusion at line 1100) argues that virtue and worth have objective grounding, not merely subjective attribution.

anchor_text: We turn not back the silks upon the merchant
summary: Troilus uses a merchant analogy to argue against returning Helen: once you have handled (and thus soiled) a bolt of silk, you cannot return it; once you have eaten your fill, you do not throw the leftovers into the 'unrespective sieve' (an indiscriminate rubbish-heap). Having enjoyed a purchase, you are bound to keep it.

The argument is circular and self-serving: Troilus implies that Helen is Troy's 'property' because Paris has used her, and that to return her would be to admit the whole enterprise was theft. The commercial metaphor is exactly what Hector has been objecting to — treating honour as a transaction.

anchor_text: for an old aunt whom the Greeks held captive He brought a Grecian queen
summary: Troilus recalls the pretext for Paris's voyage: the Greeks had previously taken Hesione, a Trojan princess (here called 'aunt'), captive. Paris went ostensibly to recover her, and returned instead with Helen, queen of Sparta, abandoning the original mission entirely. This is the Trojan claim that the abduction of Helen was a legitimate reprisal for the earlier Greek abduction of Hesione.

Caxton's Recuyell of the Histories of Troye (1474), one of Shakespeare's likely background sources, gives this version. The argument is further evidence that the whole play exposes the gap between stated causes and real motives: Paris went for Hesione and came back with someone he wanted more.

anchor_text: Wrinkles Apollo's, and makes stale the morning
summary: Apollo was the sun-god, a byword for perfect male beauty; the morning (Aurora, goddess of the dawn) was equally a standard of radiant freshness. Troilus is saying Helen's beauty is so overwhelming it makes the sun-god himself look wrinkled and aged, and makes the brilliant dawn seem dull. The hyperbole shows exactly how the Trojans have inflated Helen beyond any rational assessment.
detail: The comparison of a human woman to Apollo as an image of radiant beauty also occurs in Troilus and Cressida 4.5, where Hector addresses Achilles in terms drawn from the Hyperion image. Marlowe's famous line 'Was this the face that launched a thousand ships' (Faustus, c. 1592) is the period's most direct statement of the same Helen-overvaluation the play is systematically deflating. Apollo (Greek Phoebus, 'the shining one') was the god of the sun, poetry, and music, and his beauty was classical gold-standard.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 3.156-160 (the Trojan elders acknowledge that Helen's beauty justifies the war, while still wishing she would leave) — the source tradition Shakespeare is both using and subverting.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1010
Homer Iliad 3.156-160 does show the Trojan elders on the wall acknowledging Helen's beauty while still wishing she would leave, supporting the claim about the source tradition.

Apollo as the classical gold-standard of male radiant beauty is correct, and the reading that the hyperbole itself exposes the Trojans' irrational inflation of Helen is sound; the Marlowe parallel is properly flagged as a parallel, not claimed as a source.

anchor_text: whose price hath launch'd above a thousand ships
summary: This is Troilus's version of the most famous line about Helen in Elizabethan writing: Marlowe's 'Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships?' (Doctor Faustus, c. 1592). Shakespeare's phrasing turns it into an economic argument: Helen's 'price' is the thousand ships — but Troilus means this as praise, where Marlowe's context is horror. The echo signals that the inflated price-tag is the very problem under debate.
detail: The 'thousand ships' figure comes ultimately from the ancient Greek tradition that Agamemnon assembled a fleet of about 1,000 vessels; Ovid's Heroides 13 and 16 sustain the count. By Marlowe's day it was the fixed shorthand for Helen's value. Shakespeare's use here — in a scene that is explicitly arguing about whether she IS worth the cost — makes the familiar phrase newly ironic: Troilus is using the price as proof of worth, but the play has been showing that price and worth are exactly what cannot be assumed to be equal.

sources.name: Marlowe, Doctor Faustus
sources.citation: Christopher Marlowe, Doctor Faustus (c. 1592; publ. 1604), 5.1: 'Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1013
Marlowe, Doctor Faustus 5.1 does contain 'Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?' — confirmed at that location.

The echo of Marlowe's Doctor Faustus line is a widely recognised parallel passage, and the interpretation — that Troilus deploys the familiar price-tag as proof of value, inadvertently making the play's ironic point — is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: 'Tis our mad sister; I do know her voice
summary: Troilus immediately dismisses Cassandra's off-stage cries as madness, before she has spoken a word in his presence. In the myth, Cassandra was the Trojan prophetess who was given the gift of true prophecy by Apollo and then cursed so that no one would believe her. Dismissing her as 'mad' is exactly the curse in action — the Trojans hear accurate warnings as ravings.
detail: Cassandra's double bind (she knows the truth; no one believes her) is the structural dramatic irony that underlies the whole scene. The audience, knowing the Troy story, knows every word she speaks is accurate. The play stages the wilful rejection of accurate prophecy in favour of pride and appetite as the mechanism of Troy's destruction. Cassandra's divine affliction is referred to in Virgil (Aeneid 2.246-247) and recounted in Ovid's Heroides.

sources.name: Ovid, Heroides
sources.citation: Ovid, Heroides 5.113-120 (Oenone to Paris: Cassandra's prophecy about the ships, ignored by the Trojans).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1030
Ovid Heroides 5.113-120 does contain Cassandra's prophecy (reported by Oenone) warning of ships bringing ruin to Troy, supporting the citation.

Troilus's instant dismissal before Cassandra speaks a word is accurately identified as the curse's mechanism in action; the structural-irony reading (audience knows she is right) is the standard and defensible interpretation.

anchor_text: Aristode thought Unfit to hear moral philosophy
summary: Hector quotes Aristotle's actual opinion: in the Nicomachean Ethics Aristotle argues that young men are poor students of ethics because they are ruled by passion rather than reason, and so cannot benefit from instruction about what is truly good. Hector uses this to explain why Troilus and Paris have 'gloz'd but superficially' on Helen's worth — their 'hot passion' rules their argument, not reason.
detail: The specific Aristotelian reference is Nicomachean Ethics 1.3 (1095a2-10): 'The young man is not fitted to be a student of Politics... for he will not profit from the lessons, since the end aimed at is not knowledge but action... and emotions govern his conduct.' Hector cites Aristotle by name — uniquely anachronistic, since Troy is mythological and Aristotle lived in the 4th century BCE, centuries after the war — a deliberate anachronism that colours the Trojan debate with a Renaissance university-humanism flavour and signals that this is a play for educated audiences.

sources.name: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics
sources.citation: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.3.1095a2-10 (young men ruled by passion are not fit to hear moral philosophy).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1100

Aristotle Nicomachean Ethics 1.3 (1095a2-10) does explicitly argue that young men are unfit students of moral/political philosophy because passion governs their conduct rather than reason, exactly as the annotation states.

The specific Nicomachean Ethics 1.3 passage on young men ruled by passion is correctly identified and accurately paraphrased; the annotation honestly labels the anachronism as deliberate rather than excusing it.

anchor_text: pleasure and revenge Have ears more deaf than adders to the voice
summary: Hector draws on the biblical image of a deaf adder that will not respond to a charmer's call. The Psalms describe a wicked man who 'stoppeth his ear like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear, which will not hearken to the voice of the charmer' (Psalm 58:4-5). Hector is saying that passion and a desire for revenge are just as wilfully deaf to rational argument.
detail: Psalm 58 describes the wicked as 'estranged from the womb' and 'deaf like the adder that stoppeth her ear.' The image was a standard biblical emblem for wilful obstinacy in the face of truth and persuasion. The Geneva Bible gloss on this verse makes the adder's deafness a figure for all who deliberately shut out God's word. Its application here is precise: Troilus and Paris have been arguing from desire (pleasure) and wounded pride (revenge), and Hector accuses them of being as impervious to reason as the proverbial deaf serpent.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Psalm 58:4-5 (Geneva 1599): 'They are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her eare, which heareth not the voice of the enchanter, though he be moste expert in charming.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1105
Psalm 58:4-5 in the Geneva Bible does contain the deaf adder that stops her ear against the voice of the charmer, supporting both the citation and the quoted wording.

Psalm 58:4-5's deaf adder as emblem of wilful obstinacy is the standard and precise biblical referent; the application to Troilus and Paris resisting rational argument is directly supported by the speech's context.

anchor_text: What nearer debt in all humanity Than wife is to the husband
summary: Hector makes a formal natural-law argument: there is an obligation rooted in nature ('Nature craves / All dues be rend'red to their owners') and confirmed by the laws of 'each well-order'd nation' that a wife belongs with her husband. Helen is the lawful wife of Menelaus of Sparta; Troy holding her against this law is a violation both of nature and of the law of nations.
detail: The legal concept of ius gentium ('law of nations') — a body of norms binding on all peoples regardless of local custom — is specifically what Hector is invoking in 'laws / Of nature and of nations.' This was a recognized concept in Roman law (Justinian's Institutes defines it) and in Renaissance international jurisprudence. The argument draws not on sentiment but on formal legal theory: Helen is not a trophy but another man's property, and the law, even between enemies, requires her return. The dramatic irony is extreme: Hector proves his own case, then immediately announces he will vote to keep Helen anyway ('my spritely brethren, I propend to you'), abandoning reason for 'honour.'

sources.name: Justinian, Institutes
sources.citation: Justinian, Institutes 1.2 (the ius gentium, law of nations, as a body of obligations recognised by all peoples — the legal tradition Hector is drawing on).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1109
Justinian's Institutes 1.2 does define the ius gentium as obligations recognised by all peoples, supporting Hector's invocation of 'laws of nature and of nations.'

The ius gentium reading is sound and the dramatic irony — Hector proves his own case then immediately abandons it — is the scene's central and universally recognised interpretive point; citing Justinian's Institutes for the law-of-nations concept is appropriate.

anchor_text: fame in time to come canonize us
summary: To 'canonize' is to include in a canonical, sacred list — specifically, in the Catholic Church, to declare someone a saint. Troilus uses it metaphorically: future fame will make them holy, sacred. The religious word for saint-making is applied to martial glory, as if military fame were a form of sanctity. The irony is that the audience knows this play's debunking of heroic 'fame.'
detail: Troilus's language consistently reaches for absolutes — holy, eternal, sacred — to justify keeping Helen. The same inflation that makes Helen's beauty surpass Apollo's applies here to their 'honour': fighting a war over a stolen woman will make them saints. For an Elizabethan audience familiar with the Reformation's assault on the cult of saints, the word 'canonize' applied to warriors fighting over a queen was potentially comic or alarming. The play's trajectory — Achilles butchering Hector, Troy falling — will measure how far this 'canonization' falls short.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'canonize' v., sense 2: 'to place in the canon of saints'; the transferred secular use is attested from the late 16th century.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1136
OED s.v. 'canonize' does record sense 2 (place in the canon of saints) and notes transferred secular use from the late 16th century, supporting the annotation.

The irony of applying the Catholic saint-making term to martial glory — particularly for an Elizabethan post-Reformation audience — is a sound and commonly noted reading; the annotation does not over-claim Shakespearean intent, framing it as 'potentially comic or alarming.'

anchor_text: a roisting challenge sent amongst The dull and factious nobles of the Greeks
summary: 'Roisting' means boisterous, swaggering, loud. Hector reveals he has sent a formal challenge to the Greeks — a single-combat challenge — designed to shame their 'great general' Achilles back into action. 'Factious' means given to internal disputes and self-interest. This challenge (Hector vs. a Greek champion) will be the subject of Act 1 among the Greeks and leads to the Ajax-Hector duel of Act 4.
detail: The challenge is part of the play's sustained examination of what 'honour' produces: the same code that keeps Troy fighting also generates these formal combats — chivalric rituals amid an unheroic war. Ulysses will manipulate the challenge to his own political ends (making Ajax, not Achilles, the Greek champion, to humiliate the sulking Achilles). The tactic of the single-combat challenge to rouse a passive enemy is Homeric (Hector challenges the Greeks in Iliad 7); Shakespeare gives it a political purpose Hector does not know about.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 7.67-91 (Hector proposes single combat with any Greek champion — the source of this challenge in the play's plot).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1143
Homer Iliad 7.67-91 does show Hector proposing single combat with any Greek champion, establishing the source for the challenge referenced in the play.

The identification of the challenge as a single-combat device linked to Hector's Homeric challenge in Iliad 7 is accurate, and the political dimension — Ulysses will redirect it to humble Achilles — correctly anticipates the play's subsequent action.

anchor_text: lost in the labyrinth of thy fury
summary: Thersites compares his own rage to being trapped in the Labyrinth — the famous Cretan maze, built by Daedalus, from which escape was impossible without the thread Ariadne gave Theseus. He is so consumed by fury at Ajax's beating that he cannot find his way out of his own anger.
detail: The Labyrinth housed the Minotaur and is the classical image of inescapable entanglement. Thersites turns it inward, making his rage a maze he cannot escape. The play opens 2.3 with Thersites alone, still stewing over Ajax's beating of him (alluded to in 2.1), and the Labyrinth image captures how the powerless man is imprisoned by frustrations he cannot act on — he cannot beat Ajax back, only rail. The whole scene then demonstrates exactly this: Thersites rages and insults everyone, and nothing changes.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.155-168 (Daedalus builds the Labyrinth on Crete to house the Minotaur); Golding's English translation, 1567.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1149

Ovid Metamorphoses 8 does contain the Labyrinth/Daedalus passage, though the section begins at line 152 rather than 155; the core claim (Daedalus builds the maze to house the Minotaur) is accurate and the source is real and supportive.
The Labyrinth as an image of inescapable entanglement is well supported; applying it to self-consuming rage is a natural metaphor and the scene's subsequent stasis confirms the interpretation.

anchor_text: elephant Ajax carry it thus
summary: 'Carry it' means 'win the day' or 'have it all his own way.' Thersites likens Ajax to an elephant — a byword for immense brute strength and slow wit — to sneer at his power over him. The elephant was proverbially obstinate and unable to kneel or bend, making it a natural image for Ajax's unyielding, unsubtle force.
detail: Medieval and Renaissance natural-history and bestiary lore held that the elephant had no knee-joints and so could not bend its legs or rise if it fell (a belief Sir Thomas Browne would later debunk in Pseudodoxia Epidemica). Pliny's Natural History Book 8 is the great classical source for elephant lore, though Pliny in fact says elephants do kneel; the 'cannot bend' idea is the later popular tradition. This disability becomes relevant when Ulysses at TLN 1239 says 'The elephant hath joints, but none for courtesy; his legs / Are legs for necessity, not for flexure' -- both passages make Ajax's inability to 'bend' (to be gracious, to kneel to his commanders) into an animal joke. The association of Ajax with the elephant runs through the play.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 8 (chs. 1-12, the great classical account of the elephant's size and intelligence -- the root of Renaissance elephant lore).

The elephant-as-brute-Ajax running joke is textually confirmed by Ulysses's echo at TLN 1239, and the Plinian belief about inflexible legs is the correct scholarly context; 'carry it' meaning 'win the day' is standard Elizabethan idiom.
