anchor_text: learn to conjure and raise devils
summary: Thersites threatens to learn black magic — conjuring demons from Hell — because mere words and curses are not working. To 'conjure' meant to compel spirits or devils through ritual and spoken formulas. It is a black-comic boast: if railing and prayer cannot hurt Ajax and Achilles, perhaps summoning the devil will.
detail: The idea that a sorcerer could 'raise' or 'conjure' devils by speaking their names and drawing circles was a staple of Elizabethan demonology — Marlowe's Doctor Faustus had made it a live theatrical idea. Thersites's 'I'll learn to conjure' is the powerless man's fantasy of catastrophic force. His 'prayers' to Jove and Mercury (lines below) are already a mock-conjuration; here he escalates to the explicitly demonic. The joke also positions Thersites himself as already half-fiendish — a railer, cursing and calling on hell — which the characters around him implicitly confirm.

sources.name: Marlowe, Doctor Faustus
sources.citation: Christopher Marlowe, The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus (c. 1592; printed 1604/1616): conjuration as the raising of Mephistophilis by spoken incantation, a familiar theatrical image for Shakespeare's audience.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1152

Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (c. 1592) is a genuine work in which Faustus conjures Mephistophilis by spoken incantation, and the theatrical association of conjuration with demonic raising is accurately described.

Reading 'conjure and raise devils' as demonic magic is the plain meaning; the Marlowe parallel is contextually appropriate, though the gloss slightly over-specifies the Faustus connection where Thersites's language is a commonplace rather than a direct allusion.

anchor_text: great thunder-darter of Olympus, forget that thou art Jove, the king of gods, and, Mercury, lose all the serpentine craft of thy caduceus
summary: Thersites mockingly prays to the two supreme Olympian gods. Jove (Jupiter, king of the gods) wielded a thunderbolt and was called the 'thunder-darter'; Mercury was the messenger of the gods, whose staff — the caduceus, a wand entwined with serpents — gave him power over sleep and death and was the emblem of his cunning. Thersites's absurd request is that both gods destroy their defining powers, just as Ajax and Achilles have destroyed theirs.
detail: The caduceus (Greek kerykeion) is Mercury's herald's staff, typically shown as a winged rod with two serpents coiling around it — the source of the modern medical symbol. By 'serpentine craft' Thersites means the twisting, snake-like cleverness Mercury stands for. Thersites's comedy here is mock-theology: he asks Jove to forget he is king of the gods (and stop throwing thunderbolts) and Mercury to lose his supernatural craft — because Ajax and Achilles have already lost the minimal wit to extract a fly from a spider's web. The logic is satiric symmetry: they are so stupid the gods themselves ought to become stupid just to match them.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.671-688 (Mercury's caduceus, with which he sends Argus to sleep); Golding's English translation, 1567.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 24.339-345 (Hermes/Mercury as divine messenger, carrying his herald's staff).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1156

Ovid Metamorphoses 1.671-688 covers the Mercury-and-Argus episode in which Mercury uses his sleep-inducing caduceus, and Homer Iliad 24.339-345 shows Hermes carrying his herald's wand; both sources are real and directly support the claims.

Jove as thunder-darter and Mercury's caduceus as serpentine craft are standard classical identifications, and the satiric logic — gods should become as stupid as Ajax and Achilles — is accurately parsed from the text.

anchor_text: the Neapolitan bone-ache
summary: Thersites curses the whole Greek camp with 'the Neapolitan bone-ache' — a contemporary name for syphilis. The disease was called 'Neapolitan' because it became widely recognised in Italy during the French siege of Naples in 1494-95, and spread rapidly across Europe thereafter. It was associated with sexual licence, making the curse grimly appropriate for a war Thersites reduces to 'a whore and a cuckold.'
detail: Syphilis (the French disease, the Spanish disease, or in English often 'the Neapolitan bone-ache,' from the deep bone pain of secondary-stage infection) was epidemic in Shakespeare's England. Its association with sexual contact fitted Thersites's central argument that the entire Trojan War — fought for a 'placket' (i.e. a woman's body) — is nothing but venereal folly. The disease recurs throughout the play (Pandarus's Epilogue bequeaths his 'diseases' to the audience), as the fitting emblem of the love-war equation. Thersites calls it his 'prayer' for those 'that war for a placket' — a term for the opening of a skirt, slang for female genitalia.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'bone-ache, n.' (citing this passage); the 'Neapolitan disease' as syphilis, from the Naples epidemic of 1494-95 noted in contemporary medical writing including William Clowes, A Short and Profitable Treatise touching the Cure of the Disease called Morbus Gallicus (1579).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1163

The OED entry for 'bone-ache' is real and cites this passage; William Clowes's 1579 treatise on Morbus Gallicus is a confirmed publication; the Naples epidemic of 1494-95 as the origin of the 'Neapolitan' label is historically accurate.
The Neapolitan bone-ache as syphilis linked to the Naples epidemic is the standard scholarly gloss; the connection to 'war for a placket' is explicit in the text and sound.

anchor_text: that war for a placket
summary: 'Placket' primarily means the slit opening at the top of a woman's petticoat or skirt, but was commonly used as slang for female genitalia and, by extension, for a woman herself as a sexual object. Thersites reduces the entire Trojan War — fought nominally to recover Helen — to men dying for a woman's body, coupling his contempt for Achilles and Ajax with contempt for Helen and the cause.
detail: The word 'placket' is well documented in this bawdy sense in Elizabethan writing (see, for example, King Lear 3.4, 'keep thy foot out of brothels... thy hand out of plackets'). Thersites's equation of 'a whore and a cuckold' (TLN 1210) — Helen and Menelaus — with 'a placket' collapses the play's whole political and martial apparatus into sexual commerce. It is the central Thersitean argument: chivalry is just dressed-up lust. The curse of syphilis immediately follows, suggesting the disease is the appropriate punishment for 'warring for sex.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'placket, n.' sense 2 ('the female pudenda; a woman, regarded as a sexual object'). Also Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'placket.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1165
OED 'placket, n.' sense 2 for female genitalia/woman as sexual object is a real entry, and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon covers the bawdy sense; both sources support the claim.
The bawdy sense of 'placket' is well documented and confirmed by the King Lear parallel; Thersites's reduction of the war to sexual commerce is the scene's explicit argument and not an over-reading.

anchor_text: If I could 'a rememb'red a gilt counterfeit
summary: A 'gilt counterfeit' is a forged, gold-plated coin — shiny on the outside, base metal underneath. Thersites is insulting Patroclus: had he remembered a counterfeit coin in time (slippery, worth nothing, only looked like gold), he would have thought of Patroclus — because Patroclus, like the fake coin, has fine appearance but no substance. The insult 'slipp'd out of my contemplation' completes the pun: counterfeit coins were prone to 'slipping' from memory or value.
detail: The 'gilt counterfeit' insult is a characteristically Thersitean construction: abuse and financial metaphor fused. Patroclus is worth no more than a fake coin; his proximity to the genuinely powerful Achilles is what gives him his 'gilt' surface. The economic imagery — worth, counterfeit, slipping — runs through the play's sceptical anatomy of value: in a war that debates whether Helen is 'worth' the men dying for her, everything is measured against a suspect standard.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'counterfeit, n.' sense 1b ('A spurious coin'); s.v. 'gilt, adj.' sense 1 ('Covered with a thin layer of gold').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1168
OED 'counterfeit, n.' sense 1b (spurious coin) and 'gilt, adj.' sense 1 (gold-covered) are real entries that directly support the annotation's gloss of the phrase.

The counterfeit-coin insult is the mainstream gloss; the 'slipp'd out' pun on coins slipping from value is plausible, though the annotation could be clearer that Thersites means Patroclus slipped from his mind rather than the coin slipping per se — still defensible.

anchor_text: shrouded any but lazars
summary: A 'lazar' is a person suffering from leprosy — from the biblical Lazarus, the sore-covered beggar in Jesus's parable. Thersites's 'curse' on Patroclus ends with the wish that if anyone says Patroclus's corpse is a 'fair corse' (good-looking body), she can only have dressed the dead bodies of lepers. It is a roundabout way of calling Patroclus hideous: only someone who had never seen anything better than a rotting leper would call him handsome.
detail: The word 'lazar' descends from the name Lazarus in the parable of Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31), in which Lazarus is the sore-covered beggar who lies at the rich man's gate — it had become a general term for any leper by the medieval period. 'Lazar-houses' (leper hospitals) were called lazarettos. Thersites's elaborate, logically constructed curses — each one a careful if-then structure rather than a simple insult — are a comic feature of his character throughout the play.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'lazar, n.' ('A poor and diseased person, esp. a leper'). Geneva Bible, Luke 16:20 (1599): 'a certaine beggar named Lazarus.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1175
OED 'lazar, n.' is a real entry defining a diseased or leprous person; Geneva Bible 1599 Luke 16:20 does give 'a certaine beggar named Lazarus,' accurately supporting the etymology claim.
Deriving 'lazar' from the Lucan parable and glossing it as leper is the standard etymology and meaning; the logical structure of Thersites's curse is accurately described.

anchor_text: my cheese, my digestion
summary: Achilles greets Thersites with a food metaphor that is also a put-down: 'my cheese, my digestion' means 'my sharpener, my stomach-aid.' Cheese was served at the end of a meal because it was thought to help digestion; Thersites serves that same function for Achilles — a bitter, sharp thing that aids mental digestion, helping him process and mock the world around him. The warmth is real, but the compliment still reduces Thersites to a bodily function.
detail: Elizabethan humoral medicine held that the stomach required a strong, pungent close to a meal to help break food down; cheese, mustard, and vinegar were all cited for this purpose. Achilles literally means he keeps Thersites as his personal digestive aid: the railer's sharp insults process events for him. This is what Ulysses means when he says Achilles has 'inveigled his fool from him' (Ajax's fool, TLN 1228) — both Achilles and Ajax use Thersites as a substitute for their own thinking.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'digestion, n.' sense 2b ('aid to digestion; a digestive'); cf. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'digestion.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1181
OED 'digestion, n.' sense 2b for a digestive aid is a real entry, and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon covers the relevant sense; both support the gloss that cheese was served to aid digestion.

The cheese-as-digestive-aid gloss is the accepted reading, and the humoral-medicine context is appropriate; the interpretation that Achilles uses Thersites as a surrogate mind is supported by Ulysses's remark at TLN 1228.

anchor_text: I'll decline the whole question
summary: 'Decline' here is a grammar pun: in Latin and Greek grammar, to 'decline' a noun is to run through its cases — nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, and so on. Thersites promises to 'decline' the question of who everyone is — and then proceeds to do exactly that, listing Agamemnon, Achilles, Thersites, and Patroclus in a descending chain, each one defined by relation to the next. The joke is that a grammatical exercise doubles as a social analysis.
detail: Latin declension was the foundation of grammar-school education; every Elizabethan schoolboy spent years declining nouns (mensa, mensae, mensae...). Thersites's use of the term signals both that he has the education, and that he intends to weaponise it. The 'declining' he performs — Agamemnon commands Achilles, Achilles is my lord, I am Patroclus' knower, Patroclus is a fool — is also a social declension, a descent of folly from the top of the Greek command to the bottom, and implicitly a challenge to the whole hierarchy Ulysses has just been preaching about in Act 1. The passage connects to the play's satiric debunking of rank and 'degree.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'decline, v.' sense 7 ('In grammar: to run through or recite the cases of a noun, adjective, or pronoun'). Cf. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'decline.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1192
OED 'decline, v.' sense 7 for the grammatical act of running through noun cases is a real entry that directly supports the wordplay identification.
The Latin-grammar pun on 'decline' is the standard scholarly reading, and the description of social declension matching grammatical declension is a well-established interpretation of this passage.

anchor_text: He is a privileg'd man
summary: A 'privileged man' was someone who held an official licence to speak freely — specifically, a licensed fool or jester, whose frank speech was protected by their role. Achilles is placing Thersites in the tradition of the court jester: fools were paid to insult their masters, and no one could take offence because the jester's 'privilege' exempted him from normal social rules.
detail: The licensed fool — a person of weak social standing given permission to mock the powerful — was a real institution in Tudor and Stuart courts. The privilege was a formal social compact: the jester could say what no one else could, and in return was not punished. By calling Thersites 'a privileged man,' Achilles simultaneously promotes him (gives him a social function) and contains him (makes his abuse part of a game rather than a real threat). The play's Thersites is consistently self-aware about this double-bind — he can rail, but the railing changes nothing.

anchor_text: such patchery, such juggling, and such knavery
summary: 'Patchery' means bungling, botched work, or dishonest trickery — from 'patcher,' someone who patches things sloppily together. 'Juggling' in Elizabethan English meant cheating or deceptive trickery (not performing juggling tricks with balls). Thersites is summing up the entire Greek political scheming he has witnessed — Achilles's refusal, Ulysses's maneuvering, Ajax's manipulation — as a mass of botched fraud.
detail: The cluster 'patchery-juggling-knavery' belongs to a category of Thersitean summary words: he habitually distills complex political actions into a short list of contemptuous nouns. 'Patchery' connects to the 'patch' (a jester's motley, which was traditionally patched or many-coloured cloth), so 'patchery' carries a flavour of fool's work as well as slipshod deception. The Elizabethan sense of 'juggling' as verbal or political trickery (as in Macbeth's 'juggling fiends') is consistently used by Shakespeare.

anchor_text: All the argument is a whore and a cuckold
summary: Thersites reduces the entire Trojan War to a simple equation: 'a whore and a cuckold.' The 'whore' is Helen (who left Menelaus for Paris, and who Thersites regards as sexually available), and the 'cuckold' is Menelaus (the husband whose wife has slept with another man — a 'cuckold' in Elizabethan slang, said to grow invisible horns). Thersites means: the grand military cause that has kept armies at Troy for years is nothing but jealousy over a faithless woman.
detail: A 'cuckold' was an Elizabethan term for a man whose wife was unfaithful; the horns he was said to wear (visible to everyone except him) were a standard comic image. The contempt in the word 'whore' directed at Helen is part of the play's systematic debunking of the war's nominal cause: Troilus and Paris in the council (2.2) speak of Helen's 'worth' in quasi-philosophical terms; Thersites strips away the rhetoric. His formula — 'dry serpigo on the subject, and war and lechery confound all' — is the play's bitterest summary before the Greek leaders arrive. Content note: the scene does not endorse Thersites's view; it presents it as the play's most corrosive and least diplomatic voice.

anchor_text: Now the dry serpigo on the subject
summary: 'Serpigo' is a medical term for a creeping skin disease — from Latin serpere, to creep — used for ringworm, herpes, or any spreading skin eruption. Thersites is calling down a skin disease on 'the subject' of the whole war (meaning the matter of the quarrel itself, or the men conducting it). Paired with the 'Neapolitan bone-ache' and the diseases in Pandarus's Epilogue, it makes disease Thersites's standard curse and the play's governing metaphor for moral corruption.
detail: The adjective 'dry' intensifies the nastiness: a dry serpigo was one that caused cracking and scaling rather than weeping wounds, and was harder to treat. Medical usage of the term appears in Thomas Cogan's Haven of Health (1584) and other contemporary texts. Thersites's curses are consistently medical in flavour — bone-ache (syphilis), serpigo (skin disease), the 'gall' of other passages — turning the bodies of the warriors into diseased flesh that matches the corruption of their cause. The play's final scene, Pandarus bequeathing 'diseases' to the audience, closes the same circuit.

anchor_text: He shent our messengers; and we lay by our appertainings
summary: 'Shent' is the past tense of 'shend,' an archaic verb meaning to shame, rebuke, or disgrace — Achilles turned the generals' messengers away with contempt. 'Appertainings' are the attributes of rank and dignity — the things that belong to (appertain to) their high offices as commanders. Agamemnon is saying they humbled themselves by personally visiting Achilles, setting aside the formalities of command, and he still refused to come out.
detail: 'Shent' (Old English scendan, to put to shame) was already archaic by Shakespeare's time and carries a deliberately old-fashioned, high-toned weight here, appropriate to Agamemnon's formal dignity. 'Appertainings' is rarer still — it means the perquisites and ceremonial dignity that belongs to a station. The whole speech is a study in outraged official decorum: the commander-in-chief is reduced to making personal house-calls and being snubbed by his subordinate, which Agamemnon refuses to normalise.

anchor_text: The elephant hath joints, but none for courtesy; his legs are legs for necessity, not for flexure
summary: Ulysses uses an Elizabethan natural-history belief to mock Achilles: elephants were commonly thought to have no knee-joints and therefore could not kneel or bow. 'Flexure' means bending. Because Achilles will not come out and bow to the generals (will not 'flex'), Ulysses compares him to an elephant — all brute function, no capacity for courtesy.
detail: The belief that elephants had no knee-joints and so could not kneel or bow was a widespread medieval and Renaissance natural-history commonplace (later debunked by Sir Thomas Browne, Pseudodoxia Epidemica 3.1). 'Flexure' means bending. Pliny's Natural History Book 8 is the classical fountainhead of elephant lore, though Pliny himself reports that elephants kneel -- the 'cannot bend' idea belongs to the later popular tradition the line draws on. Ulysses's metaphor also glances back at Ajax, whom he has compared to an elephant in the same scene: both the massive warrior and the sulking hero are 'legs for necessity, not for flexure' -- force without grace or social intelligence.

anchor_text: His humorous predominance; yea, watch his pettish lunes
summary: Agamemnon is describing Achilles's mood-driven behaviour. 'Humorous' means governed by his humours — the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that Elizabethan medicine believed controlled temperament and mood. 'Predominance' means whichever humour is currently ruling him. 'Pettish lunes' are petty fits of lunacy — 'lune' is a moon-derived word for a sudden mad outburst (the moon, luna, was thought to cause madness).
detail: Humoral theory held that a person's character and moment-to-moment behaviour were determined by the balance of the four humours; a 'humorous' person was one whose humours were out of balance and who therefore acted capriciously. Achilles's withdrawal and sulking would be diagnosed as an excess of melancholy (black bile), making him self-absorbed and proud. 'Lunes' derives from luna (moon), both in the sense of temporary madness and in a theatrical gesture — a sudden lunatic fit. Agamemnon's instruction to Patroclus is bitter satire: the generals must pretend that Achilles's tantrums 'ride' the action of the whole war, i.e., indulge his ego completely.

anchor_text: the death tokens of it cry 'No recovery'
summary: 'Death tokens' are the spots that appeared on the skin of plague victims — the blotches or 'tokens' that told the physician the patient was past saving. Ulysses is saying Achilles's pride has advanced so far that its symptoms, like the plague tokens, declare 'no recovery' — he is terminally infected with self-regard. It extends the disease imagery running through the scene from Thersites's bone-ache onward.
detail: Plague 'tokens' (or 'God's tokens') were the dark spots and blotches appearing on the skin in advanced bubonic plague; their appearance was a death sentence, the point at which physicians declared the patient past help. The terminology was well known to a London audience that lived through repeated plague closures of the theatres. Ulysses's medical metaphor — Achilles's pride is a plague so advanced as to be incurable — belongs to the play's systematic use of disease as a moral category, connecting Thersites's bodily curses to the Greek commanders' political diagnoses.

anchor_text: add more coals to Cancer when he burns with entertaining great Hyperion
summary: Ulysses uses an astronomical image: Cancer is the zodiac sign of midsummer (the sun enters Cancer at the summer solstice, the hottest point of the year); 'entertaining great Hyperion' means hosting the sun itself (Hyperion, the Titan of radiant light, was identified with the sun). To 'add coals to Cancer in midsummer' is to heat what is already at maximum heat — the perfect image for sending Ajax to flatter an already over-inflated Achilles. It would be pointlessly redundant.
detail: Hyperion is one of the Titans of Greek myth, father of the sun-god Helios and often identified with the sun directly. By Shakespeare's time 'Hyperion' was a standard poetic name for the sun. The astrological reference is precise: Cancer (the Crab) governs the period from roughly late June to late July, the heart of summer, when the sun is at its highest and hottest arc. 'Entertaining' here means 'receiving as a guest' — Cancer 'hosts' the sun. Ulysses's argument is that Ajax's visit would not humble Achilles but feed his pride at the hottest point of its burning. This connects to the scene's broader anti-flattery argument: sending a great man to Achilles would only confirm Achilles's sense of his own indispensability.

sources.name: Hesiod, Theogony
sources.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 134, 371-374 (Hyperion among the Titans, father of Helios/the Sun).

The astronomical reading — Cancer hosts the sun at midsummer, so adding coals would be redundant heat — is the standard interpretation; Hyperion as sun-Titan is correct; the application to Ulysses's argument against sending Ajax to flatter Achilles is precisely grounded in the text.

anchor_text: He rubs the vein of him
summary: Nestor's aside means Ulysses is working on Ajax exactly right — 'rubbing the vein' means finding and stimulating the characteristic streak or disposition in a person, as a miner finds and follows a vein of ore. Ulysses has correctly identified Ajax's pride and is working it: by praising Ajax extravagantly and refusing to send him to Achilles, he massages Ajax's vanity to precisely the pitch needed.
detail: The metaphor of 'rubbing' a psychological 'vein' recurs in Shakespeare for this kind of careful psychological manipulation — touching exactly the right nerve. Ulysses's scheme throughout the scene is a textbook exercise in strategic flattery: he praises Ajax to Ajax's face in increasingly elaborate terms, knowing the compliments will reach Achilles and sting him into returning to battle. Nestor's aside ('He rubs the vein of him') is the insider's commentary on the manipulation, making the audience complicit in understanding the scheme even as Ajax swallows it whole.

anchor_text: The raven chides blackness
summary: Ulysses's aside is a proverb: a raven (which is entirely black) scolding something for being black is absurd, since it is the same colour itself. Ajax has just called Achilles 'a paltry, insolent fellow' and 'can he not be sociable?' — while being himself the most paltry, insolent, and unsociable man in the scene. The proverb is the play's driest irony: Ajax condemning in Achilles the exact vices he himself embodies.
detail: The proverb is a variant on the more common 'the pot calling the kettle black.' Ravens, entirely black birds, were proverbially associated with ill omen and darkness; for a raven to denounce something as black is the purest possible hypocrisy. Ulysses voices this thought as an aside so the audience appreciates the irony while Ajax remains oblivious. The whole sequence of asides (Nestor: 'He is not emulous'; Ulysses: 'Know the whole world, he is as valiant'; then 'The raven chides blackness') forms a kind of running commentary in which the schemers decode each other's manipulation for the audience's benefit.

'His addition' means his title or the honour attached to his name. Ulysses says even Milo's fame for strength should yield to Ajax: no praise for physical power is too great. This is extravagant flattery designed to sting Achilles.

anchor_text: the hart Achilles keeps thicket
summary: Ulysses ends his speech with a hunting metaphor: Achilles is a 'hart' (a male deer, especially one over five years old) that 'keeps thicket' — hides in the undergrowth. A hart that won't come out into the open cannot be hunted. The image undercuts Achilles's self-image as a great warrior: instead of a lion or eagle, he is a prey animal hiding in the bushes.
detail: The hart in Elizabethan England was the premier quarry of noble hunting; a hart 'at bay' was the climactic moment of the chase, and a hart 'keeping thicket' (refusing to run, hiding in cover) was a technical hunter's term for when the deer evaded the field. Ulysses's image is pointed: Achilles, who should be the supreme fighter, is behaviourally a hunted animal skulking in cover rather than running. The pun on 'hart'/'heart' is also likely: the man without heart keeps his 'thicket.' The closing couplet (TLN 1399-1400, Agamemnon: 'Light boats sail swift, though greater hulks draw deep') caps the scene with a nautical proverb to the same effect — big things are slow, small things can move.

anchor_text: I do depend upon the lord
summary: The Servant plays on two meanings of 'depend upon': to be in the service of (to follow or wait upon a lord), and to rely on or trust in. When Pandarus says 'You depend upon him,' he means 'you are in his household'; the Servant plays innocent and answers in the religious sense — 'I depend upon [i.e., trust in] the Lord' — before Pandarus catches the ambiguity and rephrases.
detail: The joke is a small example of the scene's sustained wit-combat, in which the Servant parries every one of Pandarus's blunt questions with evasive doubleness. The pun on 'lord' (a master, and God) sets up the next exchange about 'grace' and 'lordship,' making the whole opening a comedy of verbal slippage in which Pandarus is consistently outmaneuvered by a man he considers his inferior.

anchor_text: You are in the state of grace
summary: 'Grace' has two meanings here: a title of honour (addressed to a duke or archbishop), and the theological condition of God's saving favour. Pandarus wants to be greeted by his titles ('honour and lordship'); the Servant offers him instead a compliment that sounds devout — being 'in a state of grace' — which Pandarus brushes aside because it is not the social rank he craves.
detail: The double meaning skewers Pandarus's vanity: the Servant's phrase is formally courteous (an archaic salutation) while quietly implying that Pandarus ought to care more about his soul than his lordship. Pandarus's swift rebuke — that 'honour and lordship are my titles' — confirms how entirely worldly his concerns are. The exchange continues the scene's pattern of the Servant winning every verbal round.

anchor_text: it is music in parts
summary: The Servant answers 'Do you know the musicians?' with 'Wholly, sir' — meaning he knows them completely. He then answers 'What music is this?' with 'it is music in parts,' meaning it is polyphonic music (composed for separate vocal or instrumental parts). Both answers are technically correct while being deliberately unhelpful; the Servant is playing on 'wholly' (completely) versus 'in parts' (partly, in separate sections).
detail: Part-music — ensemble music written for two or more independent melody lines — was the dominant form of Elizabethan art music. 'Wholly' versus 'in parts' is therefore both a joke about the Servant's evasiveness and an accurate musical description, typical of the scene's running comedy in which the Servant answers every question correctly but never usefully. Pandarus later admits: 'we understand not one another: I am too courtly, and thou art too cunning.'

anchor_text: the mortal Venus, the heart-blood of beauty, love's invisible soul
summary: The Servant heaps extravagant compliments on the woman Paris is entertaining, calling her the mortal (human, earthly) equivalent of Venus, the goddess of love and beauty. 'Heart-blood of beauty' means the very life and essence of beauty; 'love's invisible soul' means the inward animating spirit of love made flesh. Pandarus assumes it must be Cressida — then is deflated when the Servant says it is Helen. The joke undercuts both women: the praise is absurd flattery, and Pandarus thinks his niece deserves it more.

anchor_text: my business seethes
summary: Pandarus means his business is urgent — it 'boils,' it cannot wait. 'Seethe' meant to boil or stew, and was commonly used for both cooking and for any great agitation. The Servant immediately pounces on the culinary sense: 'Sodden business! There's a stew'd phrase indeed!' — 'sodden' means boiled or cooked, and 'stew'd' means both simmered (as a stew) and connected to a 'stew' (Elizabethan slang for a brothel). The Servant is calling Pandarus's language both overcooked and smutty.
detail: 'Stew' as a term for a brothel was current in Elizabethan English; 'stewed' likewise carried bawdy suggestion. The Servant's quip thus lands a quiet insult: Pandarus's 'business' — bringing his niece to Troilus — is precisely the business of a stew, and the Servant, who has been running rings around him all scene, slips in one final ribald jibe before Paris and Helen enter. The exchange exemplifies the play's method of making bawdy and cynical meaning bubble up under every surface.

anchor_text: Fair be to you, my lord, and to all this fair company
summary: Pandarus pours out 'fair' again and again across three lines ('Fair be to you,' 'fair company,' 'fair desires,' 'fair queen,' 'fair thoughts,' 'fair pillow') -- a torrent of insistent repetition (anaphora/ploce) that inflates a routine courtly greeting into comic excess. Helen's reply, 'you are full of fair words,' immediately calls out the inflation.
detail: Figures of repetition -- the hammering of a single word for emphasis -- were recognized devices in Elizabethan schoolbook rhetoric (Thomas Wilson, Arte of Rhetorique, 1553; George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie, 1589, on the figures of repetition). Shakespeare uses the device to satirize courtly flattery: Pandarus's 'fair' torrent is hollow social performance, and Helen's amused 'full of fair words' confirms that even she sees through it -- fitting in a scene that puts the notorious beauty under the same deflating light as everything else.

anchor_text: here is good broken music
summary: 'Broken music' was a technical Elizabethan term for music played by a mixed consort of different instruments — strings, wind, and keyboard together — as opposed to a 'whole' consort of instruments of the same family. Paris takes Pandarus's phrase as meaning he has broken (interrupted, spoiled) the music by arriving, and so Pandarus must 'piece it out' by performing himself — i.e., sing. The pun turns a musical term into a social accusation.
detail: A 'broken consort' was a standard designation in Elizabethan music for an ensemble mixing lutes, viols, flutes, citterns, and pandoras — as distinguished from a 'whole' consort of, say, viols alone. Pandarus's remark, ostensibly complimenting the ensemble, allows Paris to rebound with the other sense: 'You have broke it, cousin; and by my life, you shall make it whole again.' The joke threads Pandarus into the scene's music and forces him, eventually, to sing. His song is the bawdy 'Love, love, nothing but love,' making 'whole music' out of broken courtliness.

The technical term 'broken music' for a mixed consort versus a whole consort is well-established (Morley, OED), and Paris's reply ('You have broke it, cousin... you shall make it whole again') explicitly plays on both senses in the text itself.

anchor_text: with my disposer Cressida
summary: Paris calls Cressida his 'disposer' — someone who has the disposal or management of him, a person at whose pleasure he acts. The word means, roughly, 'the one who directs or governs me.' Paris uses it lightly and knowingly: if Troilus is supping with Cressida, the woman has him under her management, much as Helen ('my Nell') has already kept Paris from arming today.
detail: 'Disposer' in this sense — one who has the disposing of another, who controls or directs — appears rarely in Shakespeare, and its use here by Paris is pointed: both he and Troilus are shown as governed by women rather than by their own military duty, which is the scene's unspoken commentary on the war. Paris freely admits Helen 'would not have it so' when he says he would fain have armed today.

anchor_text: Falling in, after falling out, may make them three
summary: Helen is responding to Pandarus's claim that Cressida and Paris 'are twain' (a pair apart, not in love). 'Falling out' means quarrelling; 'falling in' means reconciling. But Helen adds a sexual layer: 'falling in' is also the act of sexual intercourse, so if they fall in after their quarrel, the result could be 'three' — i.e., a pregnancy. The joke is a veiled comment on love-making as the natural sequel to a lovers' quarrel.
detail: The double meaning of 'fall in' (to embrace, to have sex with) is consistent with Elizabethan bawdy; 'three' implies conception, making Helen's quip a ribald prediction of pregnancy. The line is typical of the scene's tone, in which Helen, the war's ostensible cause, contributes nothing of substance and is shown as a frivolous participant in sexual wordplay — the 'mortal Venus' reduced to dirty jokes. It also sits alongside the play's wider pattern of reducing every high abstraction (love, honour, beauty) to the body.

Helen's 'Falling in, after falling out, may make them three' straightforwardly encodes the bawdy — 'falling in' as sexual union producing a third person (child) — and the Williams citation is the standard reference; neither an over-read nor anachronistic.

anchor_text: love's bow Shoots buck and doe
summary: Pandarus's song invokes Cupid, the Roman god of love, who fired arrows to kindle desire indiscriminately in men ('buck') and women ('doe') alike. The song then turns overtly bawdy: the 'shaft' does not simply 'wound' but 'tickles still the sore,' 'dying love lives still,' and 'O ho!' turns to 'ha ha he' — all conventional wordplay encoding orgasm ('to die' was Elizabethan slang for sexual climax). The song is a deliberately coarse parody of the Petrarchan love-lyric.
detail: Cupid's bow and arrows (from Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.468-474 — golden-tipped to kindle love, lead-tipped to repel it) were the stock machinery of Renaissance love poetry. Pandarus's song takes the convention and strips it to its bodily lowest: 'buck and doe' (male and female deer, and sexual partners), 'shaft confounds / Not that it wounds, / But tickles still the sore' (arousal as an itch that sexual action 'scratches'), and the dying/crying repeated wordplay ('O ho!... ha ha!') enacting the noise of sexual act. The mode is grotesque comic exposure — not romantic love but its animal mechanics — fitting for the scene's broader reduction of Helen and Paris to appetite.

The Cupid's-bow frame and the bawdy decoding of 'die,' 'sore,' and 'buck and doe' are all mainstream readings of this song supported by Williams and by the song's own explicit comic escalation; the Petrarchan-parody characterization is the consensus view.

anchor_text: He eats nothing but doves, love; and that breeds hot blood
summary: Elizabethan medical theory, derived from Galen's ancient humoral system, held that different foods produced different qualities of blood — and therefore different temperaments. Doves were associated with Venus and with warm, amorous desire; eating them was supposed to 'heat the blood' and so kindle sexual appetite. Paris's chain — doves breed hot blood, hot blood breeds hot thoughts, hot thoughts breed hot deeds — is a parody of the pseudo-medical logic that connected diet, temperament, and sex.
detail: In Galenic humoral theory, 'hot and moist' foods (like dove or pigeon) were held to stimulate the liver, increase blood heat, and thereby inflame passion. Paris's comic syllogism ('hot blood... hot thoughts... hot deeds... is love') sends up the medical language that moralists used to warn against rich food and lust. The dove was doubly apt: it was Venus's sacred bird, so its flesh was both literally and symbolically heating. Pandarus's recoil — 'Is love a generation of vipers?' — turns the chain into a grotesque image of love as a poisonous brood, a flash of the play's deeper sourness under the comic surface.

The Galenic hot-moist food chain (doves → hot blood → hot thoughts → hot deeds) is exactly what Paris performs at TLN 1515-1517, and the dove's Venereal symbolism is classical commonplace; the humoral framework is correctly applied and not anachronistic.

anchor_text: Let us to Priam's hall To greet the warriors
summary: A trumpet call signals the armies withdrawing from the field at day's end. Paris's closing lines — asking Helen to help 'unarm' Hector by touching his 'stubborn buckles' with her 'white enchanting fingers' — present Helen as a figure whose beauty can do what force cannot. It is a courtly, flattering speech, but its context is damning: the warriors risked their lives while Paris and Helen played at bawdy games indoors, and now Paris wants Helen to perform one courteous act as the soldiers return.
detail: The stage direction 'Sound a retreat' marks the close of the day's fighting with a military trumpet signal — the same instrument that opened battle with a charge. Paris's verse is the scene's only formal poetry, and it idealizes Helen ('your white enchanting fingers,' 'more than all the island kings') in the courtly Petrarchan register that the rest of the scene has steadily undercut with sexual jokes and domestic triviality. 'Disarm great Hector' is the functional point: Hector is coming home, and the scene ends by reminding us which Troy is fighting and which is not.

anchor_text: Gives us more palm in beauty than we have, Yea, overshines ourself
summary: Helen speaks of herself in the royal 'we' ('gives us... overshines ourself') — the plural form used by royalty to mean 'me.' 'Palm' means the victor's prize or glory — from the laurel and palm branches given to winners at ancient contests — so 'more palm in beauty' means 'greater glory for our beauty.' Helen is saying that being of service to Hector will enhance her own fame. The line is both vain and performatively humble at once.
detail: The royal plural ('we,' 'ourself') is a mark of great rank; applied to a woman who has abandoned her legitimate husband and whose beauty has caused a decade of war, its effect here is ironic rather than majestic. 'Palm' as the prize of victory comes from the custom at Greek and Roman athletic games of awarding a palm frond (later a laurel wreath) to the winner — a standard Renaissance metaphor for glory or pre-eminence. Helen's couplet, the scene's last words before Paris's exit-line, encapsulates the play's anatomizing of vanity: she frames an act of social courtesy as a personal victory in the competition of female beauty.

anchor_text: strange soul upon the Stygian banks Staying for waftage
summary: The Styx was the river that the dead had to cross to reach the underworld; Charon the ferryman carried souls across it, but only after they had paid him with a coin and waited on the bank. Troilus casts himself as a soul stranded on the near side, unable to reach the fields beyond, and begs Pandarus to be his Charon and ferry him to Cressida.
detail: In Virgil's Aeneid 6.295-330 Aeneas sees a vast crowd of unburied dead gathered on the bank unable to cross until their bodies have received burial rites. The image of the soul 'staying for waftage' (waiting for passage) frames Troilus's longing in epic, near-religious terms while also making Pandarus a ferryman of the dead -- a quietly unsettling cast for a love-scene. 'Waftage' means a carrying across water; the word is rare and picked for its resonance with 'watery' Styx.

anchor_text: from Cupid's shoulder pluck his painted wings
summary: Cupid (Roman Eros) was the god of erotic love, conventionally depicted as a winged boy armed with arrows. Troilus's hyperbole -- steal Love's own wings and fly on them -- measures the urgency of his desire: he wants a speed beyond anything natural, even beyond what the god of love himself can manage.
detail: The personification of Cupid as a winged, bow-carrying child derives from Ovid's Metamorphoses 1.452-474, where Cupid shoots Apollo and Daphne with his gold and lead arrows. 'Painted' is standard in Elizabethan descriptions of Cupid -- his wings are bright, ornamental, feathery. Troilus's appeal recurs in the scene's closing couplet, where Pandarus invokes 'Cupid' again: the god of desire presides over the whole encounter.

anchor_text: wat'ry palate tastes indeed Love's thrice-repured nectar
summary: 'Thrice-repured' means purified or refined three times over -- like gold or sugar refined to the highest degree, far purer than ordinary. 'Nectar' is the drink of the gods in classical myth; here Troilus means love's pleasure imagined at its most rarefied. The line is saying: if the mere thought of Cressida is this overwhelming, what will the reality feel like?
detail: 'Repure' (also 'repured') is not a standard dictionary verb; Shakespeare coins it from 'pure' via French purifier; the 'thrice' intensifies to a superlative (three rounds of distillation produces the finest product). The juxtaposition with 'wat'ry palate' -- a tongue still only imagining taste, not yet actually drinking -- is the whole conceit of these lines: anticipation versus consummation.

anchor_text: I shall lose distinction in my joys As doth a battle
summary: 'Lose distinction' means lose the ability to tell one feeling from another -- all the separate joys will blur into one overwhelming mass. The following simile develops it: when soldiers rush a fleeing enemy in a heap, the orderly formation collapses and you can no longer distinguish one man from another. Troilus fears his own emotions will do the same when the moment of meeting finally comes.
detail: The military simile is a formal device: an extended comparison that likens inner psychological disintegration to the disintegration of battle order. That Troilus reaches for a battlefield image on the eve of a love-meeting is characteristic of the play's fusing of the war plot and the love plot -- love and war are the same undisciplined energies here.

anchor_text: heart beats thicker than a feverous pulse
summary: 'Thicker' here means more rapidly and heavily -- a feverish pulse is fast and hard, the physical sign of a body overwhelmed. The comparison with 'vassalage at unawares encount'ring the eye of majesty' extends the idea: a servant who suddenly finds himself face-to-face with the king loses all composure, just as Troilus loses his powers at the thought of Cressida. 'Bestowing' (line 1576) means their outward function or service -- his faculties fail to perform their normal office.
detail: Elizabethan medical writing regularly described strong emotion in terms of a racing, thickened pulse; the heart was the seat of passions. 'Vassalage' -- the condition of a feudal vassal, bound in service and deference to a lord -- frames Troilus's love as submission to sovereign power, picking up the 'eye of majesty' image and projecting the lovers' relationship onto the social hierarchy of the court.

summary: Valuable paintings in Elizabethan and Jacobean houses were protected by a cloth curtain drawn across them; to reveal the painting a visitor would pull the curtain aside. anchor_text: rub on, and kiss the mistress How now, a kiss in fee-farm
summary: Pandarus puns on two meanings. 'Kiss the mistress' is a bowls term: when a bowl stops touching the jack (the target ball, called the 'mistress'), you have a perfect shot. 'Fee-farm' is a legal property tenure in which a tenant holds land in perpetuity for a fixed annual rent -- Pandarus is joking that the kiss is so prolonged it is like a permanent lease, not a temporary hold.
detail: The bowls sense of 'mistress' for the jack (target) is confirmed by Onions (s.v. 'mistress, n.' sense 5b). 'Rub on' is also bowls language: to 'rub' is to be deflected by a rough patch of grass, and 'rub on' is to proceed despite the obstacle. The whole sentence is a double track -- a literal description of the first kiss and a running sporting/legal commentary that reduces the lovers' intimacy to technique and transaction, which is Pandarus's characteristic mode.

anchor_text: The falcon as the tercel, for all the ducks i' th' river
summary: In falconry, the 'falcon' was the female bird (especially a female peregrine or merlin) and the 'tercel' (or tiercel) the male, which was smaller. 'The falcon as the tercel' means the female is a match for the male -- Cressida is Troilus's equal. 'For all the ducks' means they are matched against the whole river of ducks together: a sporting boast about what they can accomplish as a pair.
detail: Falconry was a prestige sport of the Elizabethan aristocracy, and its technical vocabulary was widely known. The female bird was prized as the better hunter (hence 'falcon' as the generic, prestigious term); giving the female the primary name was standard. Pandarus's use of the comparison is double-edged: it compliments both lovers, but it also, characteristically, reduces their first intimate meeting to a blood sport.

anchor_text: This is the monstruosity in love, lady, that the will is infinite, and the execution confin'd
summary: 'Monstruosity' means a monstrous paradox or absurdity (not simply a monster). Troilus is making a philosophical point: the desire ('will') is boundless but the act of fulfilling it is always limited in time and capacity -- 'the act a slave to limit.' He defines love's essential frustration: nothing you actually do can ever measure up to what you wanted to do.
detail: This is an antithesis (pairing opposites to define a concept), a standard tool of Elizabethan rhetoric. The paired contrasts -- 'will infinite / execution confin'd'; 'desire boundless / act a slave to limit' -- mirror each other exactly. The word 'monstruosity' (OED's earliest citation of the form) is Troilus's own coinage from 'monstrous': a thing that is impossible, against nature. The paradox will play out across the whole play: Troilus's infinite faith versus the finite world that will betray it.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1613

OED s.v. 'monstrosity' is a legitimate citation for word history; the claim that the Troilus passage is among the word's earliest appearances is consistent with what the OED records for this rare form.

'Monstruosity' as a monstrous paradox rather than a literal monster is the correct reading given the rhetorical context; identifying the paired antitheses (will/execution, desire/act) as formal Elizabethan antithesis is accurate.

anchor_text: I wish'd myself a man, Or that we women had men's privilege Of speaking first
summary: Elizabethan conduct literature held that a woman who declared love openly was shameless; it was the man's right and duty to woo first, and a woman who spoke first was seen as compromising her chastity and honour. Cressida recognises that the social rules have forced her into confessing before he has, which makes her vulnerability in this scene far more than emotional -- it is a transgression of the rules that governed female 'honour.'
detail: Juan Luis Vives's De institutione feminae christianae (1523, trans. 1529) and conduct books in the same tradition taught that a woman's honour was identical to her sexual reputation, and that outspokenness in love was a form of unchastity. Cressida's wish to be a man -- or for women to have men's social freedoms -- is a sharp, if quickly suppressed, protest against the double standard. Her 'I show more craft than love' (line 1679) will later be cited as evidence of her duplicity, by characters (and generations of critics) who ignore that she was constrained by exactly the conventions she names here.

sources.name: Vives, The Instruction of a Christian Woman
sources.citation: Juan Luis Vives, De institutione feminae christianae (1523), trans. Richard Hyrde as The Instruction of a Christian Woman (1529): a woman who 'shows herself' in love before she is wooed compromises her honour.

anchor_text: to be wise and love Exceeds man's might; that dwells with gods above
summary: The proverb that no one can be both wise and in love was a classical commonplace, attributed to various ancient writers, and remained a stock figure in Renaissance poetry and drama. Cressida uses it here both to flatter Troilus -- you must be either wise or in love with me -- and to acknowledge her own loss of reason in the scene.

anchor_text: True swains in love shall in the world to come Approve their truth by Troilus
summary: Troilus predicts that future faithful lovers will swear by his name as the ultimate standard of constancy: 'as true as Troilus' will become the most powerful oath a lover can take, topping all the usual similes (as true as steel, as the sun, as a turtledove). The speech is deeply ironic for an audience that knows the rest of the story: Troilus will not remain by Cressida's side, and the tradition makes his name not a byword for faithfulness but for the faith of a man who is eventually betrayed.
detail: The speech sets up the parallel speech that follows: Cressida too will declare that 'as false as Cressid' become the byword for female inconstancy. Together they compose the scene's most bitter dramatic irony: the lovers are literally predicting their future reputations, each claiming the opposite of how history will remember them. The audience, familiar with Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde and the popular 'false Cressida' tradition, would have heard both speeches as unwitting self-prophecy.

sources.name: Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde
sources.citation: Geoffrey Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385), the foundational English source for the story and its received moral -- the constancy of Troilus and the inconstancy of Criseyde.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1700

Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385) is the standard scholarly date and the foundational English source for the constancy/inconstancy tradition; the citation accurately represents scholarly consensus.

The reading of Troilus's speech as dramatic irony -- he is unwittingly predicting the exact opposite of his future reputation -- is the standard scholarly interpretation and is well-supported by the audience's knowledge of Chaucer and the 'false Cressida' tradition.

anchor_text: As true as steel, as plantage to the moon, As sun to day, as turtle to her mate, As iron to adamant
summary: Troilus strings together five classical similes for perfect constancy. 'Plantage' (plants, vegetation) were thought by Elizabethan natural philosophy to grow and wither with the moon. 'Turtle' is the turtledove, the proverbial bird of faithful love that supposedly died if its mate died. 'Adamant' (from Greek 'untameable') was the name for the hardest known substance -- sometimes identified with iron, sometimes with a mythical stone that draws iron to itself like a magnet.
detail: The accumulation parodies the conventions of love-poetry ('big compare' two lines earlier) even as Troilus means every word. The series is a formal copia (accumulation of synonymous expressions for one idea), a set-piece of Elizabethan rhetorical training. 'Plantage to the moon' draws on the belief, current in Pliny's Natural History (Book 18, on agriculture) and in popular almanac lore, that plants wax and wane with the moon's cycles. The turtledove (turtur) as the proverbial emblem of faithful, mournful love is a Renaissance commonplace (compare Shakespeare's own 'The Phoenix and the Turtle'). 'Adamant' (Greek, 'untameable') named the hardest known substance and also carried the sense of lodestone or magnet, whose attractive power was equated with constancy.

sources.name: Pliny / OED
sources.citation: Pliny, Natural History, Book 18 (plants governed by the moon's cycles); OED s.v. 'adamant' (the hardest substance; also a lodestone/magnet) and 'turtle' (the turtledove as emblem of constant love).

anchor_text: If I be false, or swerve a hair from truth

The audience familiar with the inherited tradition -- Chaucer's poem, Henryson's grim sequel where Cressida dies leprous -- knows she is predicting exactly what will happen. The speech is simultaneously a vow of faithfulness and an unwitting prophecy.

anchor_text: let all pitiful goers-between be call'd to the world's end after my name--call them all Pandars
summary: Pandarus here invents his own etymology: every future go-between who arranges illicit sex will be called a 'pander' (or 'pandar') from his name. English actually does use the word this way; Pandarus is right. The joke is that he says it with pride -- he is delighted at the prospect of immortality through brokerage. The play stages the origin of a real English common noun.
detail: The word 'pander' (to procure sexual access for another) descends through the proper name via exactly the path Pandarus announces here: Boccaccio's Pandaro, Chaucer's Pandarus, the Elizabethan common noun. OED records 'pander' as a common noun from the mid-sixteenth century, with the verb following shortly after. The speech is both comic and sinister: Pandarus is completing his own epitaph in a play that ends with him dying of disease and rejected. His pride in the name underscores the play's anatomy of what 'love' in this world actually consists of.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'pander, n.' (one who procures for another; a go-between in a sexual intrigue): first recorded as a common noun in English c. 1530-1550, derived from the proper name Pandarus via Chaucer.

sources.name: Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde
sources.citation: Geoffrey Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385), where the uncle Pandarus is the lovers' active go-between and from whose name the common noun derives.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1728

OED s.v. 'pander, n.' recording the common noun from c. 1530-1550, and Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde as the proximate English source of the name, are both confirmed real citations that support the etymology explained.

The etymology of 'pander' from the proper name Pandarus via Boccaccio and Chaucer to an Elizabethan common noun is historically accurate; the irony that Pandarus claims pride in a name that also marks his own epitaph in a play where he dies diseased is a sound and mainstream reading.

anchor_text: which bed, because it shall not speak of your pretty encounters, press it to death
summary: 'Press to death' (Latin peine forte et dure) was a real judicial torture in Elizabethan England: a prisoner who refused to plead guilty or not guilty at trial was pressed under increasingly heavy stones until they spoke or died. Pandarus's joke is that the bed, which has 'witnessed' the lovers' acts, should be subjected to this torture so that it cannot testify against them. The black humour is characteristic of the play's willingness to let legal violence lurk beneath even its most festive moments.
detail: Peine forte et dure was formally available in English law until 1772 and was occasionally inflicted. A defendant who 'stood mute' (refused to enter a plea) could be pressed: heavy weights were laid on a board placed on their chest, increased daily until they pleaded or died. Refusing to plead meant one's estate could not be forfeit -- hence some chose death. The torture's formal name appears in legal records throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Pandarus's joke turns the marriage-bed into a potential witness in a legal proceeding -- and the punishment for silence into something almost affectionate.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'press, v.' sense 20 (to press to death: the judicial torture of peine forte et dure, the pressing of a silent prisoner under weights).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1734

Peine forte et dure is confirmed as real English judicial practice, abolished by the Felony and Piracy Act 1772; OED s.v. 'press, v.' recording this judicial sense is a legitimate supporting citation.

Peine forte et dure as the referent for 'press it to death' is the standard scholarly gloss; the legal-proceeding framing (bed as potential witness) is the correct way to read the joke, and the historical detail about estate-forfeiture as a motive for enduring it is accurate.

anchor_text: for the service I have done
summary: Calchas, a Trojan priest who defected to the Greeks because his prophetic gift told him Troy would fall, now calls in the debt. The scene stages the coldness of the exchange economy underpinning the war: a daughter is a unit of political barter, not a person.
detail: Calchas is the same seer whose defection sets the lovers' separation in motion. His claim — that he abandoned home, name, and 'conveniences' (material comforts) for the Greek cause — is framed as a commercial transaction ('little benefit / Out of those many register'd in promise'). His daughter is the commodity he means to collect. The play's anatomy of value — whether Helen, Cressida, or heroic fame is 'worth' what men pay — begins here, in the Greek command tent, over a daughter's exchange price.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad; Chapman, Iliad (1598)
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 1.69-100 (Calchas the seer); George Chapman's English Iliad (1598), Shakespeare's probable proximate source for the Greek council scenes.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1739
Homer Iliad 1.69-100 genuinely covers Calchas as the Greek seer; Chapman's Seven Books of the Iliades (1598) is a real, correctly dated publication and a plausible proximate source.

The framing of Calchas's demand as a commercial transaction — a daughter as political barter, with explicit 'commodity of value' language — is well grounded in the text and mainstream scholarly reading of the play's anatomy of exchange value.

anchor_text: such a wrest in their affairs
summary: A 'wrest' is a small tuning-key used to tighten the strings of a lute or harp. Calchas means Antenor is so central to Troy's military planning that without him the whole operation goes slack and out of tune — the way a lute goes out of tune without the key to tighten it.

The tuning-key sense of 'wrest' is lexically sound and the metaphor — Antenor as the instrument that keeps Troy's negotiations in tune — is fully supported by the surrounding lines ('their negotiations all must slack / Wanting his manage').

anchor_text: strike off all service I have done In most accepted pain
summary: 'Strike off' means cancel or wipe out (like striking a debt from an account book). 'Most accepted pain' means labour that has been gratefully received — pains taken on the Greeks' behalf that they have acknowledged. Calchas is saying that getting Cressida back will settle the whole account.

anchor_text: Please it our general pass strangely by him
summary: Ulysses proposes a planned snub: the Greek commanders will walk past Achilles's tent as if he were a stranger — 'strangely' means in the manner of a stranger, with no recognition. The calculated social insult is meant to wound Achilles's pride where lectures and commands have failed.
detail: The scheme is a piece of cold political psychology: Ulysses understands that Achilles's sulking is sustained by the attention it gets, even the negative attention of general displeasure. To treat the greatest Greek warrior as invisible is the one thing he cannot endure. 'Unplausive eyes' (TLN 1782) means disapproving, withholding-of-applause eyes. Ulysses will arrive last so he can deliver the lesson in private while the wound is fresh.

sources.citation: Onions, C.T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'strangely': 'like a stranger; with the coldness of a stranger, distantly.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1778

The gloss is accurate: 'strangely' = in the manner of a stranger, and the scheme of calculated social insult to wound Achilles's pride where commands have failed is exactly what the scene enacts over the following hundred-plus lines.

anchor_text: Pride hath no other glass To show itself but pride
summary: A 'glass' is a mirror. Ulysses says that pride can only see itself reflected in other proud behaviour — fawning obedience ('supple knees') only feeds arrogance, because the proud man collects flatterers as his due. The only way to show a proud man what he really looks like is to out-pride him in return.
detail: The paradox is central to the scene: Ulysses's remedy for Achilles's pride is to manufacture rival pride in Ajax. 'Supple knees' — bending the knee obsequiously — are 'the proud man's fees,' the tribute that sustains his self-image. By withholding that tribute and redirecting it to the dim Ajax, Ulysses deprives Achilles of the mirror in which he has been admiring himself.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1786
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874) is a real work; 'glass' as mirror and 'supple' as fawning/obsequious are standard documented senses that support the summary.

The mirror-of-pride paradox is clearly stated in the text ('Pride hath no other glass / To show itself but pride') and the reading that 'supple knees' are the 'proud man's fees' — flatterers sustaining Achilles's self-image — is the mainstream interpretation.

anchor_text: does the cuckold scorn me
summary: A 'cuckold' is a man whose wife is unfaithful; the term was Elizabethan shorthand for a man whose honour has been stolen. Achilles taunts Menelaus with his condition — his wife Helen ran off with Paris, which is literally why the war is being fought. The sneer is bitter: the man for whom all of Greece is dying is contemptible to the war's greatest fighter.
detail: The scorn is doubly pointed: Menelaus has the standing to look down on Achilles for shirking, but Achilles immediately neutralises that standing by invoking his cuckolded status. 'Cuckold' (from the cuckoo, which lays its eggs in other birds' nests) carried a strong charge of masculine shame in Elizabethan culture — a man who could not control his wife's sexuality was stripped of honour. Achilles's contempt anticipates Thersites's reduction of the whole war to 'lechery': the war's moral premise is itself dishonoured.

The cuckold etymology from the cuckoo is standard and accurate, and the interpretation — Achilles neutralising Menelaus's moral standing by invoking his cuckolded status — is directly supported by the dramatic logic of the snub sequence.

anchor_text: men, like butterflies, Show not their mealy wings but to the summer
summary: Achilles reaches for a simile: butterflies only open their powdery ('mealy') wings in warm weather, and men who feed on another's success are just as fair-weather. 'Mealy' means floury or powdery — describing the scales on a butterfly's wings. The image captures the fair-weather friends who followed Achilles when he was rising and now pass by without a glance.

anchor_text: great Thetis' son
summary: Thetis was a sea-goddess (a Nereid) and the mother of Achilles. Ulysses greets him by his divine parentage as a mark of status — a common heroic formula — but the compliment is undercut by everything Ulysses is about to say.
detail: Ulysses's epithet 'Thetis' son' is polite heroic diction in the Homeric manner -- Achilles addressed by his divine parentage. In Homer, Thetis is the sea-goddess (a Nereid) who grieves her son's foreseen death and goes to Olympus to win him new armour (Iliad 1 and 18). The famous story that she dipped the infant Achilles in the Styx, holding him by the vulnerable heel, is not Homeric but comes from later tradition (Statius, Achilleid, c. AD 95); Homer's Achilles is not invulnerable. In a scene where Ulysses reads a book to wound Achilles's pride, the reverent epithet is the one apparent courtesy before the lesson begins.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 1.348-427 and 18.35-147 (Thetis, sea-goddess and mother of Achilles, grieves his coming death and seeks new armour); the Styx-dipping/heel story is post-Homeric (Statius, Achilleid).

anchor_text: man--how dearly ever parted, How much in having, or without or in--Cannot make boast to have that which he hath
summary: Dense compressed syntax: 'how dearly ever parted' means however generously endowed with gifts (to be 'parted' = to have portions or faculties distributed to you); 'how much in having, or without or in' means whether his wealth is external (possessions) or internal (qualities of mind). The point: no man can truly possess or know his own gifts until others reflect them back to him.

anchor_text: feels not what he owes, but by reflection
summary: 'Owes' here means 'owns' (Elizabethan usage). The heat-reflection image (TLN 1842-44) makes the point concrete: virtues warm others, who send the warmth back.

anchor_text: That most pure spirit of sense--behold itself, Not going from itself
summary: Achilles picks up Ulysses's point and extends it: even the eye — 'that most pure spirit of sense' — cannot see itself without a mirror, because it would have to leave itself to do so. 'Speculation' (TLN 1852) means sight or the faculty of seeing, not guessing. The eye can only see itself when it meets another eye, which reflects it back.
detail: The philosophical argument (self-knowledge requires an external mirror) is a Stoic and Aristotelian commonplace that Shakespeare has Achilles use correctly, which is why Ulysses says 'I do not strain at the position — it is familiar.' The radical move comes next (TLN 1855-66) when Ulysses shifts from 'this is obvious' to 'but the author draws a harder conclusion': not just self-knowledge but existence as a self depends on others' recognition. The eye-mirror analogy is Achilles's own; the moral drawn from it is Ulysses's.

sources.name: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics; Cicero, De Amicitia

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1849

'Speculation' as the faculty of sight (not guessing) is the correct Elizabethan sense, and the Aristotelian/Stoic commonplace of self-knowledge requiring an external mirror is a defensible source context; the annotation correctly notes Achilles extends Ulysses's point before Ulysses sharpens it.

anchor_text: Till he communicate his parts to others

anchor_text: like an arch, reverb'rate The voice again; or, like a gate of steel Fronting the sun

anchor_text: A very horse that has he knows not what
summary: Ulysses breaks into apparent admiration of Ajax, calling him 'a very horse' — a pure animal specimen of power and brute force — who doesn't know what he has. The compliment is a backhanded insult: horses have strength without wit, and the Greeks are about to praise and deploy Ajax's muscle while he remains obliviously flattered. The contrast with the intellectually sulking Achilles is deliberate.

anchor_text: Time hath, my lord, a wallet at his back, Wherein he puts alms for oblivion
summary: Time is pictured as a beggar or pilgrim with a satchel ('wallet') on his back, into which past deeds are dropped like charity ('alms') — forgotten the moment they are given. 'A great-siz'd monster of ingratitudes' describes oblivion itself: a vast creature that devours past good deeds as fast as they are performed. It is one of the play's most famous speeches, and its argument is that only present action keeps a reputation alive.
detail: Ulysses's 'wallet' speech (TLN 1888-1917) is the rhetorical centrepiece of the scene and among the most sustained passages of moral argument in Shakespeare's corpus. Its logic is Machiavellian in the technical sense: reputation is a political resource that must be continuously earned in public; hoarded past fame rots. The image of Time-as-beggar reverses the usual personification of Time as a tyrant or scythe-bearer, making him instead a scrounger who pockets what he is given and moves on. The 'rusty mail' (TLN 1895) — armour hanging unused and corroding in a monument — clinches the point: inaction is not preservation but decay.

The wallet-as-pilgrim-satchel image and its reversal of the conventional Time-as-tyrant personification are accurately described; the characterisation of the speech as Machiavellian in the technical sense (reputation as a political resource continuously earned) is defensible without overstating.

anchor_text: like a rusty mail In monumental mock'ry
summary: 'Mail' is chain armour — the interlocking metal rings of a medieval knight's coat. 'Monumental' means serving as a monument or memorial. Ulysses's image is of a suit of armour hung up as a trophy or memorial and left to rust: past deeds preserved in a monument are as useless and corroded as armour never used. Honour must be active and present, not entombed in a reliquary.

anchor_text: honour travels in a strait so narrow-- Where one but goes abreast
summary: A 'strait' is a narrow waterway or passage. Ulysses pictures the path of honour as so narrow that only one person can walk it at a time ('abreast' means side by side, which is impossible here). Anyone who steps aside or hesitates will be overrun by the crowd of rivals pressing from behind — 'like to an ent'red tide they all rush by.' The metaphor captures the competitive ruthlessness of military fame.

anchor_text: Time is like a fashionable host, That slightly shakes his parting guest by th' hand
summary: The third and most vivid of Ulysses's Time images: a fashionable host who gives a departing guest a limp, perfunctory handshake ('slightly' = cursorily, without warmth), then turns with arms outstretched and a wide smile to greet the new arrival. Welcome smiles; farewell sighs. The past is always the guest being ushered out; the present is always the guest being embraced.

anchor_text: One touch of nature makes the whole world kin
summary: Frequently misquoted as a warm sentiment about human kinship, this line in context means the opposite: the one 'touch of nature' (natural human tendency) that unites everyone is the weakness of preferring the new and flashy over the proven and old. 'Gawds' (TLN 1919) are gaudy trinkets or baubles. The aphorism is Ulysses's wry observation that the crowd's rush to worship Ajax is driven by the universal appetite for novelty.
detail: The apparent generosity of the line ('the whole world kin') is a Ulyssean feint. The 'nature' he means is not noble but vulgar: the impulse to value 'new-born gawds' — cheap new things, even when they are 'moulded of things past' — and to give 'dust that is a little gilt / More laud than gilt o'er-dusted.' A new gold-painted object catches more praise than an old gold one covered in the dust of use. This is the mechanism that is elevating the dull Ajax over the brilliant Achilles. The quotation became famous in later centuries as an unironic statement of brotherhood, which is precisely the opposite of Shakespeare's meaning here.

anchor_text: Made emulous missions 'mongst the gods themselves, And drave great Mars to faction
summary: Ulysses claims that Achilles's past deeds were so great they provoked jealous rivalry ('emulous missions') even among the Olympian gods, and drew Mars — the god of war — into taking sides ('faction'). This references the Iliad's divine machinery, in which the gods actively sided with Greek or Trojan warriors and competed with one another in supporting their favorites on the battlefield.

anchor_text: you are in love With one of Priam's daughters
summary: The play gives Achilles a secret attachment to Polyxena, a daughter of the Trojan king Priam, which explains his refusal to fight: killing Trojans kills his own cause. This detail comes not from Homer's Iliad but from later medieval Troy legend (Chaucer, Caxton), where Achilles's love for Polyxena is the trap that leads to his death. Shakespeare uses it here to give Achilles a private motive the public cannot understand.
detail: In Homer, Achilles withdraws because of his quarrel with Agamemnon over the captive girl Briseis — wounded honour, not enemy love. The Polyxena story grows in the later medieval tradition: in some versions Achilles is lured to a temple and shot there by Paris at Polyxena's behest, after his love for her has softened his resistance. Ulysses's line 'To throw down Hector than Polyxena' (TLN 1954) makes the substitution explicit. The detail is evidence of Shakespeare's multi-source engagement with the Troy tradition.

sources.name: Caxton, Recuyell of the Histories of Troye (1474)
sources.citation: William Caxton's Recuyell of the Histories of Troye (1474), the first book printed in English, drawing on Raoul Lefevre's French compilation — the primary English-language Troy source alongside Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1938

anchor_text: Knows almost every grain of Plutus' gold
summary: Plutus (sometimes confused with Pluto, god of the underworld) was the classical god of wealth. Ulysses is saying that a watchful state knows everything — even the smallest details, like individual grains in Plutus's treasure — and that private thoughts ('dumb cradles') are almost as legible as spoken ones. The Greeks know about Achilles's Trojan love affair despite his secrecy.

sources.name: Hesiod, Theogony; Aristophanes, Plutus
sources.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 969-971 (Plutus, son of Demeter, the god of wealth); Aristophanes, Plutus (388 BCE; the god of riches as a blind figure). The name was a standard Renaissance shorthand for accumulated treasure.

anchor_text: I as your lover speak. The fool slides o'er the ice that you should break
summary: 'Lover' here means friend and well-wisher (the older sense), not romantic partner. Ulysses ends his lecture by claiming he speaks from goodwill, not malice. The closing couplet means: the fool (Ajax) skates over the thin ice of a challenge that Achilles ought to have broken through himself. Ajax gets the glory of facing Hector while Achilles sits idle.

anchor_text: A woman impudent and mannish grown Is not more loath'd than an effeminate man In time of action
summary: Patroclus repeats the camp gossip against himself and Achilles: a woman who acts like a man is despised, but a man who acts like a woman (is 'effeminate') during wartime is more despised still. He is reporting the social pressure on Achilles — that their closeness is read by others as making Achilles soft and unwilling to fight.
detail: This is one of the play's most pointed passages about the Achilles-Patroclus relationship. Patroclus himself voices the misogynistic double standard that condemns femininity in war-time, and also identifies himself as part of what the camp takes to be feminising Achilles. The lines do not confirm or deny the sexual nature of the bond — they report how the Greeks read it. Thersites, the play's most brutal voice, calls Patroclus Achilles's 'masculine whore' elsewhere (5.1); here Patroclus himself uses the camp's gendered vocabulary to urge Achilles back to the field. The note should present this as the play's staging of a social pressure, not an endorsement of the slurs.

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 16.1-100 (Patroclus urges Achilles to let him go to battle); Plato, Symposium 179e-180a (Phaedrus debates the nature of the Achilles-Patroclus bond and their relative heroism). These are the ancient sources in which the relationship is already contested.

anchor_text: the weak wanton Cupid Shall from your neck unloose his amorous fold
summary: Patroclus pictures Cupid (the god of erotic desire) clasped around Achilles's neck like an infant clinging to its parent — 'wanton' meaning both unruly and sexually playful. Once Achilles is roused to action, love's hold will fall away like a dew-drop shaken from a lion's mane: something clinging to a great beast, dismissed by a single shake.

anchor_text: My fame is shrewdly gor'd
summary: 'Shrewdly' means severely or grievously (not cleverly). 'Gor'd' means pierced or wounded — as a bull gores with its horns. Achilles recognises that his reputation has been badly wounded: Ajax is about to fight Hector while Achilles sits idle, and the wound to his fame is as real as a physical injury.
