anchor_text: Omission to do what is necessary Seals a commission to a blank of danger
summary: A 'commission' is an official warrant or order; a 'blank' is a document with the key information left unfilled, to be filled in later. Patroclus means: when you fail to do what is required, you sign over a blank commission to danger — you leave it free to write in whatever penalty it likes. Failing to act is not neutral; it gives danger open-ended authority over you.

anchor_text: I have a woman's longing, An appetite that I am sick withal, To see great Hector in his weeds of peace
summary: Achilles uses the gendered phrase 'a woman's longing' to mean an overwhelming, almost physical craving — the sort of irrational desire contemporary culture associated with pregnancy cravings or women's appetites. 'Weeds of peace' means civilian clothing (a 'weed' is any garment). Achilles wants to see his enemy in peacetime dress, not armour — out of genuine fascination, not enmity.
detail: The speech is revealing: Achilles is drawn to Hector by something that crosses military rivalry into something more intimate. He wants to see him, talk to him, look his fill. The desire to invite Hector to his tent unarmed — 'to see us here unarm'd' — sets up the later ambush in which he will have the unarmed Hector surrounded and killed. The innocence of this longing in 3.3 makes the betrayal in 5.8 the sharper.

anchor_text: Ajax goes up and down the field asking for himself
summary: Thersites's joke: Ajax is so puffed up with his own importance (and so dazed by the Greeks' flattery) that he wanders the camp as if looking for himself — as if he has forgotten where he is, or as if 'Ajax' is a title rather than a person. It mocks Ajax's self-importance and his mental vacancy at the same time.

anchor_text: stalks up and down like a peacock--a stride and a stand; ruminaies like an hostess that hath no arithmetic but her brain
summary: Thersites piles up animal and social insults. The peacock struts and stops — all display, no movement. 'Ruminates' (chews the cud — an animal word) is the next insult: Ajax thinks slowly, as an innkeeper ('hostess') who has no written accounts and must count on her fingers does her arithmetic. The 'politic regard' (TLN 2001) — the expression of shrewd calculation — is pure performance, like fire locked in flint that produces no heat without striking.

anchor_text: He's grown a very land fish, languageless, a monster
summary: A 'land-fish' is Thersites's coinage for a creature out of its element — a fish on land is mute, flapping, and grotesque. Ajax has grown so lost in his own self-importance that he cannot speak intelligibly and has become monstrous. 'A plague of opinion!' immediately before means: look what public flattery does to a man — it turns him into a monster.

anchor_text: A plague of opinion! A man may wear it on both sides, like leather jerkin
summary: 'Opinion' means reputation, public esteem — what others think of you. A leather jerkin (a sleeveless jacket) can be worn reversed to look new again. Thersites means that reputation is reversible and superficial: a man can wear it either way, and neither way says anything true about him. The line deflates the whole scene's elaborate rhetoric about honour and fame.

anchor_text: he wears his tongue in's arms
summary: Ajax does not speak — he fights. His communication is in his weapons ('arms'), not his words ('tongue'). The pun on 'arms' (weapons / coat of arms / the limbs of the body) is typical of Thersites's compressed mockery. Ajax's eloquence is purely physical.

anchor_text: unless the fiddler Apollo get his sinews to make catlings on
summary: Apollo was the Olympian god of music, pictured with a lyre. 'Catlings' (also 'catgut') are the gut strings of stringed instruments, made from animal intestines. Thersites's savage joke: the only music that will come out of the brainless Ajax after Hector kills him is if Apollo salvages his tendons to string a lute. It reduces a hero to raw material.

anchor_text: Let me carry another to his horse; for that's the more capable creature
summary: 'Capable' means intelligent, comprehending. Thersites says Ajax's horse is cleverer than Ajax — the standard insult of comparing a man unfavorably to his own animal. anchor_text: My mind is troubled, like a fountain stirr'd; And I myself see not the bottom of it
summary: Achilles closes the scene with a simile of self-opacity: a stirred fountain is murky; you cannot see its bottom until it settles. He cannot understand his own mind — the Polyxena attachment, the professional pride, the admiration for Hector, the tactical calculation all swirl together without settling into clarity. It is one of the play's rare moments of authentic introspection from Achilles.

anchor_text: that I might water an ass at it. I had rather be a tick in a sheep than such a valiant ignorance
summary: Thersites ends the scene with two insults, one for Achilles and one for Ajax. Achilles's murky, troubled mind is only good enough to water a donkey — the lowest possible use of a fountain. 'Valiant ignorance' is Thersites's epitaph for Ajax: brave and empty, a tick in a sheep being a parasite so low that even Thersites prefers it to the pretensions of heroic stupidity.

anchor_text: By Jove, I'll play the hunter for thy life / With all my force, pursuit, and policy
summary: Diomedes casts future combat as a hunt: Aeneas will be the prey and Diomedes the pursuing hunter. 'Policy' here means calculated strategy, not just general policy. The oath 'By Jove' — Jupiter, king of the gods — is the standard strong oath in this Troy-world.
detail: The hunting metaphor for mortal combat is commonplace in Homer and the epic tradition (the hero 'stalks' his enemy like a lion after deer, e.g. Iliad 22.188-193). Diomedes's use of it makes the coming battle sound like sport, which suits the play's tone of deflating martial honour into appetite. 'Policy' carries the Machiavellian sense of cunning stratagem — the word had recently acquired that edge in Elizabethan political writing — making Diomedes sound less like a chivalric warrior than a calculating operator. 'By Jove' (Jupiter, the king of Olympus) is the Greeks' habitual oath in this play, as it is in Homer.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 22.188-193 (Achilles hunts Hector round the walls of Troy — the epic model for this kind of hunt-as-combat figure). Compare Chapman's Iliad (1598).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2070

Iliad 22.188-193 does depict the hunt-like chase of Hector around Troy's walls (a hound-and-fawn simile), supporting the claim that it models hunt-as-combat; Schmidt s.v. 'policy' confirmed to include 'cunning, stratagem' as a distinct definition.

Diomedes's 'play the hunter for thy life' is straightforwardly a hunt metaphor for combat and the text supports it; calling 'policy' Machiavellian is mainstream and non-anachronistic for an Elizabethan play, and the annotation does not over-claim the Homer parallel as a direct source.

anchor_text: by Anchises' life, / Welcome indeed! By Venus' hand I swear
summary: Aeneas swears by two things that define who he is: his mortal father Anchises, whom he famously carried out of burning Troy on his back, and Venus, the goddess who is his divine mother. The double oath signals that the Troy-story is layered with background the audience is expected to know.
detail: In Virgil's Aeneid (2.707-729) Aeneas rescues the helpless Anchises on his shoulders as Troy falls — the defining image of Trojan piety and filial devotion. Venus is Aeneas's immortal mother by Anchises (Iliad 5.247-248; Virgil, Aeneid 1.314-321), and it was through her favour that Aeneas survived the war to found the Roman line. By invoking both in a single breath Aeneas grounds his friendly-enemy greeting in the very persons who make him who he is — the son of a mortal and a goddess, survivor of Troy's ruin, now brokering its last exchanges. The audience who knew the Aeneid's ending (Troy falls, Aeneas escapes, Rome rises) would feel the weight of that future under this cheerful midnight street-greeting.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 2.707-729 (Aeneas carries Anchises from Troy); 1.314-321 (Venus acknowledges Aeneas as her son).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2074

Aeneid 2.707-729 (Aeneas carries Anchises) is confirmed; Iliad 5.247-248 identifies Aphrodite as Aeneas's mother and is confirmed; Aeneid 1.314-321 is imprecise (Venus is disguised and does not explicitly acknowledge Aeneas as her son in those exact lines, doing so only implicitly just after), but the claim that Venus is Aeneas's immortal mother is fully supported by Book 1 and Iliad 5, so the core assertion is not fabricated.

Aeneas does swear by both Anchises and Venus in direct succession at TLN 2074-2075, and the gloss correctly identifies them as his mortal father and divine mother without over-reading; the note about the audience's awareness of Aeneas's future (Trojan survivor, Rome's founder) is a defensible interpretive frame for this play's retrospective irony.

anchor_text: most despiteful'st gentle greeting, / The noblest hateful love
summary: Paris notes that the exchange between Aeneas and Diomedes is built on clashing opposites: courteous in its surface form yet venomous at the core. The figure — joining words that contradict each other ('despiteful gentle,' 'noblest hateful love') — is called oxymoron, and it captures something the whole play understands about war: enemies can admire and delight in one another precisely because they intend to kill each other.
detail: Oxymoron (Greek: 'sharp-dull') pairs logically incompatible terms to express a paradoxical emotional truth. Romeo uses the device extravagantly to describe love ('O brawling love, O loving hate,' 1.1), but there it is adolescent posturing; here it describes an actual social transaction — two soldiers who genuinely respect, and genuinely mean to kill, each other. The scene makes the chivalric truce-greeting into a form of foreplay for violence. 'Despiteful' means contemptuous or malicious (Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'despiteful').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2085

Paris's doubled oxymorons ('despiteful'st gentle,' 'noblest hateful love') are exactly what the text says at TLN 2085-2086, and the identification of the figure as oxymoron with a brief Romeo comparison is sound without constituting a structural over-reading.

anchor_text: to render him, / For the enfreed Antenor, the fair Cressid
summary: Diomedes has been sent to exchange Cressida for the Trojan commander Antenor, who is being held prisoner by the Greeks. 'Enfreed' means freed or ransomed. This swap — a man of military value traded for a woman — is the pivot on which the love plot breaks: Troilus must hand over Cressida and she must enter the Greek camp alone.
detail: The exchange of prisoners under truce was a standard institution in ancient and medieval warfare; a captive commander like Antenor had concrete strategic worth (he knows Troy's defences and councils), while Cressida is sent as a courtesy to her father Calchas who has defected to the Greeks and requested her. The exchange is impersonal and cold — nobody asks Cressida. Antenor, present in this scene but silent, acquired a later legend (found in medieval chronicles, including Caxton's Recuyell) of being one of the Trojans who actually betrayed Troy to the Greeks; if Shakespeare's audience knew that tradition, his silent presence here, worth Cressida's happiness, carries irony.

The mechanics of the exchange (Cressida for Antenor) are stated plainly in the text, and the annotation's note about Antenor's later legendary treachery is correctly flagged as a tradition the audience 'may' have known rather than as the play's meaning; no overreach.

anchor_text: Not making any scruple of her soilure, / With such a hell of pain and world of charge
summary: Diomedes says Menelaus is fighting (at 'a hell of pain and world of charge' — enormous cost in suffering and money) without any hesitation over Helen's 'soilure.' Soilure means defilement or dishonour — the disgrace of having been another man's mistress. 'Scruple' is a tiny unit of weight, meaning the slightest doubt. Diomedes is being brutally cynical: Menelaus should be too ashamed to fight for a woman publicly known to have gone to another man's bed.

anchor_text: you do as chapmen do, / Dispraise the thing that you desire to buy
summary: Paris compares Diomedes to a 'chapman' — an itinerant merchant or trader — who runs down the price of what he actually wants to buy so the seller will drop the asking price. Paris is accusing Diomedes of secretly wanting Helen and pretending to despise her to give himself negotiating cover. The metaphor also reduces Helen to a commodity being appraised for purchase.
detail: A 'chapman' (OED s.v. 'chapman, n.': from Old English ceapman, 'a merchant, a peddler') was a common travelling trader who haggled; 'cheap' as in Cheapside (London's main market street) shares the same root. Paris's self-deflating reply — 'we in silence hold this virtue well: / We'll not commend what we intend to sell' — makes Troy equally a seller trying to hide the defects of its own stock (Helen). The whole exchange about Helen thus becomes a market transaction, anticipating Troilus's question 'What's aught but as 'tis valued?' (2.2) and the play's broader preoccupation with worth, price, and false valuation. Note that Paris is also implicitly condemning himself: he is advertising a woman he intends to keep.

anchor_text: Beshrew the witch! with venomous wights she stays
summary: 'Beshrew' is a mild imprecation meaning 'curse' or 'a plague on.' Troilus curses Night as a witch who lingers tormentingly long 'with venomous wights' (evil or harmful creatures) but then flies away from lovers with 'wings more momentary-swift than thought' — the opposite of what lovers want.
detail: The word 'beshrew' (sometimes 'shrew' alone) is a weakened curse, usually implying irritation rather than genuine malice — its force was already fading in the period; cf. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'beshrew.' 'Wights' is an archaic noun for persons or creatures, often with a sinister coloring in this period. Troilus's compressed rhetoric here — Night as witch who both stays and flees, but each at the wrong time and for the wrong people — is an example of paradox: night is tediously slow for those suffering ('as tediously as hell') and impossibly swift for those in love. Chaucer's Troilus similarly laments the dawn, and the 'alba' (dawn-song of parting lovers) is the tradition behind this speech.

The gloss on 'beshrew' (mild imprecation), 'wights' (creatures/persons), and the alba-paradox structure (night too slow for the suffering, too swift for lovers) is accurate and mainstream.

anchor_text: O foolish Cressid! I might have still held off, And then you would have tarried.
summary: Cressida articulates what she said explicitly in 1.2: that a woman who withholds herself keeps a man's desire alive, while giving in causes him to leave. She is not being cynical here but anxious — she gave up that tactical position for love, and now Troilus is indeed leaving at first light.
detail: This two-line aside is a small window into the play's unsettling gender dynamics. Earlier, Cressida told her uncle plainly that 'Women are angels, wooing; things won are done' (1.2.312-313) — she knows exactly the game and its rules. Now she voices regret not that she yielded, but that yielding cost her the one instrument of power she had: the power of refusal. The play frames this as personal failure ('O foolish Cressid!'), but the system that gives a woman no leverage except delay is the problem the line inadvertently exposes. This connects to the 'false Cressid' tradition: readers trained on Henryson and Chaucer expect her inconstancy; here she is anxious about his.

sources.name: Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde
sources.citation: Geoffrey Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385), Book III, stanzas 176-189 (the night of union and the reluctant dawn-parting).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2157

The cross-reference to Cressida's 1.2 speech ('Women are angels, wooing; things won are done') is correct, and reading this aside as anxious regret rather than cynicism is well-supported by tone and text; the gender-dynamics framing is a mainstream critical reading, not an overreach.

anchor_text: How go maidenheads? Here, you maid! Where's my cousin Cressid?
summary: Pandarus greets the situation with a coarse joke: 'How go maidenheads?' means 'how is the market in virginity?' — he already knows Cressida has lost hers. 'You maid' then mocks the servant with the same pun, since Cressida is clearly no longer a maid (virgin). His calling out for Cressida as if he doesn't know where she is completes the pretense.
detail: 'Maidenhead' is consistently used in the period for virginity: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'maidenhead' (virginity, the hymen). Pandarus had engineered the entire night. His 'How go maidenheads?' turns a commodity question ('how's trade?') into a sexual one — his usual register. The speech exemplifies why his name became the English word 'pander': he reduces his niece's sexuality to a transaction and then mocks her for it. His follow-up call for 'my cousin Cressid' while Troilus is still visibly present is comic-sinister, and Cressida's 'A pestilence on him! Now will he be mocking' anticipates exactly this.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (2nd ed., 1919), s.v. 'maidenhead' (virginity).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2163

'Maidenhead' as virginity is unambiguous in the period, and Pandarus's commodity-market pun followed by mock-ignorance of where Cressida is reads precisely as the text presents it; no overreach.

anchor_text: you'll be so true to him to be false to him
summary: Aeneas presses Pandarus with a knotted paradox: you will be so loyal to Troilus (by denying he is here) that you will actually harm him — because Troilus urgently needs to hear what Aeneas brings. Being 'true' (loyal to the pretense) becomes a form of being 'false' (betraying his real interest).
detail: The two senses of 'true/false' pivot sharply: 'true' as keeping a secret versus 'true' as genuinely serving someone's good. The paradox is structurally identical to the larger plot: Troy's council is 'true' to honor in keeping Helen, but that truth is destroying them. Aeneas's line is also witty in context — Pandarus has just said he 'knew not' Troilus was there, a transparent lie. The wordplay on truth and deception is a thread woven through the whole play, from the Prologue's 'beginning in the middle' to Cressida's final vow.

'Ere the first sacrifice' means before the morning religious rites, so the transfer must happen at once. This is the plot-turn that tears the lovers apart.

anchor_text: How my achievements mock me!
summary: Troilus's single aside is the emotional gut-punch of the scene: his 'achievement' — finally winning Cressida's love after long courtship — is being undone at the very moment it was completed. The word 'achievement' carried a heraldic sense (a trophy earned), making the mockery sharper: the prize turns to nothing in his hands.
detail: In heraldry an 'achievement' is a full display of a coat of arms, particularly the commemorative tablet hung at a funeral — something won, then displayed in death. The irony is layered: Troilus 'achieved' what he pursued, and now it mocks him, as if the trophy is being instantly taken back. The compressed bitterness of a single six-word line, set among the brisk political prose of Aeneas's news, is a calculated effect — the contrast of public necessity and private devastation crystallised into one rhetorical ejaculation. Troilus's rapid recovery — 'I will go meet them' — shows the play's interest in men performing composure while their inner life breaks.

anchor_text: Make Cressid's name the very crown of falsehood, If ever she leave Troilus
summary: Cressida swears that if she ever abandons Troilus, let her name become the supreme example of a faithless woman. The audience watching in 1602 already knew the tradition: 'as false as Cressid' was a standing proverb. Her oath is written to be read as tragic irony — she is swearing by the very fate she cannot escape.
detail: The 'false Cressid' tradition had hardened for two centuries before this play, through Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde, Henryson's Testament of Cresseid (printed in Thynne's Chaucer, 1532, where she ends as a leprous beggar), Lydgate, and popular proverbial usage. Shakespeare's play is aware of its own sources: in 3.2 Troilus swears 'as true as Troilus' and Pandarus jokingly inaugurates all go-betweens in his name. Cressida's oath here is the formal completion of that self-conscious trio. The play stages the tradition while also forcing the audience to see that the 'false woman' verdict erases context: she is being traded without consent to a camp of hostile men, and the men who barter her — Troilus included — will escape all blame. Cressida's vow of absolute constancy ('time, force, and death / Do to this body what extremes you can') is real in this moment; the play withholds easy condemnation.

sources.citation: Robert Henryson, The Testament of Cresseid (printed in William Thynne's edition of Chaucer, 1532; prob. composed c. 1490), which supplied the ending — Cresseid abandoned, diseased, dying — that cemented her proverbial 'falsehood.'

The 'false Cressid' proverbial tradition via Chaucer and Henryson, the self-conscious trio of true-Troilus/false-Cressid/pander-Pandarus inaugurated in 3.2, and the reading of her oath as tragic irony are all standard and well-supported; the note that the play withholds easy condemnation is a defensible mainstream critical position.

anchor_text: her delivery to this valiant Greek
summary: Cressida is spoken of as goods to be 'delivered' — handed over from one party to another — in exchange for the Trojan prisoner Antenor. The commercial word strips her of agency: she has no say in the transaction and no voice in this scene at all.
detail: The language of 'delivery' was used for the transfer of property or prisoners of war under formal agreements. That Paris applies it to his brother's lover, in Troilus's hearing, without apparent discomfort, signals how the play frames the exchange: the men on both sides treat Cressida as an asset to be transferred, not a person with standing. The play then blames her for the choices she makes in the Greek camp friendless and without protection — the double standard the card cressida-and-the-false-woman identifies. Paris's phrase 'this valiant Greek' (Diomedes) is lightly ironic given that Diomedes's 'valour' will shortly consist in winning another man's lover.

anchor_text: Think it an altar, and thy brother Troilus A priest, there off'ring to it his own heart
summary: Troilus uses an extended metaphor: handing Cressida to the Greek is like a priest placing a sacrifice on an altar — and the thing being sacrificed is his own heart. The image casts the transfer as a religious act of self-destruction rather than a mere exchange.
detail: The comparison — Troilus as priest, the handing-over as a blood sacrifice — does several things at once. It elevates the moment to tragic ritual while also exposing its futility: the sacrifice accomplishes nothing, and Troilus is both priest and victim. The metaphor is also conspicuously private. Paris and the assembled lords hear it, but it is Troilus speaking to himself as much as to them; his public performance of the exchange will look nothing like his inner experience of it. The image of self-immolation suits the play's analysis of Troilus as a man whose idealism is so absolute it can only end in devastation. Classical sacrifice at an altar was a familiar image from the Troy tradition (Homeric ritual; Ovid, Metamorphoses), making the figure doubly resonant in this context.

anchor_text: I know what 'tis to love, And would, as I shall pity, I could help
summary: Paris claims he understands love and pities Troilus but cannot help him. The irony is acute: Paris's own love affair — taking Helen from her Greek husband — is the single cause of the war that has made this forced separation necessary.
detail: Paris's three-line speech closes the scene with a moment of pointed dramatic irony. He is the character most responsible for the situation Troilus now suffers: without the Judgement of Paris and the abduction of Helen, there would be no war, no prisoner exchange, and no separation. That Paris presents himself as a sympathetic fellow-sufferer — 'I know what 'tis to love' — while doing nothing to prevent the transfer is both psychologically true to his character (he is comfortable in his luxury while others die for his choice) and one of the play's sharpest structural ironies. The Trojan council (Act 2 Scene 2) already showed that even Hector's reasoned arguments could not move the Trojans to return Helen; Paris's passivity here is the same complicity in a smaller key.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 3 (Paris's abduction of Helen and the war's cause); compare Ovid, Heroides 16 (Paris's letter to Helen justifying the abduction).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2256

Iliad 3 is the primary book depicting Paris, Helen, and Menelaus's duel — correctly cited as the source for Paris's role as cause of the war — and Heroides 16 is genuinely Paris's epistolary justification of the abduction of Helen.

The dramatic irony that Paris — whose love affair and abduction of Helen caused the war making this forced exchange necessary — offers helpless sympathy is structurally clear and a standard scholarly observation.

anchor_text: The grief is fine, full, perfect, that I taste
summary: 'Fine' here means pure or refined — at its highest intensity — not merely satisfactory. Cressida is saying her grief is not watered down or partial but absolute and unmixed, which is why she cannot simply moderate it as Pandarus urges.
detail: The word runs through a triad ('fine, full, perfect') that escalates from quality to quantity to completion. 'Violenteth' in the next line is a Shakespeare coinage — he turns the adjective 'violent' into a verb, meaning 'rages' or 'exerts violent force.' The passage is characteristic of the play's tendency to push ordinary language to its syntactic limits.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'fine' (adj., sense 3: pure, refined, of the highest quality) and s.v. 'violent' (used as verb).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2261

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real and standard reference; the senses cited (fine = pure/refined; violent used as a verb) are well-attested in the lexicon and uncontroversial in Shakespeare scholarship.

'Fine' meaning pure or refined is well-attested in early modern English, the triad fine/full/perfect does escalate as described, and 'violenteth' as a Shakespearean verbal coinage is observable in the text ('And violenteth in a sense as strong').

anchor_text: I love thee in so strain'd a purity
summary: 'Strain'd' means stretched or pulled taut to its limit — pressed to the utmost degree of tension. Troilus is saying his love is so extreme, so refined to its pure essence, that the gods themselves are made angry by it, as if love this intense is an affront to heaven.
detail: The logic draws on a classical commonplace that the gods envy mortal happiness — a belief Cressida immediately invokes ('Have the gods envy?'). The verb 'strain' carries a physical sense of something stretched past its natural limit, which quietly anticipates the violent sundering about to happen: a bond strained this hard must break. Shakespeare uses 'strained' for things at their uttermost point in several plays (cf. Merchant of Venice 4.1, 'The quality of mercy is not strained').

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'strained' (extended to the utmost, stretched).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2281

Onions's A Shakespeare Glossary is real and covers 'strained' in the sense of stretched to the utmost; the cross-reference to Merchant of Venice 4.1 ('The quality of mercy is not strained') is a genuine parallel.

The core gloss of 'strain'd' as stretched or taut is sound, but the cross-reference to Merchant of Venice 4.1 ('The quality of mercy is not strained') actually argues the opposite meaning — there 'strained' means forced or compelled, not stretched to maximum intensity — so the parallel invoked is a false friend that may mislead rather than illuminate.

anchor_text: Have the gods envy?
summary: The idea that the gods envy or resent exceptional human happiness and destroy it is a recurring thought in Greek literature — 'divine jealousy' (phthonos) toward mortals who enjoy too much. Here Cressida immediately seizes on Troilus's claim that his love is so intense the gods are angered by it, as if to say: yes, that is exactly what the gods do to beautiful things.
detail: Herodotus throughout his Histories records the Greek conviction that divinity is always malign toward outstanding human fortune (Herodotus, Histories 1.32: the whole of human life is vicissitude, for the divinity is jealous — phthoneros). Troilus's framing — that the gods, angry at the purity of his love, take Cressida from him — is a way of absolving himself of the loss: it is the gods' fault, not his. Pandarus's complacent 'Ay, ay, ay; 'tis too plain a case' collapses any tragic dignity, reducing divine jealousy to drawing-room gossip.

sources.name: Herodotus, Histories
sources.citation: Herodotus, Histories 1.32 (Solon to Croesus on the phthonos — divine jealousy — that dogs exceptional human happiness).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2285

Herodotus 1.32 does contain Solon's speech to Croesus articulating the concept of divine phthonos (jealousy/envy toward exceptional human happiness), confirmed by multiple classical scholarship sources.

The concept of divine phthonos toward exceptional human fortune is genuinely pervasive in Greek thought and Herodotus 1.32 (Solon to Croesus) is the canonical locus; the reading that Troilus uses this to self-absolve is a mainstream interpretive observation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: injury of chance / Puts back leave-taking, justles roughly by
summary: Troilus piles up a rapid sequence of violent actions — justles, beguiles, prevents, strangles — all committed by 'chance' as if it were a rude, shoving intruder. This is personification: abstract bad fortune is turned into a thug who physically pushes the lovers apart before they can even say goodbye properly.
detail: 'Rejoinure' (TLN 2295) is rare, meaning the act of rejoining or clasping together again. 'Embrasures' means embraces — a Shakespearean spelling variant that also carries an architectural sense (the notched openings of a castle wall), lending a faint image of fortification to their locked hold on each other. The speech builds by accumulation, each new verb adding another injury, to dramatise the speed with which the separation is imposed. The climax — 'a single famish'd kiss / Distasted with the salt of broken tears' (2306-7) — reverses the erotic economy of the night before, where thousand-sigh bargaining was possible.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'rejoindure' (the act of joining again; a Shakespearean coinage), and s.v. 'embrasure' (an embrace).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2292
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is cited for 'rejoindure' and 'embrasure,' both attested Shakespearean usages the lexicon covers; the source is real and appropriate for archaic-vocab annotation.

The personification of Chance as a physical intruder, the identification of rhetorical accumulation, and the readings of 'rejoindure' and 'embrasures' are all defensible; the architectural resonance of 'embrasures' is offered as a faint suggestion rather than a primary claim, which is appropriately hedged.

anchor_text: Injurious time now with a robber's haste / Crams his rich thievery up
summary: Time is personified as a hasty thief who stuffs stolen goods into a bag and bolts. The image recurs in Ulysses's speech on fame in Act 3, where 'Time hath, my lord, a wallet at his back / Wherein he puts alms for oblivion' (3.3). Here Time steals their farewell kisses as he stole their love.
detail: The play's meditation on time and value — what things are worth, how quickly glory is consumed, how novelty displaces the fixed — finds its most intimate expression here, where the grandly abstract Time-as-thief metaphor from the public world of war and reputation invades the private world of lovers' parting. The wallet/bag image links the two passages: Ulysses's public 'wallet of oblivion' and Troilus's private bag of stolen kisses are both anatomies of how time devours what it was given to preserve. 'Fumbles up into a loose adieu' (2305) captures the thief's careless haste — the exact opposite of the lovers' careful thousand-sigh economy.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'cram' (to stuff hastily), and cross-reference to Troilus 3.3 on time's wallet.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2301

Onions is cited for 'cram' and the cross-reference to 3.3; Ulysses's 'Time hath, my lord, a wallet at his back / Wherein he puts alms for oblivion' is a genuine passage from Troilus and Cressida 3.3, accurately described.
The link to Ulysses's time-wallet speech in 3.3 is a genuine and well-noted intertextual echo within the play, and the thief/bag imagery analysis is grounded in the actual language of both passages.

anchor_text: Some say the Genius so / Cries 'Come!' to him that instantly must die
summary: The Genius in Roman belief was a man's guardian spirit, present from birth to death, that called the soul home when death arrived. Troilus compares Aeneas's urgent 'Come!' from within to this divine summons — the voice that tells a man his time is up — making Cressida's departure feel like a kind of death.
detail: Each Roman man was thought to have his own Genius (women had a Juno) — a divine double that accompanied him through life and was especially honoured on his birthday. The Genius calling 'come' to the dying is attested in Roman usage; the image makes Aeneas's practical military summons into something uncanny and final. The comparison is Troilus's characteristic move: he inflates the everyday (an officer calling for them to hurry) into a cosmic register. The irony is that the 'death' he feels will be Cressida's eventual betrayal — the loss he does not yet know is coming.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'genius' (the attendant spirit allotted to each person at birth; the spirit that summons the dying).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'genius, n.,' sense 2a: 'The tutelary god or attendant spirit allotted to every person at his birth, to govern his fortunes and determine his character, and finally to conduct him out of the world.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2309

Both Onions and the OED are real and appropriate sources; the OED sense 2a wording quoted ('tutelary god or attendant spirit allotted to every person at his birth...conduct him out of the world') matches the OED entry, and the note that women had a Juno rather than a Genius is correctly stated.

The Roman Genius as guardian spirit that escorts the soul at death is correctly described; the note that women had a Juno rather than a Genius is accurate to Roman belief; the dramatic irony that Troilus's felt 'death' anticipates the later betrayal is a mainstream reading.

anchor_text: I will throw my glove to Death himself
summary: To throw your glove was to challenge someone to single combat — the gesture that initiated a judicial duel or a fight to the death. Troilus is saying he would challenge Death itself, the supreme opponent, to testify that Cressida's heart is pure. The hyperbole is a courtly compliment but also exposes his compulsive need to assert her fidelity.
detail: The throwing of a gage (glove, gauntlet, or hood) as a formal challenge was embedded in medieval and early modern law and chivalric culture; in Richard II the entire first act turns on gages thrown and taken up between Bolingbroke and Mowbray. Here Troilus reaches for the most heroic arena imaginable — combat with Death — to make his point, yet what he is actually doing is protesting Cressida's fidelity in terms that already assume the possibility of her unfaithfulness. His 'I speak not Be thou true as fearing thee' (TLN 2322) is precisely what a man who does fear it would say.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the formal throwing of the gage as the initiating act of trial by combat; cf. Richard II 1.1.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2323
Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does cover trial by combat including the formal throwing of the gage, and the Richard II 1.1 parallel is genuine; the source supports the claim.

The glove/gage as formal challenge to single combat is historically sound and the Richard II parallel is apt; the observation that Troilus's denial ('I speak not Be thou true as fearing thee') is precisely what a fearful man would say is a defensible ironic reading, not an overreach.

anchor_text: no maculation in thy heart
summary: 'Maculation' means a stain, spot, or blemish — from Latin macula, a spot. Troilus is swearing that there is no moral stain or mark of infidelity in Cressida's heart. The Latin-derived word gives the declaration a formal, almost legal weight.

anchor_text: Wear this sleeve. / And you this glove
summary: Troilus gives Cressida his sleeve to wear and she gives him a glove — these are love tokens, the knightly practice of wearing a lady's favour (a glove, sleeve, or ribbon) as a visible pledge of devotion. The sleeve is the same token that Cressida later gives away to Diomedes, the act that makes Troilus watch her transfer her allegiance.
detail: The exchange of 'favours' — small articles of clothing, jewels, or ribbons worn to display devotion to someone — was a formalized part of medieval and Renaissance courtly culture. A knight wore his lady's favour into battle or tournament; its display was a public declaration. When Cressida later gives this sleeve to Diomedes in Act 5, it becomes the material evidence of betrayal that Troilus cannot explain away: the token is both pledge and proof. The glove she gives Troilus completes a mutual exchange, but its subsequent appearance has no parallel dramatic function — the play reserves the sleeve for its devastating reuse.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'favour' (a small token given by a lady to a knight as a mark of special regard, worn in battle or tournament); s.v. 'sleeve' (used as a love-token).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2330
Onions's A Shakespeare Glossary is a real and standard source; entries for 'favour' (love token worn in battle or tournament) and 'sleeve' as a love token are well within its scope.

The exchange of favours as knightly practice is historically accurate, and crucially this gloss correctly identifies the sleeve as the token Cressida later gives Diomedes in Act 5 — that forward reference is load-bearing for the audience and is correctly flagged.

anchor_text: heel the high lavolt, nor sweeten talk, / Nor play at subtle games
summary: The lavolt (or volta) was a fashionable Elizabethan dance involving high leaps — the man would lift his partner by the waist. It required elegance, athletic skill, and physical intimacy. Troilus is listing the social accomplishments of the Greek youths that might attract Cressida: dancing, polished conversation, witty games — the arts of peacetime courtship.
detail: The dance's characteristic high kick or leap ('heel the high lavolt') made it spectacular and somewhat daring. It appears in Henry V (3.5), where the French lords boast that English girls dance it badly. The list Troilus provides — singing, dancing, 'sweeten talk' (polished social wit), 'subtle games' (probably word games, riddles, or chess) — maps a world of sophisticated Greek leisure against which his own directness and simplicity seem blunt. The passage is the play's most explicit staging of Troilus's self-doubt: he catalogues the Grecians' gifts in language that reveals both his jealousy and his genuine fear of inadequacy.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'lavolt, n.' (also la volta, lavolta): a lively dance of Italian origin involving high leaps; in vogue in the late 16th century.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2348
The OED entry for 'lavolt' is real and describes an Italian-origin dance involving high leaps; Henry V 3.5 does contain a French lord's reference to lavoltas, confirming the cited parallel.

The lavolta as an Italian-origin leaping dance is accurate and the Henry V parallel is real (3.5.33); the reading of 'subtle games' as word games, riddles, or chess is appropriately tentative; the claim that this cataloguing exposes Troilus's self-doubt is a mainstream and text-supported interpretation.

anchor_text: Whiles others fish with craft for great opinion, / I with great truth catch mere simplicity
summary: Troilus sets himself against the play's world of manipulation and performance: where others use cunning to 'fish' for reputation and gild counterfeit coin ('copper crowns'), he lets plain truth speak for itself. 'Wearing mine bare' means not covering base metal with gold — he is authentic through and through, without flattering veneer.
detail: The passage is one of the play's sharpest statements of its central problem of value: in a world where everything is gilded and sold, what is genuine honesty worth? 'Great opinion' means high reputation — the public credit that Ulysses argues in Act 3 must be constantly renewed. Troilus claims he catches only 'mere simplicity' with his honest bait — in other words, truth attracts the simply trusting, not the clever. Dramatically this is both admirable and ironic: the play has shown his 'simplicity' as an absolute devotion that blinds him to how a world of exchange actually works. Cressida is about to be exchanged for a prisoner of war; his truthful love could not protect her from that market.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'opinion' (reputation, esteem); s.v. 'copper' (base metal, counterfeit: 'gild their copper crowns' = cover false kingship with a gold veneer).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2367
Onions is a real source for 'opinion' (reputation, public esteem) and 'copper' (base metal, counterfeit); both senses are standard and accurately applied.

The fishing/gilding metaphors are straightforwardly explained, 'great opinion' as reputation is correct, and the ironic reading — that Troilus's celebrated 'simplicity' is a devotion that blinds him to the exchange-economy of the world he inhabits — is a mainstream scholarly interpretation of the play's value theme.

anchor_text: Here is the lady / Which for Antenor we deliver you
summary: The word 'deliver' frames Cressida as an object handed over — a commodity transferred in a prisoner exchange rather than a person making a choice. This single word exposes the scene's brutal logic: Cressida has been traded for the Trojan soldier Antenor without her consent, by men who claim to love or protect her. The scene is the play's central act of bartering a woman.
detail: Troilus himself speaks the line, and the speech that follows — warning Diomedes to treat her well, threatening his throat if he does not — confirms the dynamic: Troilus presents Cressida to her new 'keeper' while simultaneously claiming to love her absolutely. He acts as both devoted lover and efficient agent of her transfer. Critics including feminist scholars of the play have argued that this scene exposes the double standard at the heart of the Cressida tradition: she is traded by men, then condemned for the 'faithlessness' that results from being placed, alone and friendless, among enemies. Present the condemnation as the critical problem it is, not as the play's settled verdict.

sources.name: Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde
sources.citation: Geoffrey Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385), Book 4: the exchange of Criseyde for Antenor, Chaucer's principal source for this scene.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2373
Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde Book 4 does narrate the exchange of Criseyde for Antenor; the date 'c. 1385' falls within the scholarly consensus range of c. 1380–1387 for the poem's composition.

'Deliver' as commodity-transfer framing is supported by the text's explicit prisoner-exchange logic and the gloss correctly handles the critical tradition — presenting the double-standard as the critical problem rather than the play's settled verdict — without overreaching into advocacy.

anchor_text: by the dreadful Pluto, if thou dost not, / Though the great bulk Achilles be thy guard, / I'll cut thy throat
summary: Pluto was the Roman god of the underworld and the dead — the most fearful oath-partner available, the lord of the realm one would enter if the oath were broken. Swearing by Pluto rather than Jupiter or Mars gives the threat its maximum weight of doom. Troilus's invoking of Achilles as Diomedes's protector also signals awareness that the Greek champion, the most dangerous warrior alive, stands between him and any revenge.

anchor_text: appointment fresh and fair, Anticipating time with starting courage
summary: 'In appointment' means fully armed and equipped for combat. 'Anticipating time with starting courage' means Ajax is up and ready before the hour appointed for the fight, his spirit leaping ahead of the clock.
detail: The phrase 'appointment' in the sense of military equipment is Elizabethan; the sense of being 'fresh and fair' emphasises that Ajax has not yet sweat or tired, so he enters the lists at his best. 'Starting' means springing or leaping — his courage already bounding forward. Agamemnon's compliment is conventional pre-combat praise, heightened to accommodate the play's general irony about epic heroism.

anchor_text: kindness but particular; 'Twere better she were kiss'd in general
summary: Ulysses proposes that Agamemnon's welcome-kiss is 'particular' (given to one person) and that Cressida should be kissed by the whole company ('in general'). The bawdy double meaning is that she ought to be sexually available to all — reducing her, the moment she enters the Greek camp, to a communal object.

'In general' was a standard phrase meaning 'by or for the whole company' (OED s.v. 'general' adj. 8). The sexual valence is developed by 'sluttish spoils of opportunity' and 'daughters of the game' in his later speech. The kiss-greeting was a real Elizabethan social custom noted by Erasmus, so the scene would read to audiences both as social comedy and as a deeply uncomfortable demonstration of how quickly the Greek camp redefines Cressida.

anchor_text: popp'd Paris in his hardiment, And parted thus you and your argument
summary: Patroclus mocks Menelaus: 'argument' means both 'reason to kiss' and 'the wife' — Helen, the 'argument' (subject and cause) of the whole war. Paris 'popp'd' in (arrived with a kiss) with his 'hardiment' (boldness), and by taking Helen took away Menelaus's right to kiss her. The war's cause is reduced to a stolen kiss.

'Hardiment' is archaic for bravery or bold enterprise; Spenser uses it in The Faerie Queene. 'Popp'd' is colloquial, deflating Paris's abduction into a quick peck.

'Argument' carrying both 'cause/reason' and 'subject of the war' is sound OED-supported polysemy, and 'popp'd' as a deflating colloquial verb reducing Paris's boldness to a quick kiss-theft is a natural reading of the comic context.

anchor_text: deadly gall, and theme of all our scorns! For which we lose our heads to gild his horns
summary: Ulysses calls Helen 'deadly gall' (bitter poison) and 'theme of all our scorns.' Then: 'horns' are the conventional Elizabethan sign of a cuckold — a man whose wife has been unfaithful. The Greeks are literally losing their heads (dying) in order to 'gild' (decorate, or restore honour to) Menelaus's cuckold's horns — a savagely ironic image of the war's absurdity.
detail: The cuckold's horns were a ubiquitous comic image in Elizabethan culture: a man whose wife slept with another man was said to grow invisible horns on his head. The joke reduces the Trojan War from epic to farce: thousands of men die to clean up one husband's humiliation. Gilding horns is also a real practice — gilded ox-horns were used in sacrificial and triumphal processions — so the image layers sacrifice and mockery together. Ulysses deploys it with deliberate bitterness.

OED 'horn' n. 18 (cuckold's horn) and Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'gall' are real standard-reference sources that support the gloss.

anchor_text: The end crowns all; And that old common arbitrator, Time, Will one day end it
summary: 'The end crowns all' was a familiar proverb meaning that the outcome of an action is the true judge of its worth — nothing can be assessed until it is finished. Hector then calls Time 'that old common arbitrator' (an arbitrator was a judge chosen to settle disputes) — time will eventually decide the war. The double irony: Hector is already marked for death, and he himself will not live to see the ending he trusts in.

anchor_text: with exact view perus'd thee, Hector, And quoted joint by joint

anchor_text: Tell me, you heavens, in which part of his body Shall I destroy him?
summary: Achilles asks the gods to tell him where on Hector's body he will strike the killing blow — as if rehearsing the murder out loud in Hector's presence. The speech anticipates the ambush: Achilles already plans to kill Hector by targeting a specific body part, which implies he does not trust himself to win a fair fight. Hector's response — dignified scorn — makes the contrast starker.

anchor_text: by the forge that stithied Mars his helm, I'll kill thee everywhere

anchor_text: She was belov'd, she lov'd; she is, and doth; But still sweet love is food for fortune's tooth
summary: Troilus defends Cressida briefly to Ulysses ('she was loved, she loved; she is, and does still') then closes with a proverb: 'sweet love is food for fortune's tooth' — everything tender gets gnawed away by fortune's randomness and cruelty. The couplet substitutes a general fatalism for a personal answer, which is itself a kind of answer — he refuses to have Cressida's reputation picked over by the man who just called her a 'sluttish spoil.' The word 'still' means 'even now' or 'always' — the love continues even as fortune devours it.

anchor_text: Achilles' male varlet. Male varlet, you rogue! What's that? Why, his masculine whore
summary: Thersites calls Patroclus Achilles's 'male varlet' (a male attendant, but with the sense of a kept sexual companion) and then glosses it himself: 'his masculine whore.' This is the play's bluntest statement of the camp gossip that the Achilles-Patroclus relationship is sexual. Thersites is the play's nastiest voice; his slur is not the play's verdict.
detail: In Homer's Iliad the bond between Achilles and Patroclus is the poem's emotional core, but whether it was erotic was discussed in antiquity: in Plato's Symposium (179e-180b) Phaedrus treats the two as lovers (disputing only which was the elder). Shakespeare inherits a tradition in which the question was live: Marlowe's Edward II had staged a king destroyed by his favourite. The play does not settle the matter -- Thersites's jeering and Achilles's own reference to a secret love for the Trojan princess Polyxena (3.3) give the audience two irreconcilable pictures. 'Varlet' (from Old French 'valet') means a male servant or, pejoratively, a rogue; Thersites strips away the euphemism in his next breath. Present this as the play's most extreme satiric voice -- scurrilous mockery, not scholarly biography.

anchor_text: rotten diseases of the south, the guts-griping ruptures, catarrhs, loads o' gravel in the back
summary: Thersites unleashes a catalogue of venereal and rheumatic diseases. 'Diseases of the south' means illnesses associated with warm climates, specifically syphilis, believed to have entered Europe from the south or from the New World. 'Gravel in the back' is kidney stones. 'Imposthume' is an abscess. 'Limekilns i' th' palm' and 'bone-ache' are signs of advanced syphilis. 'Tetter' is a skin disease (eczema or ringworm). 'Rivelled fee-simple' means shrivelled complete ownership — the disease has eaten all of you.
detail: The southern-diseases cluster was the standard Elizabethan euphemism for syphilis (the 'French disease,' 'Neapolitan bone-ache'), thought to rot from inside. The litany is deliberate: Thersites is implying that Achilles and Patroclus's relationship will bring these very diseases on them — the diseases are the wages of lechery, which is Thersites's verdict on the whole war and the whole camp. 'Imposthume' (an internal abscess) and 'palsies' (paralysis) are not exclusively venereal — rheumatism, old age, and cold could produce them — but in context Thersites means to pile the full horror of sexual corruption onto Patroclus. 'Fee-simple' is a legal term for absolute unconditional ownership; 'rivelled fee-simple of the tetter' means: the skin disease (tetter) has colonised and owns the body entirely, outright, without reservation.

anchor_text: letter from Queen Hecuba, A token from her daughter, my fair love, Both taxing me and gaging me to keep An oath
summary: Achilles reveals that he has sworn a secret oath to Queen Hecuba — Troy's queen and mother of Hector — and to Hecuba's daughter Polyxena, whom he loves. This oath to stay out of the battle is what keeps him idle in his tent, beyond the political scheming of Ulysses. It is Shakespeare's addition to the Homer story; Homer's Achilles sulks over the insult of Agamemnon taking his prize, Briseis.

Shakespeare adds and foregrounds the Polyxena love affair, drawing on later post-Homeric traditions (e.g., Caxton's Recuyell) in which Achilles was enamoured of the Trojan princess and sent messages through Hecuba. The detail transforms Achilles's idleness from heroic pride into something more morally compromised: he is choosing a private erotic oath over his public duty to the Greek army. It also introduces a tragic irony — this oath cannot last, and Patroclus's death will break it.

anchor_text: goodly transformation of Jupiter there, his brother, the bull, the primitive statue and oblique memorial of cuckolds
summary: Thersites calls Menelaus 'the goodly transformation of Jupiter... the bull' — a mocking allusion to the myth in which Jupiter transformed himself into a bull to abduct Europa. The twist is contemptuous: Jupiter chose the bull-form to get what he desired; Menelaus merely IS a bull — the cuckold's animal, the horned beast. A cuckold was a man whose wife was unfaithful; by convention he was imagined to grow horns like a bull. Menelaus's wife Helen ran off with Paris, making Menelaus the preeminent cuckold of the legend.
detail: Jupiter (Zeus in Greek) took the form of a beautiful white bull to carry off the Phoenician princess Europa (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.833-875). Thersites inverts the dignity of that transformation: instead of a god who temporarily becomes a bull to win a prize, Menelaus is a man who has permanently become the symbol of sexual humiliation — the horned cuckold. 'Primitive statue' (earliest, most original image) and 'oblique memorial' (indirect, sideways monument) mock Menelaus as the founding type and standing reminder of every man betrayed by his wife. Thersites's contempt for Menelaus is consistent throughout the play — when he meets him in battle he calls the whole war 'a whore and a cuckold.'

anchor_text: spend his mouth and promise, like Brabbler the hound; but when he performs, astronomers foretell it

The astronomical joke exploits the contemporary sense that comets, eclipses, and unusual conjunctions were portents: astronomers ('astronomers foretell it') predicted such prodigies as omens of upheaval. anchor_text: Nothing but lechery! All incontinent varlets!
summary: Thersites closes the scene with his signature verdict on the entire war: it is all lechery (lust), and every man in it is an 'incontinent varlet' (a man with no sexual self-control; a lustful rogue). 'Incontinent' means lacking restraint, particularly sexual restraint. This is Thersites's refrain throughout the play, reducing the heroic siege of Troy to nothing but appetite.

'Varlet' (Old French 'valet': servant, then knave) marks them as base. The line is the play's moral thesis delivered with maximum contempt, and it anticipates the cynical closing notes of Pandarus's Epilogue.

anchor_text: Stand where the torch may not discover us
summary: Ulysses is directing Troilus to stand in shadow beyond the reach of the torch-light. Elizabethan performances used real torches to signal night scenes and to light action; here the prop creates a plausible hiding-place. The whole scene is structured as a voyeuristic eavesdrop — two Trojans and Thersites watching and commenting while Cressida and Diomedes negotiate in the lit space outside the tent.
detail: The staging follows a well-established convention: 'we are hidden but the audience sees everything.' Three observers comment in turn — Troilus with anguished asides, Ulysses with cool management, Thersites with foul relish — while the main action plays in the torch-lit zone. The audience thus watches both the scene and the watchers' reactions simultaneously, a double perspective that gives Troilus's breakdown its ironised quality: we see him disintegrate while Thersites mocks and Ulysses steers.

anchor_text: my charge
summary: 'Charge' here means a person placed in someone's care — a ward or dependent. Diomedes was assigned by Agamemnon to escort Cressida from Troy to the Greek camp; she is his 'charge,' his responsibility. His immediate 'How now, my charge!' converts that guardianship into easy intimacy — a small but pointed signal that his claim on her has already shifted from official duty to something personal.

anchor_text: She will sing any man at first sight
summary: Ulysses's 'sing any man at first sight' means she can read any man's music at a glance — flattering his abilities as a sight-reader, but already insinuating sexual availability. Thersites immediately makes the double meaning explicit: to 'take her cliff' (her musical clef) means to read her key-signature, but 'cliff' / 'clef' also puns on a sexual opening. 'She's noted' caps the pun — 'noted' means musically notated, and also notorious.
detail: The musical vocabulary — 'sing at first sight' (sight-reading), 'take her cliff' (the clef that tells you the range of the notes), 'noted' (written in musical notation) — was standard Elizabethan sexual wordplay; the clef-as-aperture pun runs through contemporaries (Nashe, Middleton). Thersites deploys the nastiest version; Ulysses's is almost mannerly by comparison. Together they enact the play's reduction of Cressida to an object of male commentary before she has said a word to Diomedes.

anchor_text: come, tell a pin; you are a forsworn
summary: 'Tell a pin' is a contemptuous idiom meaning 'tell that to a pin' — i.e. your excuses are worth nothing, not even a pin. 'Forsworn' means oath-breaker: Cressida has sworn to give Diomedes a token (the sleeve Troilus gave her) and is now wriggling out of it. Diomedes's short, hard reply dismisses her hesitation and pushes her back toward the promised gift.

anchor_text: A juggling trick, to be secretly open
summary: Thersites mocks Cressida's half-hearted resistance as a conjuror's sleight — 'secretly open' means pretending to be closed (honest, chaste) while actually being open (sexually accessible). The oxymoron captures his contemptuous reading of her conduct: that the hesitation and the yielding are both performed, a juggler's deception.
detail: 'Open' carried a standard bawdy sense of sexually available (compare 'open' in Williams, Glossary). Thersites is the play's most reductive commentator on erotic behaviour; his gloss here pre-empts any sympathetic reading of Cressida's visible ambivalence. The play itself is less certain: from inside the tent she cannot know she is overheard, and some of her 'fooling' looks less calculated than Thersites claims.

anchor_text: adieu! you palter
summary: 'Palter' means to shuffle, equivocate, or deal dishonestly — to keep changing position to avoid committing. Diomedes's accusation is that Cressida keeps saying she will give him the sleeve and then pulling back, which is a kind of bad faith. The word carries a stronger moral charge than 'waver': to palter with someone is to deceive them through evasion.

anchor_text: the devil Luxury, with his fat rump and potato finger
summary: 'Luxury' here means Lechery personified — a morality-play devil of lust, with a fat, grotesque body. The 'potato finger' is a contemporary joke: sweet potatoes had only recently reached England from the Americas and were thought to be powerful aphrodisiacs. Thersites is picturing the god of lechery fondling Cressida and Diomedes together with a stumpy potato-finger.
detail: Sweet potatoes (Ipomoea batatas) arrived in England in the late sixteenth century and were quickly linked to lust in popular writing — they appear as an aphrodisiac in Merry Wives of Windsor 5.5 as well. 'Luxury' as personified Lechery is the same figure as the Vice of morality drama: a fat, comic devil who represents a particular sin. Thersites's imagery is the play's nastiest, but it also supplies a cultural-history footnote: the potent new-world food drops into the oldest English allegorical tradition.

anchor_text: keep this sleeve
summary: A detachable sleeve was the standard Elizabethan love-token exchanged between knights and their ladies: a knight wore his lady's token on his helmet or armour in battle as a public declaration of her favour. Troilus had given Cressida this sleeve; she now gives it to Diomedes. It is the most visible possible act of transfer — from Troilus's gift to Diomedes's trophy — and Troilus, hidden, sees it happen.
detail: Detachable sleeves were a real garment: in Elizabethan dress, sleeves could be laced on or off and exchanged as gifts. In tournament and chivalric culture the lady's 'favour' worn by her knight was a public signal of the bond between them; displaying it on the helm (as Diomedes threatens to do at TLN 2938) advertises the conquest. The sleeve thus concentrates the whole lover's-token tradition into a visible stage object whose transfer becomes the central traumatic image of the scene.

anchor_text: By all Diana's waiting women yond
summary: Diana was the Roman goddess of the moon and chastity; her 'waiting women yond' are the stars, imagined as her attendant nymphs in the night sky above. Cressida swears by them — which is itself ironic: she is swearing an oath of secrecy to Diomedes by the goddess of chastity and her star-companions, at the very moment she is breaking faith with Troilus.

The irony operates on two levels: Cressida swears by chastity's patron that she will not tell whose sleeve this was — protecting not her own chastity but her new liaison — and the solemn oath form (naming the goddess and her court) makes the betrayal of Troilus's token seem more, not less, consequential.

anchor_text: To-morrow will I wear it on my helm, And grieve his spirit that dares not challenge it

This follows the tournament convention: if a knight challenged the wearer of his lady's token for wearing it falsely, a fight to the death could result. Troilus, overhearing, immediately vows to accept that challenge.

anchor_text: by Pluto; but that that likes not you Pleases me best
summary: Pluto was the Roman god of the underworld, an appropriately dark oath for Thersites, whose commentary throughout the scene runs toward death and damnation. The quip — 'what you dislike, I enjoy' — is his signature style: he takes pleasure in watching others suffer. He swears by the god of the dead because he is, essentially, rooting for the worst outcome.

anchor_text: One eye yet looks on thee; But with my heart the other eye doth see
summary: Cressida's couplets are a brief soliloquy in which she divides herself: one eye still faces Troilus (the past), while her heart directs the other eye toward Diomedes (the future). She uses the split-eye image to describe internal division — head pulled one way by habit, will pulled another. This is her only moment of self-diagnosis in the scene, and it immediately precedes the play's harshest male commentary on her.
detail: The self-accusing couplets (TLN 2955-2960) — patterned in rhymed tetrameters, conspicuously more formal than her prose exchanges with Diomedes — function as a mini-soliloquy. They are the only point in the scene where Cressida speaks without audience pressure. The 'error of our eye' speech reads partly as internalised blame (the misogynist tradition she is trapped in) and partly as a genuine attempt to account for divided feeling. The play neither endorses nor pardons it; both readings are available.

anchor_text: To make a recordation to my soul Of every syllable that here was spoke
summary: 'Recordation' means the act of recording or committing to memory — a formal, Latinate word for recollection. anchor_text: Sith yet there is a credence in my heart, An esperance so obstinately strong
summary: 'Sith' is an archaic form of 'since.' 'Credence' means belief or credit — a readiness to believe. 'Esperance' is hope (from French esperance), used as a formal, elevated word. anchor_text: This is Diomed's Cressida
summary: Troilus's famous speech beginning 'This she? No; this is Diomed's Cressida' tries to resolve an impossible contradiction by splitting Cressida in two: the woman he loved, and the woman who is betraying him. His logic is: if souls guide vows, and beauty has a soul, then this faithless woman cannot be the Cressida he knew. The speech is one of Shakespeare's most extreme representations of the mind refusing what the eyes have seen.
detail: Troilus works through a chain of conditional propositions ('If beauty have a soul... if souls guide vows... if sanctimony be the gods' delight... if there be rule in unity itself...') to reach 'This was not she' — only to be overturned by the other half of his mind: 'O madness of discourse / That cause sets up with and against itself.' The term 'Bi-fold authority' (TLN 2996) is unique to Shakespeare and names the logical impasse: two irreconcilable verdicts occupy the same mind at once. The speech shows Troilus's idealism — his insistence that inward truth must match outward fact — collapsing, but unable to collapse.

The analysis of Troilus's conditional chain and the term 'Bi-fold authority' (TLN 2996) as unique to Shakespeare naming a logical impasse is accurate; the description of his idealism collapsing without being able to collapse is a mainstream scholarly reading, not an overreach.

anchor_text: no orifice for a point as subtle As Ariachne's broken woof to enter
summary: Arachne was the master weaver of Greek myth who challenged the goddess Athena and was turned into a spider as punishment; her 'woof' is the threads woven across the loom. 'Ariachne' blends 'Ariadne' (who gave Theseus a thread to navigate the labyrinth) with 'Arachne' — possibly a deliberate fusion, possibly a scribal error. The image means: the gap between his two contradictory beliefs admits nothing, not even the finest thread. Troilus is saying the division is total yet allows no passage between its two sides.
detail: This is one of the play's most discussed cruxes. The First Folio reads 'Ariachne'; editors have divided between treating it as a deliberate fusion of the two mythical thread-women (Arachne the weaver, Ariadne the thread-giver) and as a compositorial error for one or the other. If 'Arachne's broken woof,' a single thread of spider-silk, is what cannot fit through the gap, the image is devastatingly small: the two halves of Troilus's mind are separated by a distance that excludes even the thinnest conceivable thing.

anchor_text: Instance, O instance! strong as Pluto's gates
summary: 'Instance' here means a proof or piece of evidence. Troilus cites two contradictory instances, each 'strong' — the first ('Pluto's gates,' the gates of the underworld: absolutely shut, impossible to pass) proves Cressida is his by the bonds of heaven; the second ('strong as heaven itself') proves those bonds are now dissolved and she belongs to Diomedes. The repetition of the same rhetorical form for opposite conclusions — 'Instance, O instance! strong as X: proof A. Instance, O instance! strong as Y: proof not-A' — enacts the 'bi-fold authority' he just named.

anchor_text: The fractions of her faith, orts of her love, The fragments, scraps, the bits, and greasy relics Of her o'er-eaten faith
summary: 'Orts' are scraps of food left over from a meal — table leavings. 'Fractions' means broken pieces. Troilus heaps up synonyms for leftover food-scraps (fractions, orts, fragments, scraps, bits, greasy relics) and applies them to Cressida's faith, as if her love for Diomedes is made up of what remains of her love for him — stale, used, disgusting. The cluster of food-waste words is sustained and deliberate: love's remains are garbage.
detail: The passage is a sustained 'copia' — deliberate rhetorical amplification through synonym — but applied to the most degraded subject-matter possible. 'O'er-eaten faith' caps the image: a faith that has been consumed and left as grease and bones. The cumulative synonyms enact Troilus's disgust piling on itself. The food-scrap imagery also resonates with Ulysses's earlier warning (3.3) that appetite and value are linked: everything loses worth once possessed. Cressida's love, now transferred, becomes the play's own theme of value in decay.

anchor_text: in characters as red as Mars his heart Inflam'd with Venus
summary: Mars was the Roman god of war and Venus the goddess of love; their famous adulterous affair was a commonplace of classical and Renaissance poetry. Troilus will write his hatred of Diomedes and his love for Cressida in letters 'red as Mars his heart inflamed with Venus' — war-passion coloured by love-passion. The mythological pair condenses both his grief and his coming violence into a single image.
detail: The affair of Mars and Venus was told at length in Homer's Odyssey (8.266-366: the smith-god Hephaestus traps them in a net and calls the gods to witness) and Ovid's Metamorphoses (4.171-189). In Renaissance emblem it stood for the union of violence and desire. Troilus's image is precisely apt: his 'characters' (written letters) will be red both from Mars's war-heat and from Venus's love-heat, because his purpose is to fight Diomedes out of his grief for Cressida.

anchor_text: Were it a casque compos'd by Vulcan's skill
summary: A 'casque' is a helmet. Vulcan (Greek Hephaestus) was the divine smith of the gods, whose workmanship was supposed to be indestructible — he forged the armour of Achilles in Homer's Iliad. Troilus is saying that even if the helmet bearing Cressida's sleeve were made by the god of the forge, his sword would still cut through it. The hyperbole reaches for the very limit of human and divine craft to measure his resolve.

anchor_text: the dreadful spout Which shipmen do the hurricano call, Constring'd in mass by the almighty sun, Shall dizzy with more clamour Neptune's ear
summary: 'Hurricano' (hurricane) was a New World word for a tropical storm's waterspout, recently borrowed into English from Spanish huracán. Sailors returning from the Americas used it, and writers quickly adopted it. 'Constring'd in mass' means compressed or condensed in bulk — the sea-water drawn up into the whirling column by the sun's heat. Troilus is comparing the noise of his sword's descent on Diomedes to the crashing of a waterspout as it falls back into the sea, so loud it deafens the god Neptune.
detail: Shakespeare uses 'Hurricano' three times in the canon (here, Othello 3.3, and King Lear 3.2 — 'you cataracts and hurricanoes'). The word entered English in the 1550s from Spanish and Portuguese reports of Caribbean storms; by c. 1600 it was current in London writing and carried a flavour of the exotic, newly discovered Atlantic. 'Neptune's ear' (Neptune as the sea-god listening in his kingdom) is a classical personification that sits neatly against the New World meteorological term.

sources.name: OED s.v. hurricano
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'hurricane, n.' (early form 'hurricano,' borrowed via Spanish from Caribbean Taino huracán, first recorded in English 1555).

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid; Homer, Odyssey
sources.citation: Neptune (Greek Poseidon) as ruler of the sea: Virgil, Aeneid 1.124-156; Homer, Odyssey 1.68-79.

OED confirms 'hurricano' entered English by 1555 from Spanish/Portuguese via Caribbean Taino; Virgil Aeneid 1.124-156 (Neptune calming the storm) and Homer Odyssey 1.68-79 (Poseidon's role as sea-ruler) are both confirmed real passages supporting Neptune/Poseidon as the sea-god.

'Hurricano' as a New World loanword from Spanish huracán, entering English in the 1550s, is correct; 'constring'd' as compressed/condensed is accurate; the three-instance canon count (here, Othello 3.3, Lear 3.2) is verifiable, and Neptune as sea-god is not overstated.

anchor_text: O false Cressid! false, false, false! Let all untruths stand by thy stained name
summary: Troilus's outburst invokes the proverbial tradition in which 'Cressida' had become a byword for female faithlessness — calling all other betrayals minor beside hers. The tradition he is both enacting and extending runs from Chaucer through Henryson's Testament of Cresseid to dozens of Elizabethan allusions. But the play frames his condemnation as a critical problem: the equally faithless Troilus, who vowed eternal constancy and has already told Helen he cares nothing for the war, and the predatory Diomedes, go unshamed — only Cressida is made the emblem of all untruth.
detail: The double standard is structurally built in: Troilus brands her 'false' while himself having been the eager participant in an affair conducted in war-time under her duplicitous father's roof, in an exchange he had already been told was coming. Diomedes takes the sleeve by pressure, not seduction. Yet neither man is named 'false.' The play stages the making of the 'Cressida' legend — 'let all untruths stand by thy stained name' is a speech-act that creates the very tradition it seems merely to confirm. Content-care: present Troilus's condemnation as a problem, not a verdict.

sources.name: Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde; Henryson, Testament of Cresseid
sources.citation: Geoffrey Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385); Robert Henryson, The Testament of Cresseid (printed 1532) — the tradition in which Cressida became the proverbial false woman.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3030

Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (c.1382-1386, commonly cited as c.1385) and Henryson's Testament of Cresseid (printed 1532 in Godfray's Chaucer edition) are both confirmed real texts whose role in establishing the 'false Cressida' tradition is well-documented.

The reading of Troilus's outburst as enacting the very 'Cressida' legend it claims merely to confirm is a mainstream scholarly position (Palmer, Muir, Dollimore); the content-care framing — presenting Troilus's condemnation as a problem not a verdict — is appropriate given the double standard the annotation correctly identifies.

anchor_text: revolted fair
summary: 'Revolted' means one who has defected or turned traitor — in the political sense, a rebel who goes over to the enemy. 'Fair' is a noun here meaning a fair or beautiful woman. So 'revolted fair' = 'you, the beautiful one who has defected.' The word choice is pointed: it treats Cressida's change of attachment as treason — the same verb used for political betrayal — which echoes her father Calchas's literal defection to the Greeks.

sources.name: OED s.v. revolted
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'revolt, v.' (sense 2: to desert or go over to the enemy; used from 16th century in political and military contexts).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3039

OED s.v. 'revolt, v.' sense 2 (to desert or go over to the enemy, attested from the 16th century in political/military contexts) is a real entry that directly supports the annotation's gloss of 'revolted' as treasonous defection.

'Revolted' in the political/military sense of defection or desertion is accurate, and the gloss's pointed observation that the word's echo of Calchas's literal defection to the Greeks is not over-read — the parallel is structurally real.

anchor_text: I would croak like a raven; I would bode, I would bode
summary: The raven's croak was a standard omen of death and disaster in both classical and English popular belief — a bird that 'boded' (foretold) misfortune. Thersites says he would croak like a raven over Diomedes's coming downfall, because Patroclus will pay handsomely for news of the affair. The raven-as-omen is here used comically, but it also keeps the scene's bitter atmosphere in view: Thersites sees ruin everywhere and finds it amusing.

sources.name: OED / Pliny
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bode, v.' (to foretell, esp. evil; the raven an evil-boding bird, documented from Old English); Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 10 (the crow and the raven among the birds of ill omen; the raven's unlucky croak).

The raven as death-omen in classical and English popular belief is accurate, and the reading of Thersites's croaking as comic but atmospherically consistent with his role as bitter prophet of ruin is defensible; the Pliny reference for Roman augury is a legitimate source.

anchor_text: ungently temper'd To stop his ears against admonishment
summary: 'Ungently temper'd' means in an ungentlemanly or harsh mood — 'temper' here is a person's habitual disposition, not a sudden outburst. Andromache opens the scene by lamenting that Hector has become unusually resistant to reasonable counsel ('admonishment') on this particular morning.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'temper, n.' sense 8: the quality of mind or character in respect of its moderation or self-control; and OED s.v. 'gently' sense 1: in the manner of a gentleman, in a courteous, mild, or considerate manner.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3049
