The reading of 'ungently temper'd' as harsh in disposition (not a sudden outburst) is standard and defensible; Andromache's complaint is that Hector's mood this morning makes him unusually resistant to counsel, which the text supports directly.

anchor_text: My dreams will, sure, prove ominous to the day
summary: Prophetic dreams warning of disaster were taken seriously in both classical antiquity and Shakespeare's England as genuine communications from the gods or from God. Andromache's ominous dream is a stock feature of the Trojan-war tradition — both Homer and the later medieval retellings surround Hector's last day with ill omens that he ignores.
detail: In Homer's Iliad Hector's wife Andromache does not appear on his last morning, but the narrative is thick with divine signs that he discounts. Priam's speech at TLN 3119-3122, where he himself claims a sudden prophetic impulse, reinforces the scene's atmosphere of ignored warning. That every oracle figure on stage (Andromache, Cassandra, Priam) agrees, yet Hector dismisses them all, is the play's darkest irony: Troy's most honourable warrior chooses death by treating honour as more binding than any supernatural warning.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 22 (the fate of Hector accepted by the hero himself and by the gods despite Priam's and Hecuba's pleading); compare Caxton, Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (1474) for the medieval Troy-chronicle tradition Shakespeare also drew on.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3054

Homer Iliad 22 genuinely centres on divine omens Hector discounts despite Priam's and Hecuba's pleading, and Caxton's Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (1474) is a real and relevant medieval Troy-chronicle source.

The claim that prophetic dreams were taken seriously in classical antiquity and Shakespeare's England is mainstream; the observation that Hector ignores multiple convergent warning figures (Andromache, Cassandra, Priam) is a defensible reading of the scene's structure and its ironic logic.

anchor_text: The gods are deaf to hot and peevish vows; They are polluted off'rings, more abhorr'd Than spotted livers in the sacrifice
summary: Cassandra argues that a vow made in passionate haste ('hot and peevish') is itself impious — an unworthy sacrifice the gods reject. 'Spotted livers' refers to Roman and Greek divination: priests examined the liver of a sacrificed animal for blemishes; a diseased or spotted liver signalled that the offering was rejected and the enterprise would fail. Her point is that Hector's vow to fight is no less polluted than a defective victim.

sources.name: Cicero / OED
sources.citation: Cicero, De Divinatione, Book 1 (Roman divination, including haruspicy -- the reading of sacrificial entrails for signs of divine favour or disfavour); OED s.v. 'peevish' (childishly foolish, silly; also stubborn, perverse).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3066

Rescued in 2026-06-02 review sweep — Generalized the Cicero citation to De Divinatione Book 1 (which does treat haruspicy, though it is not the sole subject of 1.16-26 as the original implied); OED 'peevish' kept.

The haruspicy gloss on 'spotted livers' is sound and well-attested; the reading of 'peevish' as foolishly self-willed (not merely irritable) matches Elizabethan usage; Cassandra's argument — that a rash vow is itself a polluted offering — is an accurate paraphrase of the lines.

anchor_text: Mine honour keeps the weather of my fate. Life every man holds dear; but the dear man Holds honour far more precious dear than life
summary: 'Keeps the weather' is a nautical metaphor meaning to hold the windward (safer, advantageous) position — Hector claims his honour stands above his fate, commanding it rather than being driven by it. The three lines then build a chiasmus: 'dear... dear man... precious dear,' pivoting on the word 'dear' to distinguish the value men place on life from the greater value the truly honourable man places on reputation. The speech crystallises the play's central — and ultimately fatal — equation of honour with death.
detail: In sailing, the weather-gage (windward position) gave tactical advantage; to 'keep the weather' of something is to master or rise above it. Hector's rhetoric is formally beautiful and, in the play's bitter logic, suicidal: his 'honour' will lead him to ignore every prophetic warning, go unarmed at the wrong moment, and be butchered by Achilles's men. The play does not mock the speech — it makes Hector sympathetic — but the subsequent action exposes how an absolute honour-code destroys the man who holds it.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'weather, n.' sense 13b: to keep the weather (of), to get or keep the windward position relative to; figuratively, to gain or maintain advantage over.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3077
OED s.v. 'weather, n.' sense 13b (to keep the weather of, windward advantage) is a real entry that directly supports the nautical metaphor explained in the gloss.

The nautical 'weather-gage' gloss is standard and the OED supports it; the chiastic / polyptoton reading of 'dear... dear man... precious dear' is defensible as a rhetorical observation, and the annotation rightly notes the speech is sympathetic rather than satirised, which is the mainstream position.

anchor_text: you have a vice of mercy in you Which better fits a lion than a man
summary: Troilus accuses Hector of a 'vice of mercy' — an excessive, almost animal-like clemency. The lion was proverbially considered magnanimous to a fallen enemy; classical and medieval sources held that a lion would not strike a prostrate foe. Troilus's twist is that such noble restraint is appropriate to a beast by nature, but not to a soldier in a war that demands ruthlessness.

sources.name: Pliny / Schmidt
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 8 (the lion alone among wild beasts shows clemency to the prostrate and the suppliant -- 'leoni tantum ex feris clementia in supplices'); Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'lion' (the proverbial magnanimous lion).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3088
Rescued in 2026-06-02 review sweep — Corrected the Pliny chapter range (the lion-clemency passage is in Book 8's lion section, not ch. 16) and quoted the actual Latin maxim; Schmidt kept.

The proverbial magnanimity of the lion (not striking a fallen foe) is a genuine Renaissance commonplace traceable to Pliny and heraldic tradition; the connection to Hector's habit of sparing defeated Greeks, and the forward irony linking it to his fatal disarming in 5.8, is textually grounded and mainstream.

anchor_text: Let's leave the hermit Pity with our mothers; And when we have our armours buckled on, The venom'd vengeance ride upon our swords, Spur them to ruthful work, rein them from ruth
summary: Troilus personifies Pity as a hermit — a religious recluse withdrawn from the world — and consigns it to the domestic, female sphere ('our mothers'). The bitter wordplay at the end turns on 'ruthful' and 'ruth': 'ruthful work' means pitiful or lamentable work (slaughter that even the killer should lament), but then 'rein them from ruth' means hold the swords back from any pity. Both words come from Old English 'hreow' (sorrow, pity); the lines demand and then forbid the same quality in one breath.
detail: The pair 'ruthful / ruth' is a polyptoton — the same root word ('ruth,' pity) inflected two ways in adjacent clauses, used to argue opposite actions. Troilus commands swords to do pitiable slaughter and simultaneously to be free of pity. The contradiction reveals his state: grief-maddened by Cressida's apparent betrayal (reported in 5.2), he has crossed from honourable soldier to self-destructive avenger. 'Ruth' is archaic by Shakespeare's day but still current; Onions (Shakespeare Glossary) notes it as standard for sorrow or compassion in the period.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. R. D. Eagleson (1986), s.v. 'ruth': sorrow, compassion, pity; and 'ruthful': piteous, pitiable.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3099
Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (rev. Eagleson, 1986) is a real reference work and its entries for 'ruth' (pity, compassion) and 'ruthful' (piteous) are genuine and support the wordplay analysis.

The polyptoton identification ('ruthful / ruth' from the same root, used to argue opposite actions in adjacent clauses) is accurate; the personification of Pity as a hermit consigned to the domestic sphere is correctly glossed; the annotation's restraint in not over-psychologising Troilus's state keeps it defensible.

anchor_text: Not fate, obedience, nor the hand of Mars Beckoning with fiery truncheon my retire
summary: Mars was the Roman god of war, imagined wearing armour and carrying a staff of command. A 'truncheon' is a short baton or staff of authority used by commanders; 'fiery' signals divine, supernatural force. Troilus swears that not even the war-god himself, waving him off the field with a burning commander's baton, could stop him from fighting.
detail: The image of Mars as a commanding general who can order mortals off the battlefield belongs to the epic tradition where gods intervene directly in human combat. In Homer's Iliad the gods take sides and physically protect or redirect warriors (Iliad 5, 15). The image belongs especially to a play populated by the actual figures of the Trojan War, where divine intervention is part of the inherited mythology. Troilus's defiance of even a divine command measures the degree to which grief has untethered him from reason.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 5.840-861 and 15.110-142 (Mars / Ares as the commanding god of war who enters the battle directly); Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'truncheon': a short staff borne as a symbol of military command.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3107

Iliad 5.840-861 shows Ares physically present in battle and wounded by Diomedes, and 15.110-142 shows Ares arming to enter battle before being restrained — both passages support the claim of Ares/Mars as a god who intervenes directly in human combat.

The gloss on 'truncheon' as a staff of command and the Homeric tradition of gods directly intervening in battle are standard; the image of Mars beckoning with a fiery baton is accurately explained as an appeal to epic convention, and the reading of Troilus's defiance as grief-driven is supported by the surrounding context.

anchor_text: He is thy crutch; now if thou lose thy stay, Thou on him leaning, and all Troy on thee, Fall all together
summary: Cassandra constructs a chain of dependency — Priam leans on Hector as on a crutch, Troy leans on Priam — that produces a single catastrophic collapse if Hector is removed. The image turns the political fact (Troy's survival depends on its greatest warrior) into a physical figure of bodies propping each other up, then all falling together. This is also a structural echo of the 'degree' speech: the play's great chain of being, if one link breaks, brings everything down.
detail: 'Stay' is both the noun ('support,' 'prop') and a pun on the verb 'to stay' (to remain, to prevent). The line pattern 'Thou on him leaning, and all Troy on thee, / Fall all together' mimics the physical collapse it describes, each clause toppling the next. Cassandra's speech is visionary in the prophetic tradition — she sees the fall of Troy as already accomplished — and the syntax enacts it.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'stay, n.2' sense 1: a thing that serves as a prop or support; sense 4: a check or hindrance. OED s.v. 'crutch, n.' sense 1: a staff or support used by lame or infirm persons.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3115
OED s.v. 'stay, n.2' sense 1 (a prop or support) and 'crutch, n.' sense 1 (a staff used by the infirm) are real entries that support the structural metaphor analysis.

The OED glosses and the structural chain-of-dependency reading are sound, but invoking the 'degree' speech and the 'great chain of being' as a structural echo is an interpretive leap — those concepts belong to Ulysses's speech in Act 1, not this scene — and the annotation does not distinguish the metaphor's local function from that broader thematic claim.

anchor_text: This foolish, dreaming, superstitious girl Makes all these bodements
summary: Troilus dismisses Cassandra as a hysterical girl producing empty omens ('bodements' = forebodings, omen-signs). The play's bitter irony is that Cassandra is right about everything and Troilus is wrong about everything: she is the only truth-teller on stage in this scene. Her curse — to prophesy truly but never be believed — comes from Greek mythology, and Troilus here enacts it.
detail: In the mythological tradition, Cassandra received the gift of prophecy from Apollo and then refused his sexual advances; he cursed her so that her true predictions would always be disbelieved (Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1202-1212 records the fullest account). Shakespeare's audiences would know the tradition, so Troilus's contemptuous 'foolish, dreaming, superstitious girl' is audible as irony from the outset: the 'girl' is the only one in the scene who can see clearly. 'Bodements' is a relatively rare word for omens or prophetic signs; Onions cites this as one of its few appearances in Shakespeare.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. R. D. Eagleson (1986), s.v. 'bodement': an omen, a portent. Cf. Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1202-1212 (the Cassandra tradition of true prophecy forever disbelieved), known to Renaissance readers through Latin accounts and mythographers.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3138
Aeschylus Agamemnon lines 1202-1212 fall within the genuine Cassandra scene where she speaks directly of Apollo's gift and curse, and Onions on 'bodement' is a real lexicographical reference.

The Cassandra curse tradition (prophecy believed by no one) is well established and directly relevant; citing Aeschylus's Agamemnon as the fullest account is accurate; the irony that Troilus enacts the curse by dismissing her is a mainstream and well-supported reading of the scene.

anchor_text: Proud Diomed, believe, I come to lose my arm or win my sleeve
summary: A 'sleeve' was the standard love-token a lady gave her knight to wear in battle or tournament — Cressida gave Troilus her sleeve when they parted, and in 5.2 Troilus watched Cressida hand it over to Diomedes. To 'win my sleeve' means to take it back from Diomedes by killing or defeating him. The rhyming couplet frames Troilus's grief as a chivalric quest of vengeance, but the loss he also accepts ('lose my arm') makes it a death-wish as much as a war-cry.
detail: The exchange of tokens — gloves, sleeves, rings — between ladies and their champions was a central ceremony of medieval and Renaissance chivalric practice; wearing a lady's token in combat was a public declaration of service and love. Troilus himself gave Cressida a sleeve (mentioned at 5.2.68-76), so 'win my sleeve' is painfully specific: he is going to fight over a scrap of cloth that was the physical emblem of his betrayed love. The bitter irony of the whole play is concentrated here — the Trojan War, ostensibly fought for Helen, is re-enacted at the personal level as a fight over another woman's token.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'sleeve': a token of a lady's favour, given to a knight to wear or display in combat or tournament. Cf. Troilus and Cressida 5.2.70-88 (Cressida gives Diomedes the sleeve Troilus had given her).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3155
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference work and the internal cross-reference to Troilus and Cressida 5.2 for Cressida transferring the sleeve to Diomedes is accurate to the play text.

The sleeve-as-love-token custom is a genuine chivalric and tournament convention; the specific cross-reference to 5.2 where Cressida gives Troilus's sleeve to Diomedes is accurate and makes the line's bitterness legible; the reading of the couplet as both a war-cry and a death-wish is defensible given Troilus's state throughout Act 5.

anchor_text: A whoreson tisick, a whoreson rascally tisick so troubles me
summary: 'Tisick' (also 'phthisic') is an archaic word for a chest disease, most likely tuberculosis or a chronic cough and wasting illness. 'Whoreson' is a general-purpose intensifier and insult in Elizabethan English, literally 'son of a whore.' Pandarus's complaint that his disease is ruining him connects to the play's wider imagery of contagion and decay — and to the tradition that Pandarus ends the story diseased, his body the physical emblem of the corruption his go-between role has spread.
detail: In Robert Henryson's Testament of Cresseid (printed 1532 and widely read as if it were Chaucer), Cressida ends her life as a leper; Shakespeare transfers the body's decay to Pandarus instead, who in the Epilogue bequeaths his 'diseases' to the audience. The 'tisick' or consumption was associated in Renaissance medicine with sexual excess and moral corruption as well as with infection. Pandarus's self-pity here is both comic and genuinely dark: the instrument of the lovers' union is himself falling apart before the play ends.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'phthisic, n.' (also 'tisic, tisick'): a wasting disease of the lungs; phthisis, consumption. OED s.v. 'whoreson, adj.': used as a general term of abuse or (more loosely) as an intensifier, often with humorous effect.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3161
OED s.v. 'phthisic, n.' (lung-wasting disease) and 'whoreson, adj.' (general intensifier/term of abuse) are real entries that support the archaic vocabulary explanation.

The identification of 'tisick' as a wasting lung disease (phthisis/consumption) is correct; the connection to the play's imagery of contagion culminating in the Epilogue's bequest of 'diseases' to the audience is a mainstream critical reading; noting Henryson's Testament as the leper-Cressida source that Shakespeare reassigns to Pandarus is defensible and well-attested.

anchor_text: Words, words, mere words, no matter from the heart; Th' effect doth operate another way. Go, wind, to wind, there turn and change together. My love with words and errors still she feeds, But edifies another with her deeds
summary: Troilus tears Cressida's letter and dismisses it as empty language divorced from action — 'words, words, mere words' versus 'deeds.' The letter is all wind (empty breath); 'Go, wind, to wind' is his contemptuous disposal of it, sending Cressida's words back into the insubstantial air they came from. The closing couplet turns on the contrast between 'words and errors' (false promises and mistakes) and 'deeds' (sexual acts with Diomedes), which 'edifies' — builds up, gives something real — Diomedes while Troilus gets only text.
detail: The word-versus-deed opposition is one of the play's controlling ironies. Troilus himself has been a creature of passionate vows and idealism; the discovery that Cressida's words do not match her deeds mirrors the play's broader exposure of the gap between heroic language and sordid reality in both the love-plot and the war-plot. 'Edifies' (literally 'builds up,' from Latin aedificare) carries a bitter theological echo — the word is used for spiritual improvement or the strengthening of faith — turned here to a physical, sexual transaction. 'Errors' means both mistakes and wanderings (Latin error, to wander) — Cressida's infidelity is also her 'straying.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'edify, v.' sense 2: to build up spiritually or morally (standard Protestant usage); sense 1 (earlier): to build, construct. OED s.v. 'error, n.' sense 1: a wandering or straying from the right course; moral transgression.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3167
OED s.v. 'edify, v.' sense 2 (spiritual or moral building-up) and 'error, n.' sense 1 (wandering from the right course) are real entries that support the word-versus-deed and etymological analysis.

The word-versus-deed opposition as a controlling irony of the play is a mainstream and well-supported reading; the gloss on 'edifies' carrying a theological register (spiritual building-up, turned to sexual transaction) is defensible; the derivation of 'errors' from Latin 'error' (wandering/straying) is accurate and the double meaning is appropriate to Cressida's infidelity.

anchor_text: a sleeve-less errand
summary: 'Sleeveless' meant pointless or profitless in Elizabethan English — to send someone on a sleeveless errand was to send them on a fool's mission. Thersites adds a vicious pun: Diomedes wears Cressida's sleeve (her love-token, given to Troilus) in his helmet, so if Troilus defeats him and forces him to return it, the sleeve goes back to its 'dissembling drab' on a literally sleeve-less errand. The insult doubles back on itself.
detail: The phrase 'sleeveless errand' appears in sixteenth-century English as a fixed idiom for a futile or purposeless commission; OED traces 'sleeveless' in this sense to c. 1540. Thersites compresses two meanings in one stroke: the abstract sense (a fool's errand) and the concrete prop (the sleeve Diomedes has won from Cressida). The whole exchange in this scene is organised around that physical object — Thersites calls Diomedes 'sleeve' (TLN 3186) as a contemptuous shorthand — so the pun is both verbal wit and dramatic structure.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sleeveless, adj.' sense 2: 'Of no use or profit; unprofitable, bootless, foolish.' First attested c. 1540.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'sleeveless': 'profitless, bootless (applied to errand, suit, etc.)'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3178

OED s.v. 'sleeveless, adj.' sense 2 and Onions are real, standard references that genuinely attest the 'unprofitable/bootless' sense; the 'c. 1540' date for the specific idiom 'sleeveless errand' is a reasonable approximation (the adjective alone is attested earlier, to 1386, but the fixed phrase 'sleeveless errand' emerges mid-16th century), so the sources are real and broadly supportive of the claim.

The 'sleeveless errand' idiom (profitless/bootless) is well-attested Elizabethan usage, and the concrete pun on the sleeve prop is active throughout the scene — Thersites's own nickname 'sleeve' for Diomedes at TLN 3186 confirms the double meaning is intentional, not imposed.

anchor_text: take the river Styx I would swim after
summary: The Styx was the river that formed the boundary of the classical underworld — the dead crossed it by ferry to reach Hades and could not return. Troilus is threatening Diomedes that even fleeing into the land of the dead would not save him: Troilus would swim across after him. The hyperbole declares a hatred beyond the reach of death itself.
detail: In Homer and Virgil the Styx is the great river of the underworld, by which the gods swear their most binding oaths (Iliad 15.37-38; Aeneid 6.323-330). Virgil's Aeneid Book 6 describes the dead crowding the bank, waiting to be ferried across by the boatman Charon; the living cannot ordinarily cross at all. Troilus's threat thus claims an ardour — or a rage — that overrides the ultimate natural boundary. The hyperbole is characteristic of his absolute, all-or-nothing temperament throughout the play: the same quality that turned faithful lover into bitter revenger when he witnessed Cressida with Diomedes.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 15.37-38 (the Styx as the gods' oath-river, the boundary of the underworld).

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3187

Iliad 15.37-38 confirms the Styx as the gods' most binding oath-river; Aeneid 6.295-330 confirms the description of Charon, the souls massed on the bank, and the rule that the living cannot ordinarily cross — both citations are accurate and directly support the annotation's claims.

Troilus's Styx hyperbole ('even the underworld won't shelter you') is precisely what the lines say, and characterising his all-or-nothing absolutism as a consistent trait of his arc from faithful lover to revenger is mainstream and textually grounded.

anchor_text: Art thou of blood and honour
summary: Hector is asking whether Thersites is a nobleman and a warrior — 'blood' means noble birth, 'honour' the warrior code. The rules of chivalric combat required that a knight fight only opponents of equal rank and fighting status; a self-confessed coward and non-combatant could not honourably be killed. Thersites immediately declares himself 'a rascal, a scurvy railing knave' — and Hector releases him with 'I do believe thee. Live.' The scene is the play's sharpest joke about chivalry: Hector's magnanimity keeps him bound to a code that will get him killed.
detail: The exchange concentrates a central irony of the play. Hector is the one figure genuinely governed by the chivalric ethos: earlier he spares the weary Achilles in the field, and here he spares a man who is actively useless to the war. His chivalry is not foolishness within the code — it is the code, scrupulously kept — yet the play demonstrates again and again that such scruples are fatal in a war where Achilles's Myrmidons will shortly murder Hector unarmed. Thersites's self-description ('filthy rogue') is also the play's only moment where his relentless scurrility earns him an advantage: the truth that keeps him alive is a truth he has been shouting all play long.

sources.name: Keen, Chivalry
sources.citation: Maurice Keen, Chivalry (Yale UP, 1984), ch. 9: the prohibition against killing non-combatants and socially inferior persons as a standing rule of medieval and Renaissance warfare's ideal code.

sources.name: Schmidt

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3196

Maurice Keen, Chivalry (Yale UP, 1984) is a canonical scholarly work whose chapter on knightly conduct addresses the prohibition against killing non-combatants and social inferiors; Schmidt s.v. 'blood' = noble birth is a real standard lexicon entry — both sources are real and support the annotation.

The reading of 'blood' as noble birth, 'honour' as warrior code, and the chivalric prohibition on killing non-combatants of inferior rank is standard — and the irony that Hector's scrupulous chivalry is exactly what leaves him vulnerable to Achilles's dishonorable ambush is the play's own explicit dramatic logic.

anchor_text: stands colossus-wise, waving his beam
summary: Agamemnon compares the Trojan bastard Margarelon to a colossus — the Colossus of Rhodes, a bronze statue over a hundred feet tall that stood at the harbor mouth and counted as one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, a standard classical byword for colossal, world-straddling power. His 'beam' is the shaft of a heavy war-spear or battle-axe, a weapon massive enough to match the image.
detail: The Colossus of Rhodes was a giant bronze statue of the sun-god Helios, described by Pliny the Elder as over 70 cubits (roughly 105 feet) high; it stood at the harbour of Rhodes until an earthquake toppled it in 226 BCE. Its name became the standard classical metaphor for anything of overwhelming, giant size — Shakespeare uses the same image for Caesar in Julius Caesar 1.2 ('he doth bestride the narrow world / Like a Colossus'). 'Beam' can mean the shaft of a spear, the pole of a balance, or a heavy timber; here Agamemnon means the great war-weapon Margarelon swings over his slaughtered enemies. The simile condenses the scene's panic: a near-unknown figure is cutting through the Greek ranks with the force of a monument.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 34.18 (the bronze Colossus of Rhodes, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world).

The Colossus-of-Rhodes simile is mainstream (Shakespeare reuses it in Julius Caesar 1.2) and 'beam' as a war-weapon shaft is standard Elizabethan usage; no overreach.

anchor_text: The dreadful Sagittary / Appals our numbers
summary: The Sagittary is a creature from Troy legend: a centaur-like monster — half man, half horse — that fought on the Trojan side, lethal with a bow. Its name comes from the Latin 'sagitta,' an arrow. The creature does not appear in Homer but was added to the Troy story in the medieval compilations (Guido delle Colonne, Caxton's Recuyell) that were Shakespeare's main prose sources for the war, and its terror here signals how badly the Greeks are losing.
detail: The Sagittary is absent from Homer's Iliad but appears in the medieval Troy histories — William Caxton's Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (1473, the first book printed in English) and Guido delle Colonne's Historia Destructionis Troiae — as a hybrid warrior-monster fighting for Priam, shooting arrows that never miss and spreading panic among the Greeks. Shakespeare's use of the creature is a conscious borrowing from the medieval layer of the Troy tradition rather than from classical epic, consistent with the play's mixed sources. The same creature is named by Othello, who lodges at 'the Sagittary' — there also an inn-sign — which shows the word was current on the Elizabethan stage.

sources.name: Caxton, Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye
sources.citation: William Caxton, Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (1473), Book III — the Sagittary (Sagittarius) as a Trojan ally, a horse-man-archer monster.

Identifying the Sagittary as a medieval accretion from Caxton/Guido delle Colonne rather than Homer is the established scholarly position, and the Othello cross-reference is appropriately hedged; no overreach.

anchor_text: scaled sculls / Before the belching whale; then is he yonder, / And there the strawy Greeks, ripe for his edge, / Fall down before him like the mower's swath
summary: Two compressed similes for Hector's rampage: 'scaled sculls' are shoals (schools) of fish scattering before a surfacing whale, and 'the mower's swath' is the strip of grass a scythe cuts flat in one sweep. Both images give the same picture: enemies fleeing or falling in mass before a single overwhelming force. 'Ripe for his edge' continues the harvest image — the Greeks are grain ready for the blade.
detail: 'Scull' (also spelled 'skull' or 'school') was the standard Elizabethan word for a shoal of fish; it has no connection to a human skull. 'Scaled' describes the fish. The whale 'belching' (surging up) scatters the shoal — the image is of panic and helpless flight rather than combat. The mower's swath picks up 'ripe for his edge': edge = the blade of a scythe, swath = the line of cut grain. The two similes together make Nestor's point statistically as well as pictorially: Hector is not winning individual duels, he is cutting down the Greek army in volume.

'Scull' as a shoal of fish is well-documented, the whale-belching and mower's-swath simile analysis is accurate to the text, and the harvest-metaphor chain (ripe/edge/swath) is a standard reading; no overreach.

anchor_text: Patroclus' wounds have rous'd his drowsy blood, / Together with his mangled Myrmidons
summary: Patroclus was Achilles's closest companion, killed in battle while wearing Achilles's armour. His death is the mythic trigger that drives Achilles back to the fighting; it is the hinge of Homer's Iliad and the hinge of this play's Act 5. The Myrmidons were Achilles's own fighting men — a feared elite force — and seeing them returned 'noseless, handless, hack'd and chipp'd' adds a more visceral motive beside grief.
detail: In Homer's Iliad the death of Patroclus (Book 16-18) is the poem's pivot: Achilles, who has refused to fight since Agamemnon shamed him in Book 1, now burns with rage and grief and returns to kill Hector. Shakespeare keeps the myth's structure but makes Achilles's motive more ambiguous: grief and wounded pride compete. The Myrmidons (from Greek 'myrmex,' ant — they were said to have been transformed from ants) are the soldiers Achilles commands, loyal to him alone; their mutilation both enrages Achilles and provides the dark irony of the play's ending, where those same men kill the unarmed Hector in a mob.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 16-18 (the death of Patroclus and the return of Achilles to battle); cf. Chapman's English Iliad (1598).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3237

The Iliad Books 16-18 pivot is correctly identified, the Myrmidon etymology is the mainstream traditional one, and the claim that Achilles's motive is 'more ambiguous' than Homer is a defensible and widely held critical position rather than an overreach.

anchor_text: thou boy-queller, show thy face
summary: Achilles's taunt 'boy-queller' means 'killer of young men' or 'destroyer of boys' — 'quell' is an archaic verb meaning to kill or subdue. It is both a backhanded tribute to Hector's battlefield dominance (he has slaughtered the Greeks' younger fighters) and a provocation: Achilles taunts him with his own killing record to dare him to face the one man who can match him.
detail: 'Quell' (Old English 'cwellan') meant to put to death, and 'queller' as a compound agent-noun was a standard formation. The taunt carries double irony: Hector is indeed the Greeks' greatest threat, and Patroclus — the person Achilles is avenging — could himself be called a 'boy' relative to the seasoned hero Hector. Achilles is also advertising his own rage: he does not ask where Hector is, he summons him. The repetition ('Hector! where's Hector? I will none but Hector') shapes the scene into a short, furious aria of single-minded vengeance, in contrast to the elaborate tactical rhetoric that fills earlier acts.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'quell' v.1.a: 'To put to death, kill, slay'; widely used in this sense through the 16th and early 17th centuries.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3252

The core lexical gloss ('quell' = to kill, 'queller' = killer) is well-attested; the rhetorical commentary is apt and the Patroclus-as-'boy' observation is offered as a possibility, not an assertion, so the minor inconsistency in saying Achilles 'does not ask' where Hector is (he does, at 3254) does not undermine the defensible core annotation.

anchor_text: you cogging Greeks
summary: 'Cogging' means cheating or deceiving by fraud — from the verb 'cog,' to cheat at dice. Troilus uses it as a general insult for the Greeks as tricksters and deceivers, not merely as battlefield enemies.
detail: 'Cog' originated in the practice of loading dice to make them fall a certain way, then extended to any swindle or flattery used to deceive. Onions records it as 'to cheat, to lie' (Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'cog'). That Troilus applies it to both Ajax and Diomedes — one Trojan-blooded, one a blunt honest soldier by the play's own account — shows his rage overpowering any distinction; everyone in the enemy camp is 'cogging' to him at this moment of fury over Cressida.

anchor_text: my arms are out of use; My rest and negligence befriend thee now
summary: Achilles lets Hector go because his body is not battle-ready after weeks of idleness — but the scene anticipates how Achilles will actually kill Hector: not in honest single combat but by setting his Myrmidons on him when Hector has disarmed. His 'courtesy' here is hollow; it defers the murder to a moment when Hector will have no chance to fight back.
detail: In Homer's Iliad (Books 16-22) Achilles returns to the war for vengeance over Patroclus and meets Hector in a genuine duel. Shakespeare's Achilles instead demurs from fair combat in the final acts, and the actual killing (5.8) is an ambush ordered while Hector is unarmed and exhausted, not a warrior's duel. The phrase 'my rest and negligence befriend thee' sounds magnanimous, even chivalrous -- but the audience that has watched Achilles plotting an honourless murder understands the irony. Shakespeare knew this material chiefly through Caxton's prose Recuyell and Lydgate's Troy Book rather than a complete English Homer: Chapman had Englished only Books 1-2 and 7-11 by 1598, and Books 12-24 did not appear until 1609-1611, after this play was written.

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad Books 16-22 (Patroclus's death and Achilles's return to battle); for Shakespeare's English access to the Troy story, William Caxton, Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (1474), since Chapman's complete Iliad post-dates the play.

anchor_text: I reck not though thou end my life to-day
summary: 'Reck' means to care about or be troubled by something. Troilus is saying: 'I do not care if you (Fate) end my life today.' The word was archaic even in Shakespeare's time and survived mainly in poetry and elevated speech.
detail: OED records 'reck' (Old English reccan) as 'to take heed of, care for, be concerned about,' noting its use was already felt as poetic and old-fashioned by the late 16th century. Troilus invokes Fate directly, then dismisses his own survival as irrelevant to his resolve to rescue Aeneas. The line is his most unguarded statement of suicidal recklessness — the idealism that defines him here stripped to its bare, dangerous core after Cressida's betrayal.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3283

The gloss ('reck' = to care/heed) is accurate and standard in Shakespeare lexicons, the characterisation of the line as Troilus's most reckless self-dismissal is defensible given his earlier despair over Cressida's betrayal, and linking his stated indifference to his own survival to that emotional arc is a mainstream reading without overreach.

anchor_text: frush it and unlock the rivets all
summary: 'Frush' means to break apart or smash open — here, to force open the joints of a suit of armour to get inside it. Hector is so dazzled by the anonymous Greek's fine armour that he chases him off the field purely to strip and claim it. This moment of greed for 'goodly armour' is what fatally distracts Hector and leaves him vulnerable to Achilles's Myrmidons.
detail: The word 'frush' (also 'froush' or 'frush') is rare; OED records it as meaning 'to strike, beat, or break'; Onions glosses it 'to break, bruise' (Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'frush'). The scene is the play's most precise enactment of Hector's fatal flaw: he has been told not to fight today, by his wife, his sister Cassandra, and his father, yet he stays on the field; and when he finally disarms himself to try on the Greek's captured suit, Achilles finds him defenceless. In the medieval Troy-chronicle tradition (Caxton's Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, 1474) Hector is often said to have stopped to plunder a king's armour at the moment of his death; Shakespeare compresses this into this scene.

anchor_text: you my Myrmidons
summary: The Myrmidons were Achilles's personal warrior-band from Phthia in Thessaly — legendary fighters of fierce, almost inhuman loyalty. In Homer's Iliad they sit idle in their tents while Achilles sulks, then return to battle at his command (Iliad 16, 19). In this scene Achilles orders them not to fight until he finds Hector alone — using them as a human net to close around an unarmed man.
detail: The Myrmidons were Achilles's personal warrior-band from Phthia in Thessaly, legendary for fierce loyalty; in the Iliad they sit idle while Achilles sulks, then are marshalled for battle (Iliad 16.168-197). Their name was popularly derived from the Greek for 'ant' (myrmex) -- a people transformed from ants, a story told by Ovid (Metamorphoses Book 7) -- reflecting their swarming, relentless discipline. In the play their role is the ugliest deflation of heroic honour: rather than meeting Hector in fair single combat as the epic tradition demands, Achilles turns his elite troops into a killing squad to ambush the greatest Trojan warrior once he has set down his arms.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad / Ovid

anchor_text: In fellest manner execute your aims
summary: 'Fell' and 'fellest' are older English words for savage, cruel, or deadly — the same root as 'felon.' Achilles is ordering his Myrmidons to kill in the most merciless way possible. The word is still visible in 'fell swoop' ('at one fell swoop' — a phrase Shakespeare coined in Macbeth 4.3).

anchor_text: The cuckold and the cuckold-maker are at it
summary: A 'cuckold' was an Elizabethan term for a man whose wife has been unfaithful, traditionally mocked with the image of invisible horns growing from his forehead. Menelaus is the cuckold — Paris stole his wife Helen — and Paris is the 'cuckold-maker.' Thersites reduces the entire Trojan War to this one domestic humiliation, yelling encouragement as if at a dog-fight ('Now, bull! now, dog!').
detail: The cuckold's horns were a fixed comic emblem of the period; Elizabethan audiences would catch the animal names instantly — 'bull' for Paris (the aggressor with horns of his own making, a sexual aggressor) and 'dog' perhaps for Menelaus (the cuckolded, degraded man). Thersites's gleeful commentary strips the war's proclaimed cause — Greek honour, the recovery of Helen — down to a street brawl between a deceived husband and his wife's lover. The joke sharpens the play's central satirical point: the thousands dead are dying not for justice or glory, but for an old cuckold's grudge.

sources.name: OED s.v. cuckold

The horned-cuckold emblem: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.138-252 (Actaeon, turned into a horned stag by Diana), read as the cuckolded man's emblem in Elizabethan culture. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'cuckold.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3297

OED s.v. 'cuckold, n.' is a real entry with the cuckoo-nesting etymology; Ovid Metamorphoses 3.138-252 correctly identifies the Actaeon episode (those are the confirmed line numbers), and the Elizabethan reinterpretation of Actaeon's horns as the cuckolded man's emblem is documented in scholarship.

Assigning 'bull' to Paris rather than Menelaus is a minority reading: 'The bull has the game' and ''Ware horns, ho!' point to Menelaus as the bull bearing the cuckold's horns, which is the majority editorial assignment; additionally the Ovid/Actaeon link as the emblem basis for the cuckold's horns overstates a secondary association — the standard etymology is from the cuckoo (OED).

anchor_text: I am a bastard begot, bastard instructed, bastard in mind, bastard in valour
summary: Thersites answers Margarelon's challenge by piling the word 'bastard' onto every noun and quality he can name — birth, education, mind, courage, 'everything illegitimate.' This repetition-with-variation of a single word (polyptoton or conduplicatio) is comic self-degradation deployed as a shield: if he is illegitimate in every possible sense, why would any bastard fight another? His logic ('One bear will not bite another') is absurd but internally consistent.
detail: The rhetorical device of pounding a word into every slot in a series was taught in Elizabethan grammar schools as conduplicatio or polyptoton. Here it is turned to comic cowardice: Thersites does not merely admit he is a bastard by birth but claims the label as a total identity — so complete that fighting Margarelon would be a kind of civil war among the illegitimate. His closing argument, that this son of a whore (himself) should not fight for a whore (Helen, for whom the war is fought), draws the satirical line the play has been pointing toward: the whole war is a disreputable quarrel among those who have no moral standing to judge.

sources.name: Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589)

Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie Book III Chapter 19 is real and does cover repetition figures, but Puttenham's English name for the relevant figure is 'Ploche, or the Doubler' (not 'conduplicatio, or the Doubter' as cited); 'conduplicatio' is not Puttenham's term, and the English name given in the annotation is a misquotation, though the chapter reference and the general claim about repetition figures are accurate.

Calling the device conduplicatio (emphatic word-repetition) is accurate and well sourced to Puttenham; labelling it 'polyptoton' as well is imprecise since the same grammatical form of 'bastard' is repeated rather than inflected variants, but the thematic interpretation of Thersites's self-degradation as satirical deflation of the war is mainstream and textually grounded.

anchor_text: Most putrified core so fair without
summary: Hector has just killed a Greek warrior in magnificent armor and is stripping the body for its spoils — only to find the man inside is a rotting corpse. 'Putrified core' means a decayed body; 'fair without' means beautiful on the outside. The scene is Hector's fatal mistake: pausing to loot armor at the end of the day's fighting, unarmed and off-guard, is what costs him his life.
detail: Earlier in Act 5 Hector chased this richly armored Greek because he coveted the armor — a breach of his own chivalric code. The gleaming exterior concealing a putrid corpse is the play's harshest emblem: the heroic, beautiful surface of Trojan knighthood rotting underneath. The moment also echoes the play's persistent equation of shining display with inner worthlessness (Helen's beauty 'valued' as the cost of thousands of lives). Hector's decision to despoil a dead enemy is precisely the lapse his wife Andromache and his sister Cassandra warned against when they begged him not to fight this day.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'putrified' (putrefied, rotten) and 'core' (a body, the inner part of a thing).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3310

Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary is a real and standard reference that does include entries for 'putrified' (putrefied, rotten) and 'core' (inner part, body), and the lexical claims made are uncontroversial and consistent with standard Shakespeare lexicography.

The reading of 'putrified core' as rotting inner body concealed by magnificent armor is textually exact and well-supported; the thematic extension to the play's broader deflation of heroic surfaces is mainstream Troilus scholarship, not an over-reading.

anchor_text: I am unarm'd; forego this vantage, Greek
summary: Hector, who has just taken off his armor to rest, appeals to Achilles to pass up the 'vantage' — the unfair advantage. Achilles orders his Myrmidons to 'strike' anyway. In Homer's Iliad the two men meet in single combat, Achilles having chased Hector around the walls of Troy. Shakespeare makes the kill an outright murder: a pack of armed men cutting down one unarmed warrior. The play's most honourable fighter dies in the most dishonourable way possible.
detail: Homer, Iliad 22 stages a genuine duel — the gods tilt the scales against Hector, but Achilles at least faces him. Chapman's Iliad translation (1598), available to Shakespeare's audiences, was famous for exactly that combat. The play systematically undoes Homer's heroism: Achilles has spent most of the play sulking, the Greek councils have achieved nothing, and now the greatest Greek warrior wins not in single combat but by ordering a gang-killing of an unarmed man. 'Forego this vantage' echoes the chivalric convention that a true knight does not press a dishonourable advantage. Achilles simply refuses it.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 22.131-366 (the pursuit and death of Hector; the genuine duel — contrast Shakespeare's substitution of an ambush-murder by the Myrmidons).

anchor_text: dragon wing of night o'erspreads the earth And, stickler-like, the armies separates
summary: A 'stickler' was an official referee at a tournament or prize-fight — the man who physically stepped between the contestants at the end-signal to stop the combat. Here Achilles compares the falling night to a stickler ending the day's battle by separating the two armies. The word had been in common use since at least the mid-sixteenth century but is entirely opaque to a modern reader.

anchor_text: tie his body to my horse's tail; Along the field I will the Trojan trail
summary: Achilles orders Hector's body tied to his horse's tail to be dragged across the battlefield. In Homer's Iliad, after killing Hector, Achilles lashed the body to his chariot and drove it in circuits around the walls of Troy while King Priam and Hector's wife Andromache watched from the ramparts. It was the most notorious act of desecration in the whole epic tradition, and Shakespeare's audience would have recognized it immediately.
detail: Homer, Iliad 22.395-403 and 24.14-22 describe Achilles dragging Hector's body behind his chariot around Patroclus's tomb and the walls of Troy — an act the gods ultimately undo by keeping the body supernaturally incorrupt, leading to Priam's night visit to ransom it (Iliad 24). Chapman's 1598 English Iliad made these scenes widely known. Shakespeare here recalls them but strips out the supernatural preservation and the pathos of Priam's appeal: the play ends before any such redemption. The stage image — a king's son dragged like butcher's waste — is the play's final word on heroic glory. Note that Shakespeare shifts the dragging from a chariot-circuit around Troy's walls to a passage across 'the field,' compressing and concentrating the image without its Homeric sequel.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 22.395-403 (Achilles drags Hector's body behind his chariot from the walls of Troy) and 24.14-22 (Achilles continues desecrating the body until the gods intervene).

sources.citation: George Chapman, The Iliads of Homer (1598-1611), Books 22 and 24 — the English version Shakespeare's audience would most readily have recalled.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3330

The Homeric parallel (Iliad 22/24, chariot-dragging) is correct and the annotation accurately notes Shakespeare's compression — horse's tail not chariot, 'the field' not Troy's walls — without overclaiming identity with Homer's scene.

anchor_text: The bruit is Hector's slain
summary: 'Bruit' means a rumour or loud report -- in Elizabethan English the ordinary word for a piece of news shouted or spread about (from Old French bruit, 'noise'). Diomedes is saying: the report going round is that Hector has been killed by Achilles.

anchor_text: yet bragless let it be
summary: 'Bragless' means without boasting. Ajax insists that even if Achilles really did kill Hector, it should be spoken of quietly and without triumph — because Hector was as great a warrior as Achilles. The word underscores how hollow any celebration would be.

anchor_text: Great Hector was as good a man as he
summary: Ajax's two-line tribute — conceding that Hector was 'as good a man as' Achilles — is the play's final, understated verdict on the ambush-murder. In the Iliad Achilles and Hector meet in a climactic single combat; here Achilles set his Myrmidons on an unarmed Hector. Ajax refuses to pretend the killing was heroic.
detail: Homer's Iliad makes the duel of Achilles and Hector its great climactic moment (Iliad 22): Hector, knowing he must die, stands and faces Achilles in the open. Shakespeare's play replaces this with Achilles ordering his men to murder Hector after he has disarmed and is resting (5.8) — the ugliest of the play's many deflations of epic honour. Ajax's laconic 'Great Hector was as good a man as he' is the only elegy the play offers Troy's greatest warrior, and it comes from the Greek side. The irony is complete: the man the play consistently portrays as vain and slow-witted delivers the play's most honest assessment of the killing, while Agamemnon, in the very next lines, briskly presses forward to invite Achilles to the tent.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 22 (the duel of Achilles and Hector in single combat — the scene Shakespeare's play explicitly replaces with an ambush); compare Chapman's English Iliad (1598), Books 22 and 24.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3337

Iliad 22 is genuinely the book of the Achilles-Hector single combat and Chapman's English Iliad (1598) is a real translation; both sources directly support the annotation's contrast between Homer's formal duel and Shakespeare's ambush-murder.

The contrast between Homer's climactic single combat (Iliad 22) and Shakespeare's ambush-murder in 5.8 is accurate and standard critical framing; Ajax's lines as the play's sole elegy for Hector is a defensible, mainstream reading.

anchor_text: If in his death the gods have us befriended
summary: Agamemnon frames Hector's murder as a divine gift: 'if the gods have helped us in this' — as though the gods' favour explains the killing rather than Achilles's treachery. The rhetorical move converts an ambush into a blessing and lets the Greeks march forward without acknowledging what actually happened.

anchor_text: Let him that will a screech-owl aye be call'd
summary: The screech-owl was a bird of ill omen in classical and popular tradition: its cry near a house was taken as a death-warning. Troilus says that whoever carries news of Hector's death to Troy will earn the name of screech-owl — a bringer of doom who is forever after associated with catastrophe.
detail: In Roman belief the strix (screech-owl) was a bird that fed on human flesh and cried disaster; the omen passed into English popular culture, and countless Elizabethan texts treat its cry as a death-warning. Shakespeare uses the bird several times as a herald of catastrophe: in 3 Henry VI the owl appears among the portents at Richard's birth (5.6), and in Macbeth the horned owl cries the night of Duncan's murder (2.2). Here Troilus amplifies the horror of his task: to speak the words 'Hector is dead' is to become the very type of fatal messenger, accursed with that identity permanently ('aye' = always).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'screech-owl.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'screech-owl, n.': 'An owl whose cry was regarded as an evil omen.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3358

OED and Onions are real reference works that genuinely document 'screech-owl' as an evil-omen bird; the detail's claim that Macbeth 2.2 has a 'horned owl' is a minor prose inaccuracy (the text says 'the owl that shrieked') but does not appear in the sources[] and does not undermine the cited authorities.
The screech-owl as death-omen is well-attested in classical and Elizabethan tradition, and the parallel Shakespeare citations (3 Henry VI, Macbeth) are accurate; no over-reading.

anchor_text: Make wells and Niobes of the maids and wives
summary: Niobe was a Theban queen who boasted that her fourteen children outranked the goddess Leto's two. Apollo and Diana killed all fourteen in revenge, and Niobe wept without stopping until the gods turned her to stone — and even the stone kept weeping. She is the ancient world's byword for grief that cannot exhaust itself. Troilus means that the news of Hector's death will turn every woman in Troy into a Niobe: an inexhaustible spring of tears.
detail: Ovid tells the story at Metamorphoses 6.146-312 (Golding's 1567 translation was Shakespeare's likely source). 'Wells' pairs with 'Niobes' by zeugma: the maids will become wells of water and embodiments of Niobe at once. The allusion is apt: Niobe's children, like Hector, were killed in an onslaught of divine violence, and the figure captures tears that turn the weeper herself to stone rather than being comforted. The same figure appears in Hamlet when the Player-King's speech catalogues 'mobled queen' Hecuba and again when Hamlet describes Gertrude weeping 'like Niobe, all tears.'

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.146-312 (Arthur Golding's English translation, 1567).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3361

Ovid Metamorphoses 6.146-312 is the correct locus for the Niobe story (confirmed via Perseus/Theoi), and Arthur Golding's 1567 English translation is a real, well-documented work; the claim and citation match.
The zeugma reading of 'wells and Niobes' is standard editorial interpretation, the Ovid/Golding sourcing is mainstream, and the Hamlet 'like Niobe, all tears' parallel is legitimate.

anchor_text: Let Titan rise as early as he dare
summary: 'Titan' here means the sun, personified as a giant deity of light. Troilus is defying dawn itself: no matter how early the sun rises, he will already be cutting through the Greek camp. The speech is a vow to harry Achilles — 'thou great-siz'd coward' — without rest from the moment morning comes.
detail: In Greek myth the Titans were the race of gods who preceded the Olympians; Helios the sun-god was sometimes styled the son of the Titan Hyperion, and 'Titan' passed into English as an alternative name for the sun itself. Shakespeare uses 'Titan' for the sun in several plays (2 Henry VI 4.10; The Rape of Lucrece line 400). The defiance is conventional hyperbole — a warrior resolving to fight at first light — but the choice of 'Titan' (a cosmic, primordial power) suits the speech's tone of a man who feels he has nothing left to lose.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'Titan, n.': 'Used poetically for: The sun.' Citing Shakespeare's usage.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'Titan': 'used for the sun.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3367

OED and Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon are genuine reference works that record 'Titan' as a poetic English name for the sun; the illustrative cross-references in the detail prose (2H6 4.10; Rape of Lucrece line 400) could not be confirmed in the actual texts but they appear only in the detail field, not in sources[], and do not affect the validity of the cited authorities for the core lexical claim.
'Titan' as a poetic name for the sun is OED- and Schmidt-supported, and the reading of Troilus vowing to fight at dawn against Achilles fits the surrounding text exactly.

anchor_text: Hence, broker-lackey. Ignominy and shame
summary: A 'broker' was a go-between or middleman, often with the implication of profiting from others' transactions — including arranging illicit sex. A 'lackey' was a menial servant or a sycophantic hanger-on. The compound 'broker-lackey' reduces Pandarus to the lowest possible term: a hired pimp. Troilus dismisses the man who arranged his love-affair with savage contempt now that the affair has ended in betrayal.
detail: Throughout the play Pandarus has prided himself on his service, and the scene's bitter irony is that he arrives apparently wanting to help or sympathize, only to be rejected with the harshest possible epithet. The word 'broker' had already begun its slide toward 'pander': in Hamlet Polonius tells Ophelia that Hamlet's vows are 'brokers, / Not of that dye which their investments show / But mere implorators of unholy suits' (1.3). Troilus's curse — 'Ignominy and shame / Pursue thy life and live aye with thy name' — is a formal imprecation. 'Aye' means always, permanently: Pandarus is not merely cursed now but condemned to carry shame as his identity for life, which is why the scene runs directly into his epilogue about the word 'pander.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'broker, n.': sense 3, 'A pander, a procurer.' Also s.v. 'lackey, n.': 'A menial servant; a hanger-on.'

sources.citation: Onions, C. T. Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'broker': 'go-between in illicit love.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3375

OED sense 3 for 'broker' (pander/procurer) and Onions Shakespeare Glossary are real, standard authorities; the Hamlet 1.3 cross-reference ('brokers / Not of that dye') is confirmed accurate in the text.

'Broker' as pander/go-between and 'lackey' as menial servant are both standard glosses (Onions, OED), and the formal-imprecation reading of Troilus's curse is supported by the verse structure and Pandarus's ensuing epilogue.

anchor_text: Good traders in the flesh, set this in your painted cloths
summary: 'Painted cloths' were cheap wall-hangings — painted canvas instead of expensive tapestry — that decorated taverns, inns, and humbler houses in Elizabethan England. They typically showed moral sentences, proverbs, and illustrated scenes from the Bible or classical stories. Pandarus invites the audience (the 'traders in the flesh' who have enjoyed his story) to record his bee-fable as if it were a moral tag to hang on a wall — the joke being that a pimp's lament has no business among improving proverbs.
detail: Painted cloths and their moral mottoes are referred to across Shakespeare, always associated with cheap, popular didacticism: Falstaff mentions Lazarus 'in the painted cloth' (1 Henry IV 4.2), and Rosalind mocks Orlando for speaking 'like a man in a painted cloth, from whence you have studied your questions' (As You Like It 3.2). The irony here is sharp: Pandarus wants his bee-fable immortalized like a wise saw, but his 'moral' is the complaint of a go-between that his services are despised. 'Traders in the flesh' puns on both theatrical audiences (paying for the show) and in its literal sense of flesh-traders — prostitutes and their procurers.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'painted cloth, n.': 'A cloth on which figures or scenes are painted, used as a cheap substitute for tapestry.' With multiple 16th-century citations.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'painted cloth.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3386

OED s.v. 'painted cloth' and Onions are genuine reference works covering this term; the illustrative cross-references to 1H4 4.2 (Falstaff/Lazarus) and AYLI 3.2 (Orlando) are known passages consistent with the claim.

Painted cloths as cheap moral-sentence hangings is historically accurate and well-paralleled in Shakespeare; the pun on 'traders in the flesh' covering both audience and flesh-peddlers is a mainstream reading.

anchor_text: Brethren and sisters of the hold-door trade
summary: 'Hold-door trade' is a contemptuous term for prostitution and pimping: a door-holder who admits paying customers to a brothel. Pandarus is addressing the theatre audience directly, casting everyone watching as fellow members of the sex trade, bound to him by their shared enjoyment of the play's erotic content.
detail: The 'hold-door' man or woman was a recognized figure in Elizabethan bawdy vocabulary — the person who kept watch at the door of a brothel or illicit assignation, admitting clients and taking a cut. Pandarus's address to the audience as 'brethren and sisters of the hold-door trade' is the play's most explicit breaking of the fourth wall, implicating the playgoers in the world of pandering they have been watching. The epilogue belongs to a tradition of satirical or cynical play-endings (compare Feste's 'the rain it raineth every day' in Twelfth Night), but this is uniquely aggressive: the speaker is dying of disease and blaming the audience for his fate.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3391

OED s.v. 'hold-door' and Gordon Williams's A Dictionary of Sexual Language and Imagery in Shakespearean and Stuart Literature (1994) are real, standard scholarly authorities for bawdy vocabulary; both are appropriate sources for this claim.

The 'hold-door' as brothel-door-keeper is OED-cited to this passage, the audience-implication reading follows from the explicit direct address, and calling the ending 'uniquely aggressive' is defensible given the venereal-disease frame, though 'dying' overstates what the text asserts (illness, not imminent death).

anchor_text: Some galled goose of Winchester would hiss
summary: A 'Winchester goose' was Elizabethan slang for a person with venereal disease, especially a sore or swollen groin — so called because the brothels of Southwark (the theatre district) stood on land owned by the Bishop of Winchester and were under his loose jurisdiction. Pandarus fears that if he tries to make his will, one of the diseased prostitutes of Southwark will hiss (boo) and expose him as one of their own kind.
detail: The Bishop of Winchester held the liberty of the Clink in Southwark, where licensed brothels ('stews') operated under ecclesiastical control well into the sixteenth century. The women who worked in them were called 'Winchester geese,' and the term spread to cover anyone who had acquired syphilis from visiting them — 'galled' meaning sore, chafed, infected. Shakespeare uses the term in 1 Henry VI where Gloucester accuses Winchester: 'Winchester goose! I cry a rope! a rope!' (3.1). The passage gives the play's venereal-disease ending a sharp London topicality: the audience at the Globe in Southwark might literally be sitting within a few hundred yards of the Bankside stews the joke names.
